articles.title: CLOSE OF THE EXIIIBMONITS FAILURE
articles.text:
CLOSE OF THE EXIIIBMON-
ITS FAILURE

The Exhibition Showmen, Messrs. Kelk and
Lucas, with their outwitted and unfortunate
partners, Her Majesty's Commissioners, this
day finally close their monster booth at
Kensington; the former with well-lined pockets,
well-deserved censure, and minus their knight-
hood; the latter covered with ignominy and
disgrace, bankrupt alike in finance, honour, and
fame. Jobbery and robbery have been the pre-
vailing characteristics of the Show from the first
propounding of the scheme down to the day of
its final close, and it has given up its prolonged
and lingering existence without the slightest
sign of regret from anyone, except the Times,
and that "art and science" clique who have
revelled and fattened on its mismanagement.
A vile, trading, huckstering spirit has pervaded
the place, and all concerned in its management.
throughout, and it is this which has mainly
-contributed to the failure; for failure it has been.
despite the bolstering up of the Times, and the
minor satellites in the pay of the contractors
and their humble servants, tools, and dupes,
the Commissioners. Here is a building—
ugly in design, and disgraceful in execution,
it is true—but a building containing within its
uncouth shell a display of the art and industry
.of. the world far superior to that exhibited in
1851; a population of some millions more
than in that year;, a much greater amount of
railway accommodation; largely increased in-
telligence and appreciation of what is beautiful
and useful; the indefatigable, unceasing, and
unscrupulous "touting" oftheTimes; the severe
whipping up of the management; and an ex-
tension of five weeks in keeping open the shed,
and yet the total of visitors are only a few
thousands more in number than in 1851, while
the total receip t s area few thousands less, swelled
as they have been by the profits from the eat-
ing-house department, and from the numerous
paltry dodges and artifices resorted to by the
Commissioners the umbrella question, to
wit. It must also be borne in mind
that the cost of erecting this huge monstrosity
has been far in excess of that which was ex-
pended in raising the fairy-like structure de-
signed by Sir J;zph Paxton, and /that the
current expense aye been conside&bly more
than in 1851/ It is not, therefore, surprising
that instead of a surplus, as on the last occa-
-sion, of overE2oo,ooo,the Commissioners should
now be struggling against a deficiency, and that
the guarantors should be dependent upon the
Willingness of Messrs. Kelk and Lucas to dis-
gorge some of their enormous gains. On the part
of the Commissioners an amount of incapacity,

imbecility, indecision, and weakness, has- been

displayed, surprising to every one. -Jobbing in
the building contract, jobbing in the refresh-
ment contract, jobbing with the exhibitors, job-
ing with the cloak and lavatory departments,
breaking of faith with the season ticket holders,
and an utter disregard of public opinion, has
characterised their proceedings thronghout.
The DctilyNews, in a leading article on Monday
last, has the following just remark upon this
point
The Exhibition was not honestly projected nor
honestly carried out. Jobbery hovered over and di-
rected the pencil of the architect in his office, and
watched greedily the laying of the first stone. The
industrial exhibition, the review of artistic and com-
mercial progress during the last eleven years, was the
pretext; the building, the solid, permanent building,
was the object. One society wished to gain a vast
hall at the public expense; another society wished to
be provided with a winter garden for nothing; and
a third restless clique, who are scotched, not killed,
wished to secure a vast central hall for a rotten
Centralising project. Royal investors in land, job-
bing builders, adventurers who put on a showy mask
tailed Science and Art, all worked together for good
to themselves, to found a little happy island ofjobbery.
To this abode of offioial blis' q this sandy swamp in a
distant suburb, they wished to draw the British
Museum, the National Gallery, the Soane Collection—
anything, in fact, from the Monument on Fish-street-
hill to the Duke of Wellington at Hyde-park, which
they could lay their hands on. The land bought with
the surplus of the first Exhibition gave them some-
thing to work upon; the second Exhibition was their
stalking-horse, the exhibitors their tools. •
But if the Commissioners have thus laid
themselves open to this well-merited castiga-
tion, from a quarter by no means badly dis-
posed to them, what shall be said of the Con-
tractors, Kelk and Lucas? With them

jobbery and robbery—(according to law)—
has been combined jobbery in their
contract, and in the way in which they have
executed the work entrusted to them, and
robbery of the workmen in their employ, by
taking away from them, under false pretences,
all extra payment for overtime. I have so
frequently given my opinion on the conduct
and proceedings of these men in connection
with their introduction of the hour system, and
their treatment of their workmen, that it is
unnecessary for me here to repeat it. But
that they are mainly responsible for the failure
of the Exhibition is beyond all doubt. The delay
in the completion of the building, which acted
so detrimentally to its interests in the first
month of its opening, was the result of their
attempt to enforce an innovation on the cus-
toms of the trade against the wishes of their
workmen, and the " botchery" and untrades-
m_ anlike way in which the work was at last
done, was owing to the same cause. To this
also •
, a great measure, may be attributed
that enormous bill for extras, amounting to
nearly £loo,ooo—a bill unparallelled in the
building trade, and which has greatly
' contributed to create the deficiency existing.
Messrs. Kelk and Lucas are not the sort of
men to be generous, and put their hands in
their pockets to save those of the guarantors,
and if, as it is said, they are about to make up
the deficiency in the receipts by handing over
.some £20,000 to the Commissioners, it is only
another proof how enormous must have been
their gains, and how reckless the conduct of
the Commissioners, in entering into their con-
tract. Hear the Daily News again upon this
part of this most disreputable transaction :
The arrangements to construct the building have
been in keeping with the whole scheme. A firm of
- builders was admitted into partnership with the Royal
• Commissioners. Speculative tradesmen who should

but the Exhibition has done nothing in the name of

Not only has "charity" been thrown over-
board, but humanity also. A deaf ear has
been turned alike by
these chandler-shop
Commissioners and jobbing Contractors, to the
claims of sufferingindustry, or the cries of the
families of the victims sacrificed at their shrine.
While every paltry "music-hall" and "two.-

penny hop" has given its contributions to the
cotton distress fund, the returns from the
"Great International Exhibition, under the
superintendence of her Majesty's Commis-
sioners (?") for this object are " nil !" But yet
whatever there was of glory or splendour
about this Exhibition was due solely to In-
dustry's labourers. Shame and disgrace upon
these Commissioners that they so mismanaged
their business, as to be unable to sacri-
fice even one day's receipts in the cause of
charity! Shame and disgrace upon these Con-
tractors, that if disinclined to give anything
out of their bill of" extras," they did not order

set apart a portion even of one day's receipts,
for the relief of the widows and orphans made
during the erection of the building!' The
guarantors would have forgiven them had they
done so! ,

As a successful display, of art and industry,
the Exhibition has been a great success; but its
management has been one continual outrage
upon decency and propriety. It is to be hoped
that the next Exhibition will be more honestly
planned, and more sensibly, economically, and
honourably carried out, with none of the pre-
sent clique in office to mar its prospects, or
speculating builders connected with its erection,
to delay its completion by tampering with the
rights and wages of their workmen.
November 13. SCOURGE.

THE GREAT PANE" OF ENGLAND
NOTE PAPER ROBBERY.

Some very extraordinary proceedincrs have come to
li '
ght in reference to the robbery of the bank paper from
the mill, and the subsequent attempts at forgery, and
also the circumstances under which the detection of
the prisoners took place. There appears to be no doubt
that for a very considerable period a plant,' as it is
termed, was made upon the mills by the professional
bank-note forgers, with a view to get possession of
some of the genuine note paper; and it may be stated
that one of the principal difficulties that have stood in
the way of these persons putting forged notes into cir-
culation, has been the paper, a spurious note being
detected almost instantly. Every endeavour, there-
fore, was made by the gang to effect this object; and
from inquiries that have been made, there appears to
be no doubt that, for several months, schemes of all
sorts were resorted to with a view to tempt some of
the workmen employed about the mills to betray their
trust. It appears, however, that the gang were very enol
and cautious in their proceedings' and although they
had succeeded in the object they had so long contem-
plated, nothing was done precipitately, but they set about
deliberately to make all the necessary arrangements for
a grand coup, and before anything was done the forgers
resolved upon having a full supply of each kind of
paper, so that the business might be done in a regular
and systetnatic manner. It is quite certain that the
genuine bank-note paper was in their possession for a
a considerable time before any attempts were made to
print the felted notes upon it, - and it is probably
owing to this caution on their part that a much greater
amount of mischief was not effected; for, owing to the
delay in the operations of the marauders, very few
notes were printed on the genuine paper, and through
the activity of the police, and the energetic steps taken
by the officials of the Bank of England, the whole
affair was discovered before the extensive system of for-
gery contemplated could be carried out. Immediately the
disclosures took place it was palpable to the officers
employed that some one engaged upon the premises
must have abused his trust, but the difficulty was to
obtain a clue in the right direction. The detective
however' by the most persevering inquiries, at length
obtained information which led to the apprehension
of the boy Brown; and when he found that he had no
chance of escape, and that the officers were in posses-
sion of information upon all his proceedings, he ex-
pressed his readiness to reveal all he knew, and from
this time the officers had a comparatively easy task to
perform. The affair of the robbery bavingto a certain
extent been settled, the next step was to endeavour to
trace out the parties who here guilty of the more serious
offence of forgery, several forged notes—principally £lO
and £5 —printed upon a portion of the stolen bank paper
havingby this time come into the Bank of England, and
the inquiries made by the detectives led them to Bir-
mingham, where the man Griffiths was taken into
'custody. This man appears to be an extraordinary
character. It will be remembered that, when he was
taken, he was found in the act of engraving forged
Bank of England notes; and when he saw there was
no chance of escape, he freely admitted his guilt, at the
same time stating that he had been engaged in the
same nefarious pursuit for a period of seventeen years.
It will be hardly credited that the ostensible occupa-
tion carried on by this prisoner was that of a farmer,
and he occupied a small farm a few miles from Bir-
mingham, where all his forging operations were
carried on; and it would seem that, although the
detective officers of Birmingham—who are probably as
shrewd as any men of their class—entertained some
suspicion as to the nature of his proceedings, they did
not consider there was sufficient to justify them in
interfering with him until the present occasion.

A STEEL PADDLE STEAMER.—Are SSTS. JOIISS and
Quiggin, of Liverpool, will shortly launch a steamer of
250 tons burden, built of steel plates only 3-16ths of an
inch in thickness. The Liverpool Journal of Commerce
states that she is intended for a peculiar trade,' and that
she will steam 20 knots an hour. The peculiar trade is
understood to mean the running of the blockade.
PAINFUL CASE OF DESTITUTION AND DEATH. On
the 12th Mr. IL Rallies Walthew, held an inquest at
the Maid and Magpie Tavern, Wellington-place, Step-
ney, on the body of Edith Loney, aged 56 years,
who died from destitution at 4, Annie-street, near the
Thames Police-court. It appeared by the evidence
that deceased was a charwoman, but for some time she
had been unable to follow her occupation through ill-
health. She occupied one small room, for which she
paid 2s. per week, but was in arrears of rent to her
landlady to the amount of £1 ss. On Saturday last
deceased did not make her appearance 'as usual, when
one of the lodgers finding the key in her door, it was
opened, when deceased was discovered lying upon the
floor a corpse. She had a quarter of an ounce of tea
in her hand, and it is supposed that when she returned
on the previous evening she must have fallen down
from exhaustion, as she had complained to a neighbour
of weakness, which she attributed to her distress.
Mr. Horton, the divisional medical officer, said he was
called by the police, and found that the deceased had
been dead several hours. He believed that the de-
ceased had died from disease of the heart, accelerated
by poor living and the want of suffi lient nourishment.
The weather had no doubt acted upon her condition.
The room where deceased lived was poverty-stricken,
but clean. The jury returned a verdict in accordance
'with the medical testimony.

articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 15, 1862.

TEE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

THE EAST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL
EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE.

On Monday last the usual weekly meeting of this
Committee took place at the Committee-rooms, Speak-
buildings, Padiham. The Rev. E. A. Verity, 8.D.,
rector of Habergham, presided. Deputies present:
Messrs. Pinder, Shackleton, and Crompton, Burnley;
Messrs. James, Heap, Whitehead, Hargreaves, Haberg-
ham ; and Messrs. Denbigh, Haworth, Wilkinson, and
Peacock (Secretary).
The Minutes of the last meeting were read and con-
firmed.

The Secretary in his report gave a very hopeful
account of the progress of the charity, and a deplorable
picture of he distress; blankets, coals, and clothing
were becoming necessaries of life. Another remittance
had been received from Mr. Potter of £B, and £lO
promised from Bristol. The Wolverhampton work-
men had voted them £23, and £4O collected for them
after a concert. in Aberdeen. Other places were in
present communication with him, such as Newcastle,
where the shipwrights were collecting; and the colliers
of Yorkshire were about to send them a Christmas
gift. It would be well for all friends to hasten their
gifts as the snow and frost of winter had already
arrived. The report was adopted.
The President observed that three other localities
were desirous, as soon as possible, to participate in the
grants, Bacup, Ramsbottom and Great Harwood.
Applications from these places had been received, and
Local Relief Committees formed. In Bacup the dis-
tress was felt very severely by the co-operators, for
the Guardians had rejected as many as 1,700 from
relief, and they could not dispose of their scrip, except
upon terms such as would ruin them. He wished help
could be sent them.

Resolutions were passed that deputations visit Liver-
pool and. Leeds to stir up the working classes there.
Mr. Denbigh suggested that funds might be set
apart by each Local Relief Committee to redeem the
clothing in the pawnshops.
Mr. Shackleton described Burnley as being in a very
destitute state.

Mr. Wilkinson declared that those receiving relief at
ls. 6d. per head were better off than thos.) working full
time—the work was so bad—many preferred breaking
atones.

Other resolutions were passed, and the usual grants
made, after m hich the meeting broke up.

The following letter as to the conduct of the Com-
mittee in connection with the Manchester Central
Committee has been received from the secretary of the
above committee :

TO THB EDITOR OP THE BEBEIVE.

Sir,—lt may not generally be known that a poor
operative cannot obtain aid from the Committees in
connection with the Manchester Central without first
filling up a form, which upon his application is given
to him. This form contains his age, family, trade,
pariah, circumstances, income, debts, and finally, con-
cludes with a recommendation from his last employer,
who is to describe the man, how long in his employ,
what disposition ho is of, &c., &c., &c. If he cannot
bring such a recommendation he is not relieved. I
cannot describe to you the pain which is felt at having
to undergo such mental tortute in order to get bread.
A high spirited and independent minded workman
told me the other day that all this red tapism and
inquisitorial proceedings were in his judgment in-
tended by the mill-owners to crush their hands and
reduce them in spirit so that when times mended the
operatives would fear to strike for higher wages. lam
sorry to say that such cruelty now practised toward
the working classes is fast alienating the good will of
the workpeople from the millowners, for they can
plainly see it is not only their intention not to subscribe
themselves in proportion to their wealth, but even to
go so far as to prevent the subscriptions of others
readily reaching them. lam glad to inform you that
the relief administered by the East Lancashire Central
in Burnley, Habergham, and Padiham is doing noble
service to the distressed sufferers; and though little in
extent, is drawing out more liberal grants, both public
and private, from others. Since we began to relieve
the incumbent of Padiham has established a soup
kitchen, the poor law authorities have increased their
wages to Is. 9d. per head per week, and the middle
class committee is more liberal in wages. We are the
only body in East Lancashire that gives bona fide
relief; all other bodies give labour (stone breaking,
&c.) at a shilling per day. A few private individuals
sell cheap soup, bread, blankets, and clogs, but I hear
of none who part with them in pure charity. It is a
shame for the Manchester Central to receive charitable
gifts and then require hard labour in return for the
pittance.

I am, Sir, yours respectfully,
JOSEPH PEACOCK, Hon. Sec.
Padiham, Nov. 6th, 1862.

PROPOSED MEETING AT NOTTING HILL.—A corre-
spondent informs us that a public meeting of the work-
ing classes of Notting Hill and Kensington will be
held on Tuesday evening next, the 18th inst., at 8
o'clock, at the Horbury School Rooms, the gratuitous
use of which has been granted by the committee, to
take into consideration the best way in which the
working classes of the district can aid in the relief of
the great distress now prevailing in the cotton dis-
tricts. The provisional committee, composed of work-
ing men, would be happy, to see Mr. G. Howell and a
deputation from the Trades Council present, with any
other friends to the cause.

LECTURE BY THE REV. E. A. VERITY.--011
Thürs-
day evening week a public lecture was delivered by the
Rev. E. A. Verity, 8.D., Rector of Habergham, in the
School-room of the Public Hall, Burnley, under the
auspices of the East Lancashire Central Relief Com-
mittee, to inaugurate the establishment of an Opera-
tives' Local Relief Committee in connection with the
Central. There was a good attendance of the working
classes, chiefly heads of families. Mr. Lawrence
Shackleton was called to the chair. _ _

PA.DDINGTON.—A public meeting of the inhabitants
of Paddington was held on Tuesday evening, in the
Vestry Hall, for the purpose of promoting a general
parochial subscription in aid of the distressed operatives
in the North. The Rev. Canon Boyd, who was unani
,
saous.ly called to the chair, eloquently appealed to the
meeting on behalf of the suffering classes in Lancashire
and read several letters he had received from gentle-
men of local influence, inclosing donations. The rev.
chairman also announced it to be his intention to have
collections in his church, an example which he trusted
would be followed by the incumbents of other churches
in Paddington. Vice-Chancellor Sir Richard Kinder-
sley proposed the following resolution: Resolved, that
this meeting, deploring the deep and wide-spread
distress in the cotton manufacturing districts, considers
it the duty of the inhabitants of Paddington to express
their sympathy with the sufferers 17 raising a general
subscription throughout the parish in i9sl of their relief.'
B. Shaw, Esq., seconded the resolution, which was
warmly supported by Baron Channel), and carried
unanimously. The Rev. Dr. Manning moved, and the
Rev. Harvey Brooks, seconded the appointment of a
committee to carry out the intention of the foregoing
resolution in such way as they may think 'best, with
power to make a house to house collection. The sub-
scriptions announced in the course of tta evening
amounted to £2OO.

articles.title: .RA VISION OF THE BACKN.EY VARBIAGE ACT
articles.text:
.RA VISION OF THE BACKN.EY VAR-
BIAGE ACT

The following are the clauses proposed to be substi-
tuted for those existing in the present Hackney Carriage
Act, and which are considered to bear unjustly upon
the drivers of cabs in the metropolitan districts; with
the new clauses it is intended to incorporate into the
amended Act. These clauses were adopted at delegate
meetings of the drivers representing the following dis-
tricts :—Clerkenwell, Paddington, Highbury, West •
minister, East London, South London, and Eastern
Counties Railway, and were submitted for considera-
tion and discussion at district meetings, to which the
proprietors and drivers were invited to attend, and
having been returned to the delegates were by
them finally adopted at a meeting held at the BEEHIVB
Office, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street, on the evening
of Wednesday, November 5. These clauses, after
being prepared in a legal form, will be submitted, with
other propositions for redreesing the grievances under.
which cab-drivers are labouring, to the whole body of
London cabmen at an aggregate central meeting to be
held on the 3rd of next month, when the delegates will
call on the drivers generally to take up the question
in earnest.

That all clauses relating to the Metropolitan Stage
Carriage Act be expunged from. the Hackney Carriage
Act; each act to be a separate one.
That no driver shall be compelled to let his cab for
less than one shilling; a driver to be compelled to go
two miles for that sum if required.
Police commissioner shall grant licences to act as a
hackney carriage driver to any person producing a
certificate that siall satisfy the commissioner of his
fitness to hold such licence, which shall not be revoked
or suspended except only by a police magistrate or
alderman of the City of London. The Commissioners
not to have the power to refuse the renewal of a
licence unless by an order of a justice of: the peace.
Drivers to receive a certificate instead of wearing the
metal ticket at present in use. Commissioners to give
a certificate to each driver with his licence as follows:
—License ; No. . This is to certify that A. 8., age,
height, ; eyes, ; hair, ; complexion,
; is the driver to whom the above licence, No.
was graßted.—(Signed) C. D., Police Commissioner.
[The certificate will answer all the purposes of the
badge, if carried by the driver in his pocket, to be
produced when required by the police or the public;
and it will be a guarantee that the driver is the party
holding the licence. At present, any man can lend his
badge to another, but he could not do so with a certi-
ficate containing his description. The degradation of
the badge will be abolished, while its only real use will
be retained.]
That no SUM be recovered from a driver by a master
on account of the earnings of a cab, except on a written
agreement, and then only such sum as may be due
for the last day's employ, any sum paid upon that day
to be considered part payment of that day, the same to
be recovered at the police court.
Magistrates and aldermen to have power to revoke
the licence of any driver convicted of stealing, or
knowingly receiving stolen property; and to suspend
licence for the first offence of furious driving, detain-
ing property left in a cab, refusing to attend before a
justice of the peace, or being drunk during his employ-
ment, with power to revoke licence for the second
offence of any of the above; but that it shall not be
lawful for any justice, magistrate, or alderman, to re-
voke or suspend licence for any offence committed by a
driver out of his Occupation, except in case of felony.
[Where a driver cominits an offence, such as drunken-
ness, assault, &c., when not engaged in his occupa-
tions, he should be treated as any other tradesman. It
is a manifest injustice to endorse his licence with his
conviction and punishment, for an offence not com-
mitted by him as a driver; by so doing he is doubly
punished for one offence.]
That no cab shall be deemed plying for hire unless
standing on some place authorised by the police com-
missioners.

[This clause will not prevent any driver who may
be driving along the streets, on his return to his yard
or elsewhere, taking up a fare if he feels so inclined,
but will relieve those drivers who may not feel so in-
clined from the liability of being summoned for refusing
to carry, on the ground of their horse being knocked
up, &c.]
That every driver of a hackney carriage who, by
any wilful misbehaviour, shall cause any obstruction
in or upon any public place, or street, or road, shall
for every such offence forfeit the sum of twenty shil-
lings.

['This clause will affect all those drivers who may be
loitering or attempting clandestinely to take fares from
cabs on the rank.]
Drivers not to be bound to deliver a ticket unless
asked for.

That the clause relating to lost property in the Act
2 Will. IV. be restored, and the clauses 16 and 17
Vict. be erased,,with the exception that twenty-four
hours stand in place of four days.
That all agreements between drivers and hirers for
purposes beyond the limits of the act shall be binding
on both parties.

That w- hen the hirer of a cab refuses to pay his fare,
or make compensation to the driver for any damage
done to the cab, it shall be lawful for the driver to
compel the fare to go to the nearest police-station,
where he shall be bound to deposit the amount of suith
fare or damage, or to give satisfactory security for the
same, previous to going before the magistrate at his
next sitting.

That the- distance of four miles new measured by
the radius be in future measured by the road from
Charing Cross.
That the fare of 6d. per mile cease at the end of four
miles, and that beyond that distance the fare should
be is. for every mile or part of a mile.
_ _ . .

That when hired by time, and discharged beyond
the four miles as measured by road, the driver may
charge 6d. per mile extra for every mile or part of a
mile in addition to his fare by time, _
_

That 3d. be charged for ea-ch child under ten years
of age when two or more persons are carried in or upon
the carriage. Two children under ten years of age to
be considered as an adult.

[This will place children riding in cabs under similar
regulations as those adopted on railways.]
That all packages be charged for when carried out-
side 2d. each. Proprietors not to be responsible for
lost property to a greater amount than £5.
That all dogs carried in or outside cabs shall be
charged 6d. each.

That any carriage plying at a railway station,
except a metropolitan stage carriage,, shall be deemed a
hackney carriage within the meaning of the Act, and
liable to all its provisions.
That any driver unlawfully summoned before a
magistrate, the magistrate shall give compensation to
such driver and his witnesses.

That on any driver pr.eving, his case before a magis-
trate, such magistiato, shall allow him his costs and
expenses.

It is. very frequently the case that although &

driver may prove himself in the right the magistrate
wilt not allow him his costs and expenses. This is a
gross injustice. For example, a driver summons a
fare for a disputed 61. He proves his legal claim, and
the magistrate orders payment, but generally either
refuses the cost of the summons or loss of time. Thus
a driver may et the 6d., but baying paid 2s. for his
summons, is Is. 6d. out of pocket. This is no uncommon
occurrence.]
That the price charged to the driver for the book of
fares should not exceed Is.

That the fines inflicted by the Act in the City of
London should be made uniform with those in the
metropolitan districts. _

[A Present the fines can be made as high as £5 in
the city, and 40s. in the country.]
That every driver of a hackney carriage shall
receive notice of the unfitness of his carriage or horse
for public use before becoming liable to prosecution.
That proprietors of hackney carriages shall not be
l;able for prosecution for any cab or horse kept out by
his driver and unfit for use, without his knowledge.
That none but hirers be empowered to prosecute in
any dispute' or for any supposed or real offence con-
nected with such dispute with which the driver may
be charged.
That the clause relatinz to the signing of the licences
of drivers by proprietors be erased from the Act.
That every driver shall be served with the summons
for misconduct, &c., within seven days after the
alleged offence may have been committed, and three
clear days before the day of hearing.
That the power of appeal from magisterial decisions
be granted, such appeal to be cheap and effictual.
[The exact mode in which this appeal should be
made, and the court to which it should be taken, is a
question involving legal points, and the delegates con-
tented themselves with affirming the principle that a
cheap and effective appeal was necessary. At present
no appeal can be prosecuted without being taken to the
Court of Queen's Bench, at an expense of £2O, which
is equivalent to having no appeal at all.]

A meeting of the sub-committee of delegates was
held at the BEEHIVE Office on Wednesday evening,
Mr. Cook in the chair. Present—Messrs. Towel!,
Walton, Harris, Bates, Earle, and Miles, with
Mr. Bennett, as secretary. A letter was read
from Mr. Smith, of South London, stating that
Captain Hawes was willing, with himself and Mr.
Bennett, to go over the old act and the new clauses,
and work them both in together in the shape of an
amended act to go before the House of Commons. It
was resolved that the offer of Captain Mawes, made
through Mr. Smith, be accepted. The time and place
for the aggregate meeting of drivers was then discussed,
and it was ultimately agreed that the meeting should
take place at the Whittington Club, Strand, at 7 o'clock
on the evening of Wednesday, Dec. 3, and Mr. Ben-
nett was instructed to write to several gentlemen,
members of Parliament, and others, requesting their
attendance, and to obtain the services of one of them
as chairman. It was also resolved that the admission
to the meeting should be by tickets, charged 6d. each;
the proceeds to be devoted to the payment of the ex-
penses of the meeting, and the surplus to be paid over
to the treasurer to be used in support of the movement
generally. It was also resolved that the general body
of the delegates should be summoned for Wednesday
evening, Nov. 26, at 9 o'clock, at 2 Bouverie-street,
Fleet-street, to decide upon the resolutions and pro-
gramme for the public meeting.
The committee then adjourned.

FRANTIC FREAKS OF A BULLOCK. SEVERAL ACCI-
DENTS.-At an early hour on Wednesday morning a
young bullock broke from a herd that was being
driven along the Holloway-road. It dashed at full
speed towards the metropolis, creating the greatest
terror and alarm amongst the inhabitants and persons
going to work. The animal was pursued by a few
drovers and butchers, with an intent to turn him back
to the drove; but the pursuers being joined by a
number of boys and others be was driven into a
frantic state by their yells and shouts, the barking of
dogs, Fec. The infuriate animal rushed with tail erect,
and horns ploughing the ground, down a turning
through which there was no outlet, and turning round
he made a furious dash through the crowd, who were
guarding the entrance, and imagined they had him
secure; but in this they were deceived, as with a
frantic bound he escaped, overturning several persons,
two of whom—John Best, a butcher, and a lad named
Wilson—were much injured by the beast trampling
on them. On ward the animal sped at an increased
rate of speed, and coming into contact with the tail
grating of a waggon loaded with hay, a severe gash
was inflicted on his shoulder. This occurrence ren-
dered him more furious and after bellowing for a
moment or two he set off again, and in his mad career
caught a woman on his horns; fortunately her
clothes, which were torn to pieces, saved her life. His
mad race was soon after this terminated, for in en-
endeavouring to pass between two waggons he got
jammed, and being released fell panting and worn out
to the ground, in which position he was secured by his
pursuers.

THE LONDON GENERAL PORTERS' BENEVOLENT As-
sociATiox.—On Wednesday evening the quarterly

the George Hotel, Aldermanbary. Mr. F. T. Isitt,
the chairman of the board of management and a vice-
president of the association, presided. The room was
crowded. Mr. Bennett, the secretary, read the report,
which stated that the funds of the association now
amounted to £4,523 15s. 7d. During the year 190 new
members and subscribers had joined the association.
The honorary subscribers had purchased a library of
800 volumes, and had made a free gift of it to the
porters of London under condition that its management
should be in the hands of the association. Mr. Uttley,
in a few remarks, moved the adoption of the report.
Mr. Mills seconded the motion, and Mr. Whitlock
supported it. It was then put and carried unanimously.
Mr. Gurney, M.P., was then re-elected president of
association. The various officers were next appointed,

THE LA.NCASHIRE REVOLUTION.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE " BEE-HIVE."
SlR,—The world is as full of troubles as Dr.
Cumming's expected, at the present time. Kings
and Queens appear to have no secure tenure of their
possessions; but make only a step to a nunnery
from a palace, or from a throne, to being wanderers
by the way. Now there is that dashing heroine,
the ex-queen of Naples, who would have been a
more suitable helpmate for General Stonewall
Jackson, or General Stuart—l beg the pardon of
Mrs. Jackson and Mrs. Stuart, good Virginian
matrons, no doubt, if these ladies should ever see
the BEE-HIVE, for iinking of such a thing,—than
for the Bourbon whom she married—has taken a
notion of the veil ; and the Queen of Greece, another
of the Munich girls, or somehow connected with
Munich, has flung away a classical kingdom, and
taken to singing melodiously on the sea, "as the
sun goes down," and "as the Kye come harne,"
"the isles of Greece." People who have good
berths will not keep them, and persons who would
keep them cannot get them. Depend upon it the
world is getting out of joint. It is said that the
lady who gave the law to Europe, and all the globe,
on bonnets, with grievous detriment of female
teeth, and the increase of ear-ache, has become a
newspaper proprietress. I read that in some
journal, and I thought perhaps that you might in-
duce this terrible Eugenie to take some of your
shares. Only imagine an Empress attending a
meeting of shareholders in a newspaper, and perhaps
taking the chair, more especially, too, a newspaper in
opposition to her husband's journals. Did you ever
hear of a more daring act of matrimonial disobedi-
ence? I know that if my grandmother had ever
been told of such a thing being done she would
have lectured on female improprieties an hour of
every evening for the next six months. I don't
know "anything of anything" political, but only I
believe that something most be off the hinges,
and that we must be well-nigh some great
revolution. What with the comets and the
meteors, the presidents, and the Queens,
and everything else in the form of signs,
we seem to have very dangerous symptoms. Al-
though I know nothing of these great people be-
yond and except what the newspapers tell me, I
occasionally think their revolutions small, indeed,
contrasted with those going on around us in common
life. lam stepping out of my usual course—the
even tenour of my way—into a region that I do not
profess familiarity with, in saying anything regarding
Lancashire females and their troubles. I know
nothing of spindles, and less of goods and yarns,
except threads, if they be yarns ; but I do know
how far is, 3d. weekly goes to feed a human crea-
ture, and it is not far, not much beyond Monday's
cold dinner, beginning with the first day of the week.
I could never see fifteen pence go much farther with
me or mine at any rate. Now, in Lancashire, some
people have discovered that Is. 3d. will keep each
person in coals and food, or say food only, for a
week. It is the most remarkable revolution of our
time. No discovery has exceeded this hit in
possible results. Some aid in addition is given,
it appears, from charitable funds, but it is not
much, and so I fear the operatives will perish under
experiments in cheap living.
People do not go on the parish so long as they
can support themselves from their own resources.
Fifteen pence weekly in return sometimes for labour
done, is not even a great inducement to the idle;
and to the industrious it is an insult; yet the
parish does not give this aid until the family be
nearly naked, and all their furniture sold. This
is the revolution which will tell long on the comfort
and homes of these people. After work has re-
turned, if ever it returns, years will pass away
before all the devastation of months be restored.
Already a deficiency of day and night clothing is
experienced in the more suffering districts,- and we
are on the border of winter. No deficiency in these
necessaries existed in the manufacturing counties, as
a general rule, until the present year. All these
articles that could be spared during summer have
probably been sold or parted with for food. In
many cases they have not been sold, and could be
recovered for a comparatively small sum of money.
One way of meeting the revolution, therefore, might
be managed by some of the charitable associations
redeeming blankets and clothes, stored away, per-
haps, at no great distance from the cottages to which
they belonged. No doubt the proprietors could
seize them for rent—the proprietors of the cottages
—but some arrangement might be made to prevent
that, and house•owners are not worse tempered than
other people. Their property has been greatly de-
preciated, and they deserve pity, but they are not
entirely destitute of sympathy. Many of the cot-
tages belong to the mill-owners, and in them any
gift or loan of this nature would be perfectly safe,
and the idea, if it could be carried out by any
society, would cheaply and effectually help the
sufferers over the year. What is to be done with
them then? Will the same risk be run over a
second time, even if the cotton-growers and their
neighbours stop from fighting, and take once more
to peaceable pursuits. I suppose not, for when
people get a taste for a loose way of life, they often
continue in it, so that the Americans may fight
again, and at any rate some men say that they will
not grow much cotton hereafter. The plant is said
in books to be easily cultivated in many healthy
countries. Any newspaper reader may learn that it
can be grown profitably in Southern Africa, and
Northern Australia. To both countries families
within my own knowledge have gone from our large
towns and prospered. They were not acquainted
with farming, but their garden knowledge served
them well. I remember to have known a trades-
man, with a wife and two children, who were always
poor somehow. They went out to South Africa
some years ago, and have become
.quite independent
from the cultivation of arrowroot. A number of
Manchester overseers and their. families purpose
to go to Australia and cultivate cotton. It is a
great revolution in their circumstances, but the best
muse, perhaps, that could be taken, for another
season of the present suffering would cause dreadful
disease, and diminish the population. Surely then
there is sense and spirit enough even among the
trades to help in going to the root of the reyolution
now commenced, and instead of depending hereafter
for bread and life on the smaller part of a large
trade, to place the business in the hands
.of our own
people, and provide for future time against a repe-
tition of this year, by cultivating a crop that
can only be profitably cultivated, it appears, where
there are plenty of females and children to gather
the harvest ; not harder work in this case than
gathering flowers or gooseberries, or pick iug pears,
although it may be managed to last over the half of
each year; leaving planting, hoeing, and weeding,
harder work, but healthier than spinning, for the
other half. EVELYN LEE.

ARRIVAL OF A LIVE GORILLA IN LIVERPOOL.—By
the arrival of the African mail steamer Armenian at
Liverpool there has been brought to that port a finemale
specimen of the gorilla, lie appears quite docile, and
amuses himself in dancing round the room at Mr.
Newby's (the eminent naturalist) and attempting to
sew pieces of blankets together. His skin is of an
olive colour, and, as he is yet very young, only
slightly covered with hair. He is remarkably fond of
good living, and appears to have an especial relish for
beefsteaks, mutton chops, and fruit. Young Mr.
Gorilla is about three feet and a half in height, very
broad and thick across the chest, while his arms and
legs are long and sinewy, displaying great strength.
He has a habit of putting his feet into any stray boots
and shoes which may be lying about, and when he is
discovered in his freaks he invariably runs for protec-
tion to ady lady who may be present. His face,
unlike the generally entertained opinion, is not fierce
or repulsive looking, although the Jaws are both broad
and heavy. This is the only live specimen of the go-
rilla ever brought to this country.
PRICE Two PENCE,

AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.

(From the Mark Lane Express.)

The weather continues to have much influence on
agricultural pursuits wheat-sowing being proceeded
with at every favourable period, and the first three days
of the week were mostly dry, foggy, and cold. In the
earlier districts nearly all has been finished; but the
heavy soils have not gone on so well, the drenching
rains at intervals rendering the land in an unfit state for
the reception of the seed. In Lincolnshire, on Tuesday,
our report states :---4 Since our last, the farmers in this
neighbourhood have been busily engaged in sowing
wheat, the weather having been most favourable for
that purpose.'
In Scotland there is harvestliwork still to be done.
From the west coast on Wednesdoy it was stated: "The
weather has been better this week, and some portion of
the outstanding crop secured; but much still remains
out, and, as we fear, is greatly injured.' The wheats
there secured in the earlier districts have come forward
poor both in quality and condition, and supplies of better
qualities will be required in larger quantities than dur-
ing the past two years; but these will be obtained prin-
cipally from the Baltic, hiad prices may not materially
vary for some months to come. Their barleys are coarse,
but possess good malting properties, and will in consequence
command a ready sale again throughout the malting sea-
lon. As to their oats, many will be soft and poor, requir-
ing to be dried before shipped in bulk, or sent away by
steamers, to ensure a quick passage. Their wheat-sowing
will be very late, but they will have a good quality of
seed. Amongst the red, 'Nursery' was the finest;
Spaldincr°," BrowicK," White-straw Red,' and' Golden
Drop,' have been forwarded; and of the white sorts,
Chidham," Taunton Dean,' and 4 Rough Chaff.' These
kinds will prove a good change to the Scotch farmers,
and the red descrip ions will most probably be sown more
extensively than usual, from their own whites not having
turned out well this season in any of their districts.
On Wednesday au unfavourable change in the weather
took place, th it day h.vig been a thoroughly wet one;
and on the afteri.oon of Thursday a good deal of rain
fell, so that, where this was the case, two days would
be lost, as far as field work was concerned. All wheats
now sown may be considered got in late, which is noL
looked upon as fav,,urable for another season.

The de-liveries of barley will now be On the increase
-weekly, and, most probably, will continue so up to
Christmas; maltsters being generally now at full work.
The demand will no doubt be good, particularly for the
choicest qualities, which are most run after, and, being
a small portion of the cr,p, these may command fair
prices. The intermediate qualities have been more
abundant, and easier to purchase; but, as these germi-
nate well, they will go steadily into consumption, for
want of a greater quantity of the better sort. Foreign
qualities do not yet arrive freely; but some of the
French are very good, and give the maltsters satisfaction.
The Seale qualities do not work so kindly as usual;
Moravian samples are well spoken of; and the Danish
new will only be fit for brown malt.

The weatlier on Friday and Saturday was raw and
cold: the barometer, having been up to 30.30, was
falling steadily, the thermometer as low as 40 deg. ;
wind westerly, and the week did not cease with good
promise of favourable weather. The Agricultural
Prospects' are not very cheering; the low prices of
wheat give poor encouragement to the farrue,s, and if
brought out in bad condition, this must continue to sell
at rates far from remunerating. The best plan would
be to allow it to remain in stack until spring, when the
coßdition might 1-,e imp/eyed, and prices could not well
be worse, and may be much better. Attention winnow
be directed to the feeding of cattle; for the Christmas
show will soon be here, and there is plenty of food to be
obtained of a suitable quality for this purpose, amongst
the rest, Indian corn may be considered the cheapest of
any, at about one-third the price of condiments.

articles.title: LORD MAYORS' SHOWS IN THE OLDEN TIME.
articles.text:
LORD MAYORS' SHOWS IN THE
OLDEN TIME.

The yearly inauguration of the Lord Mayor was kept
with infinite splendour, the various companies vying
with each other, and that to which the new civic king
belonged asserting its precedence by the most lavi-h out-
lay. The simple procession of minstrels and beadles on
horseback, of which we have already spoken, gave place
to far more elaborate displays. For a time water
spectacles, chiefly in the nature of sham fights, grew
vastly popular. In 1566, on the Mayor-day of Sir
William Draper, a pageant was arranged by one
J. Tailor, which had no scenic representations, but had
a foist, or barge, sviih ten pair of oars and ninsts,' but
whether they had sails or flags does not appear. 'The
Queen's arms flowed from the maintop, and a red trosse
from the foretop; long pendants were added to these
and two ancients displayed on the pope (poop) or baste.'
This vessel had a master and a gunner, with squibs
sufficient for the time, well painted and trimmed, with
20 pavases and two half-barrels of gunpowder on board.'
A little later, on the same occasion, in the Grocers'
pageant there was a large ship, rigged and manned,
with Galatea at its bows, a sea n\ mph, drawn on a
sea chariot by dolphins, accompanied by ss rens, tritons,
sea lions, which saluted the Lord Mayor on the river,
near the Temple.' In 1568, Sir Thomas Rae, a merchant
taylor, being elected, the company voted him £4O for
his expenses. The wardens were charged to see the
tables at Guildhall properly arranged for the feasts, and
' sixteen ' of the Bachelors' Company were ordered to
carry up the service to table. The pageant embodied an
allegorical representstion of the patron saint, John
baptist. He was attended by four boys, whose duty it
was to deliver complimentary speeches. St. John's
speech began thus—' I am that voyce in the wilderness
which once the Jews did call.' Sir Thomas Middleton,
Grocer and Mayor, 1613, was among the first who
attempted a scenic representation. Ile gave a water
spectacle with five islands, artfully garnished with
all manner of Indian fruit, fruit-trees, drugs, spices,
and the like. The centre island was embellished with
'a faire castle, especially beautified,' probably in
allusion to the East India Company' then newly estab-
lished. From this period to 1708 the Lord Mayor's show
derived its chief magnificence from the great Livery
Companies, and assumed quite a dramatic tone. Poets
were hired to compose set pieces. They received the
aid of the painter, mechanist, and dressmaker, and were
exhibited on moveable stages. The lions of the show
were always furnished by the company of the 111,1yor
elect. The music consisted of the King's trumpeters
and the city waits. On the water it was chiefly drummss
and ffiffes." The aim-men, in gownes, coattes, and
caps, bore the banners and streamers, accompanied by
their own beadles, and the beadles of the four _Hospitals,
who wore long cappes and ribbons; whiffiers, in velvet
coats and gold chains, marched, bearing white staves:
marshalmen, javelinmen, anyneyent bearers, tristiens,
with long swordes.' The Bachelors and Liverymen.
new and old Lord Mayers, Sheriffs, Aldermen, and
visitors of rank, composed the cavalcade. The water
pageant was very attractive. To increase the effect of
the show small guns, called peales ' or chambers,'
kept firing salutes from the shore.—Gity Press.

TEARFUL DEArrt.—A fearful death has just occurred
at Rhondda Val+ey, near Pontypridd, Glamorg,inshire.
On Sunday evening, the 2nd inst., a young woman
-named Jane Lewis, left her uncle's house to attend

DEATH OF 'run AMERICAN COMMODORE HUDSON.—
The American papers report the sudden death of Com-
modore William L. Hudson, well known to many in
England as having commanded the Niagara while lying
the Atlantic telegraph cable. -.New York corresponden:
says:—He was in our navy yard on Wednesday,
apparently in good health, and in fine spirits. He con-
ducted worship in hi, family, according to his custom,
that evening, retired to his bed at the usual hour, and
in two hours thereafter was dead. He was a good man,
and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith.' Re was an
ornament to the navy, both as an officer and a man of
science and as a Christian. He was buried at Green-
wood, the public religious services having been con-
ducted at St. Ann's (Episcopal) Church (Dr. Cutler's),
a which for more than 31 years he had been a member.
Dr. Cutler, assisted by Bishop M'llvairu3 ana Drs.
Vinton and Johnston, condi.cted the service.

articles.title: CONFEDERA7'ES IN VIRGINIA
articles.text:
THE CONFEDERA7'ES IN VIRGINIA

From Baltimore we have, under date the 25th, the
following information respecting Gener Lee's army
'Their ranks, like those of our old regiments, had been
fearfully thinned by the various casualties of war, and
many of them were reduced from 1,000 to 500, and in
some cases to 300 men. The new conscripts were sent
at once to fill up the old regiments, and the consequence
is that by this time nearly all the old regiments are once
more restored to their original strength. This is espe-
cially the case with the regiments composing the Con-
federate army near Winchester. In addition to this means
of recruiting his forces, General Lee's effective strength
has been gradually and steadily increased during the
last four weeks by reinforcements of old regiments
which were not under his orders at the battle
of Antietam, but which since that time have been
drawn from other points. His effective strength a
week ago to-day was fully 130,000 troops. During the
last month the Confederate Government has established
four immense depots of army supplies in Virginia—
namely, at Lynchburgh, at Burkesvitle, at Gordonsville,
and at Staunton. The depots at Lynchbugh and Burkes-
ville were used for the storage of bales of blankets,
woollen clothing, and other articles of -that discription,
which, being of foreign manufacture, must of course, have
been brought in vessels that ran the blockade. In these
storehouses, too, are immense quantities of salted meat,
flour, beans, corn, and oats, brought from Kentucky and
Tennessee. Several of the large buildings formerly used
for tobacco warehouses are now entirely filled with these
commodities. The depots at Gordonsville and Staunton
also coutain smaller puantities of these articles, but they
are principally used for the storage of the grain, fruit, and
other productions of the rich and feetile Shenandoah
valley, which have been pouring into them during the last
six weeks. At these places there are immense herds of
cattle, which have been collected in the valley. The
valley, however, has been by no means drained of its
productions. At Staunton, Georgetown, Furleytown,
Harrisburg, and at several other places, the names of
which I forget, there smaller depots of supplies of the
more perishable articles, which are forwarded to the
army, near Winchester, as they are needed. The engi-
neer department of the Confederate army has been
actively employed for a month past in improving the
roads leading from Staunton, Gordonsville, and Culph p-
per to Winchester. There are no sick or wounded sol-
diers in any of General Lee's camps. All such were
sent South as soon as they became disabled. Since the
battle of Antietam hundreds of them have been restore.l
to health and hive rejoined their regiments, but there
are still several thousatids at the great hospital at Char-
lottesville. It is stat, d that then will be no lack of
blankets or of comfortable clothing this winter in the
Confederate army, and that all of General Lee's soldiers
either have or are teeeiving these articles.'

'SPEECH OF TiE FRENCH CONSUL A.T Monmn.—'The
French residents of 'Mobile, Alabama,' says the.Nsit

was now stronger than ever in his mind, from the tenor
of his recent advices." '

The general business of the port ofiondon last week

two to New Zealand of 1708 tons, one to Moreton Bay
of 1347,t0n5, and one to Port Phillip of 1326 'tons.
The total tonnage amounting to 4281.
A COGENT REASON FOR DECLINING A MAYORALTY.—
Apropos of the present election of !mayors throughout
the cout.try, the Kendal ifereury publishes a letter .ex-
tracted from the Booke.offitecord 'of the Corporation
of Kendal, in which a mayor elect in 1746 declines
the office for a very singular reason. He says, that
when nominated I was in hopes to have served the
Town in my Capacity But 1 .now fital my family
affairs are such as wiii. not admit ,of it without great
inconveniency for at the time I should be Sworn Mayor
my wife will, I apprehend be lying inn (! ! !) I must
therefore be oblidged to pay my fine for resigning the
place of Alderman And have accordingly sent you
twenty pounds to be paid into the Court .for that pur-
pose.' The excuse was held to be valid (as how indeed
could it be otherwise?) and consequently the resigna.
tien—togethav with the SW—was accepted by the
Corporation.

The new over the Thames between Lambeth
and :Westminster, which has occupied a year short of a
day in its construction, was opened on the 10th. There
was no ceremony attending it further than that its
.strength was tested by driving some fire engines at
full speed across, one of which was so mismanaged

Tne bridge is a cvire-rope and girder structure on three
spans. There are no remarkable features about it
except the cheapness of its construction. A. small toll
as to be levied on foci passemvers.

articles.title: bUEL AT CHARLESTON, SOUTH
articles.text:
THE bUEL AT CHARLESTON, SOUTH

CAROLINA.

The duel between Major A. Rhett and Col. Calhoun,
briefly alluded to in our American news, is thus de-
scribed by the Mobile Advertiser :-
- .

Beside e the pmcipals and their surgeons, it is said
there were six gentlemen present at the meeting, three
State Senators, the Speaker of the House of Represen-
tatives of North Carolina, a leading member of the
State convention, and a captain. Two of the senators
also hold commissions as officers of the army. The ar-
rangements of the meeting were conducted throughout
with the nicest regard for the etiquette of the 'code,'
and I have heard of several of those who were on the
ground, who express their belief that a more fairly
fought duel never occurred. Major Rhett, the chat-
lenged party, waived the drop' shot, which he pre-
ferred, and shot the rise.' He was dressed in full
uniform; Colonel Calhoun in citizen's dress. Both
fired almost simultaneously, Major Rhett in an instant
after Colonel Calhoun. Tne latter missed-and fell with
a ball through the middle of his body. lie survived
only about an hour.
The quarrel which led to this unfortunate result is
said to hese had its origin as tong ago as April, IS6I,
at the time of the bombardment at Port Sumter' in
What Major Rhett considered repeated official tres-
passes of his interior officer. These lei to the use on
his part of offensive language; and the repetition
aim* of these alleged trespasses, and the offensive
words by which they were met, have aggravated and
complicated the affair. No explanation wig asked or
given. The immediate cause of-meeting was a recent
duel betiveeei Major Rhett end a friend of Colonel
Calhoun, Who, though aware of 'existing difficulty, had
eulogised Colonel Calhoun in the presence of Major
Rhett. Therefore Major Rhett repeated his former
denunciations of Colonel Calhoun, which the friend of
the latter resented as an insult to 'himself and de-
manded iiatislaction. In this first duel Major Rhett
received twit. fires of 'hie advetsary, he himself firing
his second shot in the sir. Here the meeting ended.
In both duels Major Rhett was peremptorily challenged.
It is said that in the latter affair, it was proposed on
the part of the challenger, that firing in the air 'should
not be allowed.'

articles.title: LORD MAYOR'S PRESENTATION:
articles.text:
THE LORD MAYOR'S PRESENTATION:

On Monday the new Lord Mayor (Alderman Rose)
was presented, with the u.ual ceremonies, to the Barons
of the Exchequer in Westminster Hall.

The proce-iion started from the Guildhall-yard at
half-past eleven o'clock, and, notwithstanding the
excessive coldness of the morning, and several smart
showers of rain, a vast number of persons assembled
along the whole line of route. _ _

O leaving the Guildhail-yard the precession passed
through Gresham•street, St. Anne's-lane, St. Martin's-
le-Grand, Cheapside, the Poultry, King William•street,
Cannon-street, Queen-street, Upper Thames-street,
Bridge-street, Blackfriars, Keet-street, and along the
Strand to Westminster Hall. In the Ward of Queen-
hithe, of which the Lord Mayor is alderman, the chief
magistrate received a most enthusiastic welcome.

The procession itself differed little from those of pre-
vious years. First came the police, who cleared the
way, followed by the band of the London Volunteer
Rifle Brigade, a hundred men from the Naval Reserve
force, three trumpeters, and the band of the Royal So-
eiety for the Protection of Life from Fire. The banners
of the respective companies were abundant and hand-
some, as were also the banners of the arms of past Lord
Mayors, Prime Wardens of Companies, and others
whose names are seldom heard except in connection
with this annual show. The splendid carriages of the
Sheriffs attracted general attention, and the men in
armour, some of whom had a slight military appearance,
had to encounter the usual amount of joking. A few of
the aldermen who have not passed the chair were in the
procession, which was brought up by the Lord Mayor in
the cumbrous civic coach.

At half-past one o'clock the Civic party arrived in
Westminster-hall, and forthwith made their way to the
Court of Exchequer, where they were received by the
Lord Chief Baron.

The Recorder, addressing the Court, said he had the
honour to introduce Mr. William Andersen Rose' who
had been elected by his fellow-citizens to the high office
of Lord Mayor of the City of London. .h 1 r. Rose had
been, like many of the most distinguished of the chief
magistrates of London, engaged in commerce and by
strict integrity had gained the confidence of the Ward
of Queenhithe, who eight years ago elected him as their
alderman. He had also tho honour to introduce Mr.
Alderman Cubitt, who had served the office two years
with great satisfaction to the city over which he
presided. •

- The Lord Chief Baron congratulated the Lord Mayor
on his elevation, and expressed the gratification he ex-
perienced in again meeting Alderman Cubitt, after his
honourable term of office.
The Recorded then, in the name of the Lord Mayor,
invited the learned barons to the banquet to be held that
evening in the Guildhall.
. _ _ _

The Lord Chief Bare!' said that some of their lord-
ships would attend.
The Lord Mayor then visited the other courts for the
purpose of inviting the judges to the dinner.
As soon as this ceremony-was concluded the proces-
sion was re-formed, and moved back to the City by the
same route. The Lady Mayoress, in her state car-
riage, joined the procession on its return from West-
minster. At Temple-bar the London Rifle Brigade met
the procession and preceded the Lord Mayor to Guild-
hall, where they formed a guard of honour in Guilihull-
yard and King-street.
AN INTERCEPTED LETTER.

A party of Confederate cavalry made a dash on the
10th of October at a house near Charlestown, in Vir-
ginia, and captured amongst other things a packet of
letters addressed by Federal officers to friends in the
North. One of these was addressed to Mr. Seward by a
nephew with the Army. It has been published in he
Richmond Despatch, and runs as follows :
Near Charleston, Va., Oct. 19, 1862.

'Dear Uncle—l got here from the Ferry yesterday
afternoon. I have not time to write you but a few
lines now, but will write more fully in a day ortwo.
'I send -you -half a dozen copies of various of the
Richmond papers, captured by some of our cavalry last
night. By them you will see that the rebels are not yet
fully convinced that they have not been routed in Ken-
tucky. The Whig's editorial says it never expected
success there while the rebel army was under such in-
competent generals. And the Examiner is still in a state
of painful anxiety about the battle of Perryville.
It seems that they have received dispatches from
tteneral Forrest and numerous other Southern sources,
telling of their victory; but Bragg's official report has
not been received, and they have seen the Federal
papers, and as 'these do not admit a defeat to the Union
army, the Southerners really doubt whether any has
occurred. Is not this another evidence of the wisdom
of your policy in regard to the Northern press? Gene-
ral Scott was right in saying that falsification was a
necessary part of the machinery of war. In this war
it is a powerful aid, as the Southern press -republish and
seem to credit so much of what we choose to give to
ourya pers.

' l'usl your policy as to the press still further. Make
themltate every tight a glorious victory, and stick to
it. It will do great good North and South. No time
for inore.now. Bob Verplank is hero and well.—Very
affectionately, your ,nephew,

WILLIAM 11. VANPELT.

Hon. W. H. Seward!

TILE POST OFFICE.—The Post Office is both falsely
accused and falsely condemned. It does much that it
is not bound to do, and it is remiss in doing much that it
is bound to do. It -shows a perverted ingenuity in
discovering the true aim of curt and scarcely decipher-
able addresses, and it absorbs packets which are
addressed in full, and in the most round and intelligible
hand. For instance, we select two cases out of many
that we have recently' heard of. In one, a letter dated
only Temple,' signed 'B. C.' addressed to a foreign
hotel, and reaching it after the person addressed had left,
actually founclits way back rightly4to the wiiter through
the mere clue 'B. C., Temple' In the other case, a
packet of tanniscript for these columns, 'posted at Derby.
10 days ago by the writer's own hand, addressed in a
hand as clear, though uot as good as copperplate, and
tied up with the tenderest care, has beea simply en-
gulfed; and, in spite of •every inquiry, never since
seen. Why will the Post Office employ genius on use-
less problems, and neglect to employ common care and
honesty—no common tasks !—Spectator.
CITIES OF THE DEAD.—A recent visitor to the cata-
combs near 'Rome details his descent into one of them—
that of St. Sebastian—and says:—' To give some idea
of the vast number deposited in this city of the dead, it
has been reckoned there are upwards of 170,000 bodies
in the crypts of St. Sebastian only. The atmosphere is
close and stilling, and 'smelling of earth. Not a living
thing, not an insect, not even a spider, is found therein.
It is, in every sense, the abode of death. Many s
narratives have been related of persons who have ven-
tured into these passages without proper guides, and
have been hopelessly lest l'—The Quiver.
