articles.title: LO.RI) MAYOR'S BANQUET.
articles.text:
THE LO.RI) MAYOR'S BANQUET.

The great civic banquet with which from time imme-
morial the accession of a new Lord Mayor has been cele-
brated in the City of London, came off with undiminished
eclat. Guildhall, the scene of so many festivities of
the kind, once again assumed the gorgeous livery with
which Mr. Bunning, the ingenious and skilful corpora-
tion architect, is uniformly so successful in its embel-
lishment.
As his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales had, on the
previous day, attained his majority, the decorations in the
noble old hall itself bore especial reference to that
event, and the ariangeinents in design and execu-
tion were characterised by equal magnificence and
good taste. In the centre of the eastern window, at the
upper end of the hall, was a fine statue of her Majesty
the Queen, by Durham, over which was displayed the
feathery plume of the Prince of Wales, composed of
spun-glass. To the right of the Queen was a full-
length portrait of the Pi ince, and to the left a corre-
sponding portrait of his Royal Highness's fiancee, the
Princess Alexandra of Denmark.
Dinner was served up soon after seven, the Lord
Mayor presiding, with the Lady. Mayoress on his left,
and the late Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress on his
right. His lordship was supported by his Royal High-
ness the Duke of Cambridge, Lord Palmerston, the Duke
of Somerset, Earl Granville, and Eail Russell.
Grace before meat was said by the Rev. Canon
Lupton, the Lord Mayor's chaplain; and after the
loving cup had run the circle of the tables, the grace
from the Laudi Spirituali' was sung.
The Lord Mayor then rose and said—My lords, ladies,
and gentlemen, the first toast that I have the honour to
submit for your acceptance is, The health of her most
gracious Majesty the Queen.' (Cheers.) Few of ui
actually realise the b'essings we enjoy in living as we
do in this free country; but those blessings which
spring from our constitution have been enhanced to
us in our having a Queen who has been a model
for other monarchs, a model wifb and a model
mother. (Cheers.) We have to lament that in the
dispensation of Providence her Majesty has had to meet
with affliction; and I am sure I shall have your sanc-
tion when I say that she has the utmost amount of
affectionate sympathy from her subjects, and that she
may rest satisfied that she is surrounded with a free,
an enlightened, and a loyal people. (Loud cheers.)
Toe National Anthem.
The Lord Mayor said the next toast which he had
the honour to propose was, The Health of his Royal
Highness Albert Edward Prince of Wales, and the rest
of the Royal Family.' (Loud cheers.) There was such
a speciality in this toast that he was certain he shoula
have the approval of that distinguished company when
he expressed his wish that the illustrious Prince who
had that day attained his majority, and had conse-
quently taken upon himself the responsibilities of a posi-
tion which was second to none below the Throne, would
fulfil the hopes and expectations that the country had
formed of him. (Cheers.)
Song—Miss Parepa, The Shadow air.'
The Lord Mayor next gave The Army, Navy, and
Volunteers,' with which he coupled the names of his
Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge, the Duke of
Somerset, and Colonel M‘Murdo.
The Duke of Cambridge, who was received with much
applause, in returning thanks for the army, said that it
always felt flattered by the kind sentiments which were
invariably expressed towards a by the citizens of
London.
The Duke of Somerset returned thanks for the navy;
and Colonel IPMurdo for the volunteers.
The next toast was Prosperity to the City of London
and the Trade thereof,' which was followed by The
Health of the late Lord Mayor,' who briefly acknow-
ledged the compliment.
The Lord Mayor proposed 'The Health of the
Foreign Ministers present,' and the Honduras Minister
returned thanks.

The Lord Mayor gave the The Health of the Bishop
of London,' and the right rev. Prelate responded.
His Lordship next proposed Her Majesty's Ministers
and the Health of Lord Palmerston' (loud cheers).
Lord Palmerston, who on rising was received with
loud and reiterated cheers, said :—I can assure you there
is nothing that can be deemed a greater reward by those
who are engaged in the public service than testimonies
of the good :ill and approval of their:fellow-country-
men for the performance of their duty; and when I my
the performance of their duty, I say all that can be said
for any public man, for there can be no higher praise
than the performance of duty, and no public man can
do more than perform the duty which is incumbent upon
him (cheers). Happy are those men who are able to
fulfil the task. They must be presumptuous indeed who
think they have the power of doing more. It is
peculiarly gratifying and flattering to men who are
engaged in the public service to be honoured by invita-
tions to the se annual commemorations, for in the
first place, I may say without fear of exaggerating,
that there is hardly any sovereign in Europe who
could give a more splendid banquet, when you consider
the company assembled in the hall in which we are met,
than that which we this day have had the honour of
being invited to assist at (hear, hear). There is one
circumstance which is not devoid of interest connected
with these anniversary days, and that circumstance is
more peculiarly called to mind by what fell from the
Lord Mayor this evening, for it is a remarkable, and I
trust an auspicious omen, that the day on which the
municipal corporations of this vast kingdom are called
uron to elect what my Lord Mayor will allow me to
term their sovereign for the year, is also the anniversary
of the day on which this country was blessed by the
birth of a prince who one day—Gcd grant it may be
long distant (cheers)—will be the Sovereign of this
country, and who, by the qualities with which nature
and Providence have endowed him, is destined, I
trust, to be a source of happiness to the nation over
which he may be called to rule (loud cheers). The
Lord Mayor has adverted to a topic which must excite
the deepest feelings of sorrow on the part of every
man and woman in the country. I allude to Ihe dis-
tress which unfortuately prevails in a part of our mann-
factruing districts. Let us hope that the cause of that
distress may not ion..' continue—(cheers).—although it
must be owned that there is not at present any imme-
diate prospect that more humane feelings and more
kindly sentiments are likely to prevail between the con-
tending parties on the American continent; but we may
trust that India will supply to a certain degree that raw
material which is essential to the industry of our manu-
facturing population; and if those products which
India may send us should be sedulously used in this
country, and we be not tempted by the wants of other
nations to send that cotton away as fast as it arrives—
(hear, hear, and laughter)—l trust that India may find
the means of supplying in some measure the wants
which the civil war in America has created. 'Cheers.)
In other respects it is satisfactory to know that the
country is in a good and sound condition. (Cheers.)
Our harvest has not been bad, and, though farmers are
unwilling to confess that their harvest has been good, it
is at least a consolation Vat we do not hear from them
that their harvest has been bad (hear, hear, and laughter).
Our trade and commerce have found vents in one direc-
tion to make up for the obstacles which have been

opposed to them-in others, and upon the whole balance
of productive industry we have no reason to complain
that we are this year in a worse position than that in
which we have been in the years gone by (cheers). Our
finances are also in a sound cond tion, and we are
reaping in our intercouse with all the nations of the
earth that harvest of prosperous trade which has been
sown in those doctrines of freedom of trade and un-

restricted intercourse which have won their WaTin this
country by the for e of reason, after long and continued
discussions. We trust the example of England will
diffuse these doctrines over other cnuntries which

hitherto have been deaf to the VOi—e-e-ofre;;;;;-th-t- We
shall find that our prosperi y
,serves as an example to
the other riations of the earth, and that we are not only
_ _

return you, for myself and my colleagues, our most
benefiting ourselves, but spre ,ding over the rest of man-
kind the same advantages and the same blessings which
our own wise policy has- secur, d for ourselves (cheers).
My Lord Mayor, ladies, and gentlemen, I beg again to
sincere thanks foe the honour which you have done us.
I beg to propose, therefore The Heath of the Lord
Mayor.'
_ _

The lord Mayor returned thanks, and gave the
'House of Lords, and the Health of Earl Granville.'
Earl Granville responded to the toast.
The Lord Mayor gave Her Majesty's Judges,' and
Mr. Justice Wightman returned thanks.
.The Lord Mayor proposed The House of Commons,
and the Healtq of Mr. Cardwell,' And Mr. Cardwell
acknowledged the toast
The Lord 'Mayor, in complimentary term, gave 'The
Health of Lord Brougham (cheers.)
Lord Brougham, in conclusion, gave The Health of
the Lady Mayoress.'
The toast as received with warm plaudits, and briefly
acknowledged by the Lord Mayor.
Othertoasts were 'subsequently proposed and nsponded
t 9) after which the company adjourned to the ante-rooms,
where dancing was c.aninued until a late hour.

articles.title: SIIITHFIELD CATTLE SHOW
articles.text:
THE SIIITHFIELD CATTLE SHOW

FOR 1862.

The opening of the New Agricultural MR at Isling
ton, the future home of our great annual metropolitan
Christmas cattle shows, and the sixteenth anniversary.
ofithe Smithfield Club, is appointed to take place this
year on Monday, the Bth of December, and four fol-
lowing days. The arrangements for this purpose are
now so rapidly approaching towards completion that
even the stalls for the cattle and the pens for the sheep.
end pigs, &c., are in course of erection, and the space
appropriated being something like three times the
amount of that obtained at the Baker-street Bazaar,
opportunities will be afforded not only for a great in-
crease in the specimens entered for competition, but.
also for the accommodation and convenience of the,
public.
The Agricultural Hall occupies an area closely
approaching to three acres. It has two entrances, the
grand one being in the Liverpool -road, and the minor
one facing Islington-green, nearly opposite the newly.
erected fountain and statue to Sir Hugh ityddelton.;
The western facade, which is very bold, is in the
rnedireval style of architecture. It has two lofty
towers and capacious central and side entrances. The
main hall is 384 feet in length by 217 feet in breadth,
and the span of the central portion of the glass roof,
which is 76 feet in height, is about 125 feet. This
hall is surrounded by galleries 36 feet in width, ap-
proached by five sets of double staircases, each 10 feet
wide. There is also a minor hall 100 feet square. One
thousand tons of iron were used in its construction, and
the roofing contains nino miles of iron sash bar, upwards
of one acre of glass, and two acres of slating, whilst the
space afforded by the galleries is considerably above
an acre. There is, therefore, no lack of light during
the day, whilst at night the area will be illuminated
by 14 large central gaseliers, of 48 lights each, and 60
smaller ones of 24 lights each. The ventilation and
drainage are two points to which the greatest attention
has been paid, thetowers referred to being constructed
with a view to seoure perfection with regard to the
former point; and as respects the latter the iron pillars
'Which support the -central platten of the-fabric,- form
draining tubes from the roof to the basement, and the
drainage appliances beneath. A reservoir, capable of
containing 50,000 gallons of water, has been erected,
with which hydrants are connected in various parts of
the building, E 0 that in case of fire, or any other require-
ment, Ihey can be immediately ma& available. Ca-
pacious refreshment rooms are provided in various
pats of the building, where refreshments are to be
supplied at a fixed tariff; and, amongst other accom-
modations, there will be a letter-box, lavatories, &c.,
for ladies as well as gentlemen, with a room for
depositing parcels, coats, and other articles. The
architect is Mr. F. Peck, of the firm of Peck
and Stephens, of Maidstone. So far as the
building itself is concerned, it is in every way
adapted for the purposes for which it is intended, and
the only doubt which has been raised as to ita success
as a speculation, is the locality in which it is situate.
Objections have been raised that the show of the
Smithfield Club will not obtain that popularity amongst
the upper classes of society which it enjoyed (and that
increasingly year after year) during its sojourn at
Baker-street, on account of it being so far away from
the West-end. In reply to that, the promoters point
to the late metropolitan dog show, at which, not-
withstanding the then unfinished state of the building.
and all the drawbacks attendant upon it, upwards of
60,000 or 70,000 persona visited the exhibition, and on
the five shilling days the carriages of the aristocracy
are stated to have crowded the Liverpool-road and
blocked up many of the adjacent thoroughfares. Be-
sides the increased accommodation for the public, in
other respects the convenience of the avenues, espe-
cially for ladies' is far greater than at Baker-street, the
central avenue being twenty-three feet wide, and the.
others in proportion. With regard to the facilities
for the public to reach the show from all parts of
London, it is stated that omnibuses going to and
from every district of the metropolis and the site of the
Agricultural Hall make no less than 1,600 journeys daily.
It is also understood that arrangements are likely
to be made to put on special omnibuses to and from
various parts of London and the hall during the show.
In addition to this, the Agricultural Hall is within a
mile of the Great Northern terminus at King's-cross,
and a tmile and a half from the North-Western Rail-
waY, and within an eighteenpenny cab-fare from any
one of the Metropolitan Railway termini except that
of the Great Western Railway; and by means of a
very excellent map, executed under the direction of
Mr. S. Sidney, the Secretary of the Agricultural Hall
Company, and which will be on the back of all the
tickets and documents issued with regard to the
the route is pointed out for reaching the grand en-
trance in the Liverpool-road, thus avoiding the toll,
which is still in existence on the road between the
Angel and Islington-green.
'With regard to the general arrangements for this
anniversary of the Smithfield Cattle Show, the club
have made 'very considerable alterations. Instead of
the awards of prizes by the judges and private view
taking place on Monday, as formerly, they will take
place on Saturday, the 6th of December; and an ex-
periment is about to be tried of making Monday, the
Bth, a Si. day, and still continuing to give four other
days at the ordinary charge of Is. The new building
has had the effect of stimulating the agriculturists in
all parts of the kingdom to take a more active part in
the metropolitan competition, and the entries in every
department are larger than on any previous occasiou.
The visitors generally will not be the less pleased to
know that their personal comforts have not been lost
sight of. The Agricultural Hall Committee of ,
Management have entered into a contract with the
caterer for the Grand Stand at Epsom and the Batter-
sea Perk Agricultural Meeting to supply the refresh-
ments during the ensuing show.

_RECENT WILLS 41N1) BEQUESTS.

The will of the lion. Sophia Ryder, of llambledon,
Henley-on. Thames, Bucks, bearing date 1858, was
proved in the London Court on the 21st ult. the exe-
cutors nominated being her son-in-law, the Right Hon.
Sir G. Grey, Bart., G.C.8., and her sons T. Dudley
Ryder, Esq.' and R. Calthorpe Whitmore Ryder, Esq.,
barrister-at-law. The testatrix was the daughter of the
late Thomas March Phillips, Esq., and married, in 1802,
the Hon. and Right Rev. Henry Ryder, D.D., Bishop
of Lichfield and Coventry, who died in 1836, leaving a
large family. The Hon. Mrs. Henry Ryder, by virtue
of a power of appointment under the will of her late
husband, Dr. Ryder, disposes of certain funded property
amongst her three daughters; to her daughter Harriet
Amelia she has bequeathed a sum of £7,000, and also
an equal share with her six sons in her own personal
estate (estimated at £6,000), leaving the whole of her
library equally amongst her sons.
The will of Lieutenant-General Sir Richard Doherty
was proved in London by the executors, Alexander
George Milne, Esq., of St. Michael's House, London,
and Paymaster I. D. Blythe, the General's personal
property in England being sworn under .£12,000. Sir
Richard Doherty was late Lieutenant-Governor cum
manding the troops in Jamaica, and Colonel of the 11th
Foot, and attained to the advanced age of eighty-five,
and was left a w.dower in 1354. The testator executed
his will in August last, and died the month following.
Sir Richard has charged his estates w‘th the payment
of annuities to his sisters and a brother, as well as an-
nuities to some other of his relatives and personal
friends, amounting. to upwards of £5OO per annum.
The residue of h,s property is also made chargeable
with annuities of £5O each to four distant relatives, the
surplus remaining to be equally divided between the
Royal Free Hospitl and King's College Hospital.
The will of Wyatt George Gibson, Esq. of Saffron
Walden, Essex, banker, was proved in London, under
£250,000 personalty, by the affirmation of Mrs.
Deborah Gibson, the relict, and G. S. Gibson, Esq., the
son. The will is very brief, and bears date 30th of the
St,' month, 1862. The principal legatees are his relict
and son. To his relict the testator has bequeathed an
immediate legacy of ..-C20,000 and a life interest in the
residue of his property. To his son he leaves a like legacy
of £20,000, also his capital and interest in the bankinc,
business, and the residue of his estate on the decease of
his relict. Mr. Gibson has also left legacies to his
nephews, nieces, grandchildren, and some personal
friends, as well as the following bequests to charitable
and religious institutions :—The British and Foreign
Bible Society, £500; British and Foreign School Son
eiety, £200; London City Mission, £200; the London
Missionary, Baptist Missionary, and Wesleyan Mis-
sionary Societies, as also the Saffron Walden Town
Mission, each £100; the Ackworth, Croydon, Wigton,
and Subford schools, and the Saffron Walden British
Schools for Boys and Girls, £lOO each; and £2OO to the
Thaxted monthly meeting of Friends.

earitties,

Visits of privileged parties to the Exhibition en Sun..
days are reported to have been quite common.
You will soon hear of somtthing in the Monitor
way. The Magenta has been ordei ed to run into an
old vessel in the port of Brest, and try the efficacy oi
her ram of steel, which weighs about 40,0001b5., and is
massive.

A camellia, belonging to a gentleman at Pittville, tc
whom Mr. Stoneman is gardener, has recently been.
shown us, bearing nearly 1,000 double buds and blos-
soms. These, at a moderate computation, are word:.
is. 6d. each; or a total of £75 for the tree's produce.
Mr. Morrish undertakes the great hotel at Charing.
cross which is to be erected. Ile has shown he is able
to cater on a grand scale, make money, and prevent
grumbling—difficulties that stagger most when they
come to close quarters with a large undertaking.
The marriage of the Prince of Wales with the Prin-
cess Alexandaa of Denmark will take place in the
Chapel Royal, St. James's Palace. The first mailing°
that ever was solemnised there was between Prince
George of Denmark and the Princess Anne, daughter of
James IL, afterwards Queen Anne.
His Grace the Duke of Newcastle was appointed
Lord Warden of the Stannaries' in the room of the late
Prince Consort; and the Lord Warden, the Treasurer
and Receiver-General, and other officials of the Council
of the Duchy of Cornwall, have been busy, during the
week, making up the accounts of the Duchy preparatory
to their Duke, i. e., the Prince of Wales, coming of age.
It is no longer possible,' says the Honiteur -of
Saturday, to dispute the practicability of this canal,
now that the part between Port-Said and Timsek has
been executed. That part is the only one that has never
before been constructed; it is the only one, therefore,
about which there could have been a doubt, and regard-
ing which difficulties and unfavourable anticipations
might have been suggested.'
There is a curious family difference spoken of at
Munich. Some opulent member of that Royal House
had constituted an annual endowment of several millions
of florins for the second son of the reigning Sovereign.
This would have lapsed to Otho, as King Ludwig's
second boy, but on election to the throne he made it over
to the second son of King Max. He now claims to in-
validate that cession by loss of the consideration therein
covenated.
A letter from Palermo says--' A valuable treasure has-
just been discovered in the palace of the Marquis -de
Vasto, who recently died here. In a secret hiding placer
formed in the wall of his study, thfze has been found,
piled up in the greatest ,disorder, a vast quantity
ancient plate, candelabra, candlesticks, 60,000 ducats in
gold coins of the old sovereigns of the Bourbon dynasty,
and a considerable number of old colonnades, a coin
bearing the effigy of Charles 111. This treasure was-
collected by one of the ancestors of the Marquis, who,
filled the highest posts at the Court of Spain under the-
Emperor Charles V.'
Mr. Frederick Perkins, the present Mayor of South-
ampton, who received the Premier with such magni-
ficent hospitality, is a very young man, the son ot an
auctioneer and upholsterer in that town, who has built
up a large fortune by his enterprise and integrity, and
who often declares, with honest pride, that he began
the world without a shilling.
Mr. Mayo, the financial officer of the Exhibition, ;to
whose zeal, energy, and organising skill the guarantors
are so much indebted for their present comparative
safety, has, we are happy to learn, been appointed
Registrar-General of Seamen, an office in which his-
special abilities are lady to prove of the highest
advantage to the public service.
The Charivari publishes a woodcut representing Old
Father Time looking on with great satisfaction at a
figure intended to represent America, which is in the
act of taking up and swallowing a number of armed
men belonging to both the Federal and the Confederate
forces. Underneath is inscribed a line declaring that
Old Saturn beholds with pleasure that he is not the only
one that devours his children.
The fright and inconvenience of the public has been.
almost ludicrous compared with the actual danger, since
the whole amount of forged notes brought in up to the
present time is believed to have scarcely exceeded £3OO,
one-half of which were circulated in America before
notices of the robbery had been promulgated, while:the
amount .of gold withdrawn from the Bank in conse-
quence of the prevalent distrust is calculated at not much
short of half a million.
On the railway between Alexandria and Cairo time is
well kept now by the trains, but it was not always so.
When the railway was first established, the Pasha was.
in the habit of using the line whenever the idea took
his fancy, and so interfering with the regular traffic.
He was cured of his whim by a slight reminder of his
own danger. One day he felt sleepy, and ordered the
train to stop for his nap; it did so an was run into by
another train, which rudely woke
e his Highness, and
convinced him of the propriety of sleeping elsewhere.
The Prince of Wales takei possession of his newly..
acquired estate in Norfolk, purchased by his Royal
Highness's solicitor, Mr. White, of Great Marlborough.
street, on Monday. It was purchased from the Right
Hon. William Cowper, M.P., for £220,000. The
of the mansion contains 3,000 volumes of
valuable and rare books. The furniture is all nearly
new, having been recently-supplied by Gillow. There
are thirty bed-rooms, and a ,proportionate number of
reception-rooms. In the purchase, all the timber on the
estate is included, which is some of the finest in Eng-
land. There are also 100 acres of wooded land, and
£7,000 a-year from rents, which is secure, as the tenants
are all respectable and well off, one tenant alone paying
.Ll,OOO a-year. The fishing is excellent, and the shoot-
ing, like most shooting, in Norfolk, first-rate, includ-
ing black cock amongst other game. The railway
is within two miles. ,
Amongst the mechanical contrivances etbiliited.at
the International Exhibition, few .attracted more
attention than the -washing machines. Simple and
efficacious as many of these were, by far the best wash-
ing, wringing, and mangling machine yet constructed.
was not there, owing to peculiar circumstances. The
one to which we allude is that constructed ,by Mr.
Tindall, of the Scarborough Iron Works, which. is
rapidly gaining the confidence of the public. The
finest fabrics are treated by this machine with the
greatest delicacy, and the heaviest clothes are turned
out beautifully clean. Its motion is that of a xecking-
horse and a child is competent to work it.
The Editor of-the Lan-cet vouches for the truth of.the
following statement :—Late one evening a person came
into onr office and asked to see the editor of the .Zraiceet.
On being introduced to our sanctum, he placed, aharatle
upon the table, from which he proceeded to extract a
very fair and symmetrical lower extremity, which had
evidently belonged to a woman.'There!' said•he,
is there anything the matter with that, log? Ditl you
ever nee a handsomer? What ought the man to be
done with who cut it off?' On having the meaning of
these interrogatories put before us, we found that it
was the leg of the wife of our evening visitor. Hs had
been accustomed to admire the lady's leg and foot, of
the perfection of which she Was, it appears, fully
conscious. A few days before he had excited her anger,
and they had quarrelled violently, upon which she left
the house, declaring she would be revenged On'him-
. ,The /text thing he heard of
.her was that
and that he should-never see the objects of his admire- -
tion
she was a patient in Hospital, and hadhad her,
leg amputated. She had declared to the surgeons
that she suffered intolerable pain in the knee, and had
begged to have the limb removed—a petition -the
surgeons complied with, and thus became the instru-
ment of her absurd and self-torturing revenge upon
her husband!

The Manchester papers state that great indignation if
felt at the gross manner in which Indian cotton is now
found to be adulterated with stones, dirt, and refuse is
all kinds; yet, although every one at Bombay is cope-
milt of the evil, and there is every disposition to check
it, the task presents great difficulties. About eight *
weeks back Mr. Scott, of the firm of Ritchie Stewart,
and Co., moved in the Bombay Legislative Council for
leave to bring in a Bill
c i
or the better Suppression of

The nature of the local and palliative measure which he
intends himself to propose has not yet been stated. That
it cannot reach the root of the mischief seems apparent
from an emphatic statement which he made that the
best remedy must consist in the establishment by
European firms of agencies in the ut?-country producing
districts for the nurpose of dealing direct with the ryots,
and that no prudent European merchant dare, in the
establish such agencies on a
existing state of the law,
large scale.' 'Without some efficient aid for the prompt
enforcement of contracts, he averred that whatever might
be the efforts used, a mercti ant in entering into such
operations 'would be going to certain loss.' His own
firm had tried the experiment, and after
.fighting
against all difficulties for ten years, and expending large
sums in machinery and in the importation of foreign
cotton seed, they were obliged to withdraw their
agencies.' The insecurity of contracts was stated to be
the sole cause of the result. 'Give us the means,' said
Mr. Stewart, 'of summarily enforcing them, and we will
commence again, and so will many others. Without
these means we can do nothing.'

ARIISTIWNG AND WillYWuiCill

GUNS.

Mr. Whitworth, writing to the Tintes on Monday la
leply to the recent letter of Sir William Armstrong,
says:—

With the arrangements of Shornelifie I had nothing
Whatever to do except that I went there t xpecting to
See my guns officially tried, and before going I was
ianaware that some Armstrong guns wtre to be fired on
that occasion. Sir William ahimadverts s%rongly upon
the account of the trials which was quoted in the Timss
from the Army and Navy Gazette, but he does not point
to any of the facts as being incorrect, though he has, of
,I:eurse, every facility for ascertaining theii truth. It is
!iecessary to advert to this, because it mighf be inferred
from Sir William Armstrong's letter that the trials at
iShorncliffe we. e of a parti tl and one-sided character;
fior he says, It would seem that Whitworth and Arm-
Stmng fiel- t guns wtre fired in the presence of Mr.
Whitworth, Colonel Boxer, and their friends, omitting
to add, what was diAinctly stated in the article quoted
by you, that the trials were really official, ;,n4 took place
in the presence of the Inspector General of Artillery,
General Bloomfield, arid a large staff of officers.'
Among these were Colonel Cuppage, Colonel Bingham,
representing the Horse Guards, Colonel Mardutt, and
other officers.
Sir William, without pointing out any errors, ex-
presses in general terms his doubts as to the accuracy
of the statements quoted in your papr, observing, that
on other occasions, different results had been obtained
with his guns. This is possible, hut I should ask
whether iii these instances the trials were public or pri-
vate, and under what conditions they took place. On
various occasions public trials of my guns have been
made, and the actual results of those irials were all pub-
lished at the time.

It would be very satisfactory if Sir William would
Rola to resit ts obtained by him which he is ready to
'compare with them; for example, after the Armstrong
32-pounder gave a range of 9,175 yards, I obtained
with one of my small 3-pounders a range of 9,700 yards,
and with a 12-pounder a range of 10,200 yards. Again,
my 70-pounder gave a range of 3,000 yards at 5 deg.,
and a range of 5,000 yards at 10 deg. Although Sir
William undertook (as stated in Parliament by the
Minister of War, the late Lord Herbert) to produce
a gun expressly for range, which should surpass mine
(not made expressly for range), I have never heard of
kis _ guns having equalled the results given above.
When results such as these are openly published, there
are surely ampie means for making a comparison, each
gun being allowed to do all it can, without their being
fired actually side by side. Why has not Sir William
availed himself of this mode of comparison, which was
open to us both, .had be so desired it
With reference to my 7-inch gun, which penetrated
the Warrior target at Shoeburyness, Sir William com-
plains that I have not recoglr sed my obligations to kim-
zelf.

If he will st-ite which of his inventions has been used
in the construction of that gua I shall be very glad to
express my acknowledgments for them. He probably
supposes that its inner tube, like that of his gun, is made
of welded coiled bars. This is not the case; it is formed
of a solid bar, bored out—a construction of which he, I
believe, does not approve. It is true the gun is built up,
and its hoops are made of welded coiled iron, but so were
those of guns made by me in 1855.
Guns built up of welded coiled hoops were, as Sir
William must admit, well known in this country before
he introduced his rifled ordnance. Though for practi-
cally carrying out the system he is entitled to claim full
merit, he equally with myself is indebted to those who
went before us for the principle of what is termed the
coiled construction. He has used it in his way for his
purpose; I used it in my way for mine.
For the ready and able assistance afforded me by Mr.
Anderson in the manufacture of my gun at Woolwich I
kave already expressed my thanks; but it is only due
to myself to state that the gun, besides ;being rifled on
my system, was made to drawings supplied by me. It
was of too large a size for my works at Manchester at
present to undertake to make it, and for that reason I
asked for permission to have it made at Woolwich.
Similar permission, it should be remembered, has been
readily accorded by the War Office to many others
besides myself. I iave before stated I should have pre-
ferred the gun to be made of hoops cast in one piece.
and hammered, instead of being formed of welded
-coiled bars, and gave my reasons for my preference, to
which I adhere.

articles.title: CLUBS IN SCOTLAND.
articles.text:
CLUBS IN SCOTLAND.

A most important decision, under the Public-house
Act for Scotland, passed during the last session of Par-
liament, has just been pronounced by Sheriff Hallarc
of Edinburgh. The effect of it is that every 'club' in
Scotland is in the eye of the law a shebeen,' and the
keeper must have a license in order to legalise the sa/b
of excisable liquors' to the members.
The decision was given in the cases of John Hunter,
246, Cowgate, keeper of the Freeman's Club ; ' David
Lees, of the West End Club;' ani Charles WArthur,
of The Southern Club.' Two of these three cases were
under the 20th section of the new Act. The charge was
use and occupancy of premises in which excisable
liquors were illegally kept for the purpose of being
trafficked in at the said premises.' The other case
(MArthur's) was a charge of contravening the 17th
section of the statute by trafficking in excisable liquors
without a certificate. In all the cases the ques-
tion was, whether the sale of excisable liquors by the
defendants was legal or not. The clubs named, of
which the defendants were the keepers, are alleged to be
3hebeens, assuming the name and form of clubs, in order
to evade the provisions of the Scotch Pablic-house Acts,
which require the closing of public-houses after eleven
p.m. on Sundays; and contain various other stringent
provisions. When the ease was argued it was main-
tained by the defendants that they did not sell to the
public for their own profit, but they were merely the
paid servants of an association or club, to whom the
liquors belonged, and to whom alone the liquors w ere
individually retailed, and that they were not liable to be
prosecuted any more than the keepers of club-
houses in the wt st-end of Edinburgh, which were con-
stituted in a similar way. Though the regularity of the
constitution of the defendants' clubs was denied by the
prosecutor.
Sheriff Hallard rested his decision on the assumption
that they were really clubs. He said, 'Clubs have a
place in or social history, and in the history of our
literature; they have none, so far as I know, in our
jurisprudence. They have none in this Act of Parlia-
ment. Tee term itself is an English one, with a
meaning assigned to it in our dictionaries, and with
little ambiguity in its common and conversational use.
But if, as a lawyer, I am asked to say what a club is,
Ely reply must be that I cannot tell. Clubs are
not in the statute, but shebeens are. Their existence
and character are not left to depend on mere re-
pute. The word shebeen,' so runs the interpretation
clause, shall mean and include every house, shop,
room, premises, or place in which spirits, wine, porter,
ale beer, citrafficked intd
e
tr
,
Perry, or other excisable liquors are
y retail without a certificate and excise
licence in that behalf '—a definition wide enough to
include any club, high or low, reputable or disreputable,
where excisable liquors are retailed without certificate
. • The club Laving disappeared, nothing
. •
remains but the bare fact of sales of excisable liquors by
one man to other men within the premises mentioned in
the complaint. These sales being without licence are
illegal. I, therefore, adopt the plea of the prosecution,
and repel that of the defence. In all the cases there will
be conviction in terms of the statute.'
The Sheriff then sentenced Leei and Hunter to pay a
fine of -e2, or suffer imprisonment for ten days; and
APArth ur, -P7, or six weeks' imprisonment.
By the Act of Parliament the excisable liquors seized
in the case of Hunter and Lees are forfeited, and will
be sold and the proceeds added to the police funds.

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, N OVEM BE H 15, 1862.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, N OVEM BE H 15, 1862.

1111_E.4DFUL EXPLOSIOY.

On the 6th, at a qusrter before 6 o'clock, many of the
inhabitants of the district extending from Paddington to
Rex:sal- green were startled by what they supposed to be
the shock of an earthquake, followed by a terrific crash.
Later in the morning it became generally known
throughout the neighbourhood that one of the enormous
broad gauge engines belonging to the Great Western
Railway Company had burst and killed two men on the
,Tot, besides badly injuring some others, and destroying
a large amount of property. The explosion took place
in the company's principal engine-shed, which is situate
about a mile and a quarter down the line from Padding-
ton, near the end of Westbourne-park-road, and close
to the Lilleshall Coal Depot. This shed is an
eighth of a mile long, and, with its long lines
of locomotives, presents an extremely imposing
appearance in the interior. The large body of
engine-drivers and firemen do not arrive to com-
mence work till 6 o'clock in the morning, but some
of the cleaners and fire-lighters come in at 5 in order
to prepare the engines for the early trains. On Satur-
day morning it became their duty to get the Perseus
ready to pilot out the 6 o'clock down train from the
London terminus. Though this engine was to have
done pilot duty it was a first-rate locomotive, and at
10 a.m. on the same day it was to have drawn a train to
Swindon, from which station it would have brought up
another in the course of the afternoon. Dy a quarter
before 6 its steam must have been up, for in a second
after its boiler had burst, it had scattered death and
destruction around, and its own huge form was in
piecemeal. When it blew up it was standing, tender
foremost, on the up line of rails, within about 10 feet
of the great wooden. gates at the Paddington end of the
shed, and immediately under a window in the side wall
of the shed. After the explosion the tender was found
driven through a portion of the gate, one side of the
enginewas do Ain in the pit between the rails, while the
wheels at the other side were still above, though off the
rail. The window, one about 16ft. by 12ft. had been
blown clean out, and many of the great iron girders
and frames of the roof, which was about 30ft above the
engine, had been wrenched from their fastenings and
thrown in all directions about the main line. Every
slate had been driven off the roof for a length of 150 ft.,
and for at least the same distance beyond that not one
had been left in its proper place. The boiler gave way
at the smoke-box or funnel end, and was there torn like
paper in the direction of the fire box. It may be well
to observe th it the boiler-pi ites are of very thick iron,
closely rivetted ; over these plates are placed wood and
felt, and the whole is encased in what are technically
called 'cleading' plates, which formed the external
coveting of the body of the engine. The boiler plates,
wood, felt, and cleading plates were blown high into
the air. Most of the numerous pipes which are placed
horiy, Jotally along the engine remained, but they were
blown back into so many perpendiculars, and the remains
of the locomotive had some a hat the appearance of a
monster porcupine. Some idea may be formed of the
terrific force with which the boiler was rent asunder
from this fact—that a piece of boiler plate, weighing at
least three quarters of a ton, was shot through the
roof and across the main line into a carriage yard at a
distance of about 100 yards. On entering the yard it
struck a truck, carrying away some heavy iron railing
that surrounded the latter; but this did not stop it.
It proceeded till it met a train of waggons, two of which
it smashed before falling to the ground. Attached to
a corner of this piece of boiler plate was a wrought
iron bracket, weighing about 2001 b. Other pieces of
plite were driven into the coal shed, a distance of
100 feet beyond the carriage yard, and a portion fell close
to a private house at a point nearly a quarter of a mile
from the company's premises. The funnel of the Per-
seus, after an ascent, in which it did considerable
damage, reached the earth within the shed mid not far
from the engine itself. There is little more than the
wheels and the axles left of the Perseus, which had cost
the company £2,500. It is almost incredible that the
fire-lighter, Christopher Thompson, was found in the pit
beneath the engine, not dead, though badly scalded. Two
cleaners, named James Wilson and John Eiriclge, were
killed on the spot. Wilson was not much disfigured, but
poor Elridge was so multilated that his remains had to be
collected in a bag. His head was found in one place and
his limbs scattered about in co her directions. Thompson
and another injured man named Bishop were removed
to St. Mary's Hospital in a very dangerous condition. A
thud man also received some injuries, but not such as
to prevent him from walking home. Mr. Luxmore, the
resident superintendent of the locomotive department,
lives within a short distance of the shed in which the
explosion took place. He heard it; but, like other per-
sons who heard it but did not see it, believed it to be an
earthquake. lie was, however, soon on the ground, and
set men to work to clear the main line of the obstructions
caused by the pieces of iron that had been flung every-
where about. Mr. Gooch, the chief superintend-
ent, arrived at the shed soon after, and early
in the fop-noon labourers were on the side walls
removing the loose slates which here and there
lay dangerously balanced on the portion of the
iron framework that had not been carried away. Cala-
mitous as this accident has been, there can be no doubt
that the loss of life would have been much greater if it
had taken place after six o'clock, wheat all the workmen
had arrived. As the officials of the company have not
yet concluded their own inquiry into the cause of the
bursting of the boiler, it would be unreasonable to ex-
pect from then any expression of opinion on this point;
but among non-official persons the impression at present
ia that the occurrence may be attributed to the thinning
by wear of a portion of the boiler plates. It is but right
to state that the company have shown every disposition
to have the circumstances of the occurrence made fully
known to the public.

articles.title: GARIBALDI'S WOUND.
articles.text:
GARIBALDI'S WOUND.

SURGICAL REPORT.

The exploration of General Garibaha's wounded foot
has furnished us with the following results :-
1. The articulation of the foot is opened by the ball
on the internal side.

2. The two malleoles, together with the internal por-
tion of the articulation, are tumefied.

3. As far as we can judge by external exploration, the
ball will be found towards the external part of the arti-
culation, fixed in the bone.

4. The suppuration is sufficiently good, .and not
abundant.

5. The foot is slightly turn.!d inwards.

6. The distance between the two malleoles is greater
on the wounded side by 11 to 11 than on the uninjured
side.

7. The exploration of the wound, either with the
finger or with instruments, is only indispensable when
the certainty is reached that the ball his become mobile,
and has neared the surface; such exploration should be
followed immediately by the extinction of the ball.
8. The general health of the patient is excellent.
9. The expectative method—i.e., patience—is the one
and only method to be followed in the present moment.
It must be changed when the quality of the pu., the
detachment of splinters,
.or the formation of an abscess
prove the evilent necessity of the extraction of the ball.
10. The method of dressing the wound by the acting
doctors leaves ilothing.to be desired.

11. It is indispensable that the Patient he kept in
spacious and well-aired chamber, and that he pass the
winter in a warm and dry climate.

PIROGOFF.
R. PARTRIDGE.

Spezia, Oct. 31.

The following letter has just been received by the
Mayor of Gravesend from the Lord Chamberlain,
Viscount Sydney :
Frognal, Foots Cray, Nov. 7.
SIR—I have the honour to inform you that their
Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess Louis of
Hesse will land a: Gravesend on the 14th instant, on
their arrival from Antwerp in her Majesty's- yacht
Victoria and Albert, and I have to request that you
Will be good enough to cause the necessary preparations
to he made for the proper reception of their Royal
Higt.nesses on their first arrival in this coun'ry, and
the Princess Alice's first return to her native 1. nil since
her marriage. I shall be plesent to receive their Royal
Highnesses.

have the honour to remain, Sir, your obedient
eervant,
SYDNEY.'
A meeting of the Corporation of Gravesend has
been convened to take the necessary steps for the recep-
tion of the distinguished visitors.

FOLLY OF HoARDING.—The Independanee Beige says:
The loss sustained by hoarding up money has just been

She had, she said, laid it by for him in 1820, on the
day of his first communion. The son found in the bag

old lady placed the sum at compound interest, her son
would now have had, a fortune of more th ,n 100,000f.'

articles.text:
FEE PRISONEBS UNDER SEArIEATE

OF DE21711:

No intimation has yet been given on the r art of the
futhorities at the Home-office of any intentim to in-
3rfere with the course of the law in n sped o. the the two
Bulprits, Samuel Gardiner and Robert Coiper, the
former of whom was convicted of the murder of his
wife, under very extraordinary circumstances, and the
Litter of the same offence upon a young woman with
whom he had cohabited. The first-mentioeed prisoner
still centinues to assert his innocence of the crime for
which he is to suffer, and he declares most solemnly that
if any murder at all was committed the young woman
Ellzabeth Humbler was the person who committed it.
It is stated that he exhibits an appearance of indiffe-
rence almost amounting to hardihood, and he has re-
peatedly declared that he has no fear of dying, stating at
the same time, however, that he is innocent, and that he
had no motive for destroying the life of his wife. In
support of this statement the prisoner says that, as to
the girl Humbler, there were no obstacles in the way of
his continuing his connecton with her, and, in point of
fact, he wanted to get rid of her, and he suggests that
she had a direct motive for getting rid of the deceased,
because she thought that in the event of her being
removed by any cause she might have been permitted
to remain in the house with him. Another rather
singular fact has recently come to light, which, if true
(and there does not appear to be any reason to doubt it),
would go to show that the deceased had no legal claim
upon the prisoner as his wife, from the circumstance
that she was origin illy married to his brother, and that,
in consequence of an improper intimacy having sprung
up between her and the prisoner, she separated from her
husband, and afb:rwards married the prisoner, and a
marriage between persons so situated would, of course,
not be a legal ceremony. On Friday afternoon Mr.
Lewis, the solicitor who defended Gardiner, tran-mittect
a statement of his case to the Home -office, praying for a
reconsideration of the matter, and asking that the
clemency of the Crown may be extended to him. The
grounds upon which this application is made are, that
the evidence is entirely circumstantial, and that it doe,
not at all exclude the possibility of the crime having
been committed by the girl Humbler; and in support
of this view of the case Mr. Lewis states that when
the matter was investigated by the coroner's jury, they,
in the first instance, returned a verdict of Wilful
murder' against both prisoners; that they were both
committed by the magistrate, and that the grand jury
als• returned a true bill against both for the same
offence, and that but for the interference of the Lora
Chief Baron, when the case came before him to be dis
posed of, they would both h ive beea put upon thei
trial, and the jury would have been called upon to sa3
by their verdict which of the two, or whither boh,
were guilty. -Upon all these gr ounds Mr. Lewis urge:
strongly upon the Home Secretary that there is, at all
events, so much doubt in the case as will justify him in
recommending that the clemency of the Crown shall be
extended to the prisoner, and that his life may be spared.
As to the other prisoner, Robert Cooper, his demeanour
appears to exhibit a strong contrast to that of his
wretched companion. Ever since his conviction
he has been dreadfully depressed. and his despondl
ency appears to increase as the fatal moment
approaches nearer. He was visited, one day las:
week by his sister, and the interview is stated to have
been most distressing. The other prisoner, Gardiner,
was visited on the same day by his brother, and it
would seem that his fortitude was quite unshaken, and
he conversed with his brother with perfect coolness,
and the latter, at parting from him, was the more
affected of the two. The prisoner Cooper still appears
to entertain the impression that he was, to a certain
extent, justified in what he did by the conduct of the
deceased, and it appears quite impossible to impress him
with the idea that, as he was a married man at the time
he went through the ceremony of marriage with the
deceased, the latter was not his legal wife, and that he
had no claim or right over her in that capacity. It appears
that a memorial im behalf of the prisoner has been
transmitted to the Home Office from the inhabitants of
Isle worth, where the crime was committed, but it is not
likely that any answer will be sent eitker to this or the
one sent by Mr. Lewis, on behalf of Gardiner, until the
latter end of this week. In the case of Corrigan, who
was convicted of the murder of his wife in the Mina-
ries, and who was left for execution, it will be remem-
bered that a respite only arrived on the Saturday even-
ing before the Mond,...e appointed fur the execution, and
when the barriers had been erected and other prepara-
tions made for carrying out the sentence.

articles.title: DEATH. OF THE MARQUIS OF
articles.text:
DEATH. OF THE MARQUIS OF

BREADALBANE:

As might have been anticipated front the unfavour-
xble aceounts received from Switzerland by telegram,
ilready published, the illness of the Marquis of Bread-
ilbane has terminated in death. For tlas last eight days
preceding his death, which occurred on Saturday after-
noon, at Lau-anne, all hopes were abandoned of his
ultimate recovery.

The late Right Hon. John Camp'fell, was the only
son of Lieutenant-General John, first Marquis of Bread-
albane, by Mary Turner, eldest daughter and co-heir of
the late Mr. David Gavin, of Langton, by Lady Eliza-
beth Maitland. He was born the 26th of October, 1796,
and married, 23rd of November, 1821, Eliza, eldest
daughter of Mr. George Baillie, of Jerviswood, and sister
Df the Earl of Haddington. For a short perind he, as Lord
Glenorchy, represented Perthshire in the House of
Commons, being elected after the passing of the Reform
Bill in 1832. On the death of his father, in March,
1834, he succeeded to the titular honours of the family,
and took his seat in the House of Lords. During the
time he was in the Lower House, and subsequently in
the House of Lords, he uniformly supported the Whig
Governments. In Scotland he was a warm support.;r of
the Free Church, and was deservedly popular. From
September. 1848, to March, 1852: the late Marquis
occupied the high office of Lord Chamberlain of the
Queen's Household, and again filled the same office from
January, 1853, to February, 1858.

It is said that Lord Palmerston had an interview with
Prince Napoleon, and of course a long political t,ll-.
Doubtful, though a general rumour.
TRH FORTIFICATIONS OF Sr ETTIN. —The Kreuz-Zei-
tung of Berlin states that the proposition for the de-
molition of the fortifications of Stettin, has been defini-
tively rejected by the military commission appointed by
the King.

A DANGEROUS DESCENT.—The aeronaut Dragnet
made a balloon ascent a few days back at St. Remy
(Ain), during a violent gale of wind. Having attained
a considerable height, he performed. different exercises
on the trapeze suspended from the balloon, andlet down,
several animals in parachutes; he was then carried by
the wind into the mountains where the balloon fell.
Being without assistance, M. Briquet, in order to save
the balloon, hung on, by the cords, and followed it, some-
times banging and sometimes bounding along across the
mountain for a distance of about 2,000. metres. As in
leaping he did not always alight on his feet, he was at
length so much bruised that he was forced to relax hi::
hold and abandon the balloon. M. Braquet obtained
shelter in a. cottage, in the mountains. The balloon was
found,on the following day, and not much injured.
CRUELTY TO AN APPRENTICE.—On the Bth John
Roins, the ma .ter of the fishing smack Gauntlet, of
Barking, accused of cruelty to a parish apprentice, was
again brought before the Ilford. Petty Sessions. It was
stated by various witnesses at the former examination (are-
port of which appeared in the Times, of the. 4th curren)
thatthe prisonerhad repeatedly beat the boy, 'knocked him
down, and caused his back to be tarred and varnished..
It was further stated that he was kept for 24 hours with-
out food, within two days of his death. Om Saturday,
the Beach having intimated that the case must go to a
jury, Mn Young, for the prisoner, said he should reserve
his defence. The prisoner was then committed for trial
at the Quarter Sessions, bail being accepted for his
appearance.

ALLEGED WIFE MURDER NEKR DUDLEY..—On the.
Bth an old man, 09 years of age, named William Ockold,
rby trade a tailor, was taken into custody by the police
at Oldbury, near Dudley, on a. charge of murdering his
wife. Sophia, aged .7.3. From what.the police have been
able toascertain it appears that atabout four o'clock on
Saturday morning a carter, named Yeremiah Bradley,
heard voices in altercation in the house occupied by-
Ockold and • his. wife. He heard the woman goaning,
and heard her s :y, Have-mercy upon me, don't kill me.'
Knowing that-they frequently. quarrelled, the man took
very little notice of the matter until subsequent circum-
stances recalled it to his memory. At about eight o'clock,
in the morning a girl named Maria Grazebrooki who
lived next door to the Ockolds, went in to inquire after
the health of the old womm, who had. been.unwell the
previous.day. The old man was sittingon his board at
work, and the girl noticed that one a his hands was
covered with blood, and that there wasa: large abrasion
of the skin. Upon asking him how this occurred; he
said that he had struck the old woman for getting drunk.
The girl then called upstairs, and receiving no answer
she was übout to proceed to the bed room, when Ockold
said,' You shan't go up there; but she ran past him' and
reached' the bed-room, where she found the woman
lying dead on. the floor, her face being covered with
blood, and her body fearfully bruised. She at once ran
to the police, station, and. to, an adjoining surgery, and
upon Sergeant Simmonds uriving, the man was taken
tato custody as he was in, the act of (Lagging the body
f4-om the fluor to the 'bed. Upon being, charged by the
sificer, he said, It's a bad job.' He also said that he
had injuredhis hand against his wife's teeth. He seemed
treat thematter very lightly' and showed no major.
a any kind.

articles.title: ! !MEAT COMMERCIAL FRAUD&
articles.text:
! !MEAT COMMERCIAL FRAUD&

At the Mansion-house, on the Bth, a well-dressed
foreigner, wearing beard and moustache, who was
seprehended on a warrant under the name of Hugh
Dullens, but who has a great many aliases, under
which it ie believed he has been carrying on a mo,t
extensive aystem of fraud upon the mercantile com-
munity, was brought before Alderman Carter and
Alderman Hale, charged with larceny, and obtaining
goods by false pretences from a number of wholesale
houses in the city..
Mr. Lewis in opening tkie case said that the charge
he had to make against the prisoner at the bar %Till
that of having, by means of fraud and contrivance and
false pretences, obtained goods from a number of re.
spectable wholesale houses in the City, and he proposed
in the first place- to give a brief outline of the career of
the prisoner, in order that the bench might see what
sort of a person he was. It appeared that he had
originally carried on some sort of business, and in 1852
was made a bankrupt; he did not obtain a certificate
until the month of January in the present year, and
then only a third-class one. In June of the present
year he was again a bankrupt, and was committed to
Whitecross-prison, where he remained until August
last. After his release he appeared to have taken
an office at 13, Little Britain, and set up a. firm
in the name of Teed, Leicester, and Co., call-
ing himself Mr. Teed, and started in business ob-
taining goods by every possible means. After he had
been at Little Britain some short time he started
another firm, of Berthold and Co., having that name
painted on the door of an inner °ace on the same floor
he occupied. The firm of Berthold and Co. he called
umbrella makers. Not satisfied with obtaining goods
in the name of these two firms, he started another at
the a Ime place, as Hugo Dullens and Co., so he had in
existence three firms, the whole of which he himstlf
constituted. Irrespective of obtaining goods from
different firms, he appeared to have been in the habit
of drawing bills upon the different firms which he re-
presented. For some time past the prisoner had kept
an account with the firm of Messrs. Jones and Web-
ster, who carried on the business of a banker and loan-
office, in Newington-causeway. In the first instance
he had opened an account with them in the name of
Hugo Dullens, but subsequently in the name of W.
Berthold and Co., and they had furnished him with
cheques. Mr. Lewis said he did not wish to say any-
thing against Messrs. Jones and Webster, as he must
say they had afforded the prosecution every assistance
in their power, but it appeared that they were in the
habit of receiving goods from the prisoner as deposit,
and allowing him to draw upon them against the goods.
Mr. Alderman Hale—That's what they call banking.
Mr. Lewis continued, and sail—That at the time
the prisoner drew the cheque which was the subject of
the present charge he was already indebted to Messrs.
Jones and Webster in the sum of £BO, having over-
drawn to that amount. Within a very short period
the prisoner had obtained goods from different firms to
the amount of at least £7OO, for which he had given
cheques drawn upon Messrs. Jones and Webster, and
all of which on being presented were returned marked
no assets.'

A gentleman, who said his name was Tolkien, of
King William-street, pianoforte naannfacturer, stated
that the prisoner came to him in a great hurry on Wed-
nesday morning, and ordered a piano, which he wanted
packed and soldered in a tin case immediately, as it
was to be sent on the Continent the next morning. The
prisoner said his pay day was Saturday, but he told
him he should require references or cash down, and the
references he gave did not satisfy him, and he conse-
quently declined to take the order; if he had, he had
no doubt he would have been served in the same
manner.

Mr. John Shackrah said he was the London agent to
Shackrah Brothers, of Leeds, woollen warehousemen,
and he carried on business at 20, Lawrence-lane. Eirly
in the present month the prisoner called at his ware-
house and wanted to purchase some goods. He gave
references, and ultimately went to him on the 4th inst.,
and he (witness) told him his terms would be half cash
on delivery of the goods. The prisoner selected goods
to the amount of £ll4, and promised to pay him £5O
at the time of delivery. He said he would send for the
goods, and if he (witness) went with him he would
pay him the fifty pounds. In the course of the day the
prisoner sent for the goods, and he went with them
to the prisoner's office in Little Britain, and the
prisoner at first gave him a cheque for £5O, which was
crossed, and to which he objected, telling the prisoner
he wanted a blank cheque, and the prisoner then wrote
another which he dated the Bth November. He asked
him to alter the date, as he wanted some of the money
on the morrow, and he altered it to the sth, asking
him at the same time not to present it till the after
part of the day. He presented the cheque on the sth,
and it was returned marked no assets.' He went to
the prisoner about it, and he said he would call upon
him, but he did not do so. It was not his intention to
part with the goods without the money, and when he
took the cheque he thought it was their money's worth.
Mr. George Simpson, of 14, Little Britain, said the
prisoner called on him in May last, and took a ware-
house in his house, No. 13. He gave the name of Teed,
and the name of the firm painted on the door was Teed,
Leister, and Co. The prisoner occupied that ware-
house until he was apprehended.. The mane of Waiter
Berthold and Co. was afterwards put on the door of
an office. He was not aware that the prisoner's name
was Hugo Dullens. About the 24th of otob :r the
prisoner gave a cheque, which he produced for
£4 7s. 6d. on Messrs. Jones and Webster, dated sth
November, and signed Walter Berthold and Co. The
ch, quo was given for balance of rent, which he had
asked for several times, and the prisoner said ha was
short of money as a reason for his post diting it. He
paid the cheque into his bankers, and it was returned
dishonoured. The prisoner had. previously given him
a cheque for £5, which was paid.
' Mathew Wilson, assistant to Messrs. Taplin and
Co., carpet manufacturers, Gresham-street, said the
prisoner called at their warehouse on the 18th of
October. He selected goods to the amount of £26 16.5.
61, and said he would pay ready money for them, and

money back, and he brought back a cheque with a sub-

By Mr. Beard: He did not know whether the goods
were in the hands of the police or not.
Mr. said the goods were gone.
Mr. Robinson, porter to Messrs. Taplin, said he
took some goods, by direction of the last witness to 13,
Little Britain. He saw the prisoner at the warehouse,
and delivered the goods to him with the invoice, which
had a stamp on it, but was not receipted. He gave the
prisoner the invoice and asked him for the money. The
prisoner then went into another room, and brought
out the cheque, which was produced, for £26 16s. 6d.,
on Walter Berthold and Co. He believed the, cheque
to be worth the money, but he did not notice that it
was dated the 30th of October instead of the 18th. If
he had he should not have left the goods.
Mr. Lewis said he could note ntirely complete the case
then, and asked that the prisoner might be remanded.
The prisoner was remanded accordingly.

NOVEL ROBBERY AT BRALYORD.—About half-past'
seven o'clock on the 6th, Mrs. Thorpe, of the Cowmen-
cial Rotel, Tyrrel-streer, Bradford, had her attention
called by a person of gentlemanly appearance (a cus-
tomer in her house) to a broken pane in one of the win-
dows in the commercial-room. He stated that a stone,
thrown from the street through the window, had struck
him on the head, which, as he alleged it was bruised,
he invited her to examine. She did. so for a moment,
but observed no wound. She thought little more of the
circumstance; but,about nine o'clock she discovered.: she
had had her pocket picked of her purse, containing- £25
in gold. The person she suspected of the robbery had,
DI course' disappeared, and the police have not been ablf
detecthim.—Miinchester /examiner.

larriage of the Marchioness of Bute, travelling to Turin,
was stopped by a number of these men, who carried
)ff all her valuables and diamonds. For a long time
:)efore this, attempts had been made in vain to capture
he brigands). but that day the gendarmes were more
luccessful. Lady Bute had with her some opium, whi: h
the was accustomed to take in order to assist her in sleep-
ingby the way. The robbers thought that they had dis-
covered a bottle of liqueur, and some of them drank of it.
In alittle while they grew drowsy, and lay down among
the corn near the wayside to rest a little. There sleep over-
same them, and they were found some hours of or by
the gendarmes who were in search of them. Almost all
the band were discovered, and it was learnt with astonish-
ment that many men belonging to the noblest families of
Nice had formed a part of it, and lived upon their
plunder, even in viting the authorities of the town to
dinner who never had the least suspicion of the
connexion of their hosts with the famous bandits. The
robbers had the wit to take care that tl.eir dinners were
always given the day after some remarkable robbery,
the further to evade suspicion ; and, had it not been for
Lady Bute's limit:mum. they would probably have never
been found out. Three of them were condemned to
death. Mzny of Lady Bute's diamonds- were never dis-
covered. One of the band alone esesped to Fiance.
Many years after, his son and daughter-in-law returned
to Nice in good circumstances, and the lady appeared at
a ball wearing a magnificent diamond ornament. 'Ah,

LEAMINGTON.-Nevertheless' if a man were seeking
the bustle of society he might find it more readily ix)
Leamington than in most other English towns. It is s
permanent watering-place—a sort of Institution to which
did not know any close parallel in American life; for
such places as Saratoga bloom only for the summer
season, and offer a thousand di-similitudes even tnen ;
while Leamington seems to be always in flower, and
serves as a home to the homeless all the year round. Its
original nucleus, the p!ausible excuse for the town's
coming into prosperous exi-tence, lies in the fiction of a
ehalybeate well, which, indeed, is so for a reality that
out of its magical depths have gushed streets, groves,
gardens, mansions, shops, and churches, and spread
themselves along the banks of the little river Learn.
This miracle accomplished, the beneficent fountain hasre-
tired beneath a pump-room, and appears to have given
I up all pretensions to the remedial virtues formerly attri-
buted to it. I know not whether its waters are ever
tested nowadays, but not the less does Leamington—in
plets oat Warwickshire, at the very midmost point of
England, in a good hunting neighbourhood, and sur-
rounded by country seats and castles—continue to be a
resort of transient visiars, and a more permanent abode
of a class of genteel, unoccupied, well-to-do, but not very
wealthy people, such as are hardiy known among our-
selves. Persons who have no country houses, and whose
fortunes are inadequate to a London expenditure, find
here, I suppose, a sort of town and country life in one.

THE FOREIGN OLD GENTLEMAN.—Your little old
men abroad live, when they are to be found extant at
all, to a prodigious age. They seem to be subject to the
same mummifying nfluences as the bodies of the old
monks in Sicily. They grow very yellow, very withered,
their bones seem to crack as they walk, but they don't
die. Take my friend Estremadura, for instance. I have
known Senor Ramon de Estremadura ever since I can
remember the knowledge of anything. That Hidalgo
knew my papa, and he has been dead five-and-thirty
years. Estremadura was so old when I was a child that
the nurses used to frighten me with him. I have met
him off and on in almost every capital. in Europe. Only
this summer, drinking tea with certain friends, there
came a brisk though tremulous little knock at the doar.
' Ecoutez,' cried the lady of the house; that surely is I
Estremadura's knock.' Estremadura! There was a cry
of derisive amazement. Everybody agreed that he had
been dead ten years. Somebody had seen an account of his
funeral in the newspapers. But the door opened, and
Estremadara made his appearance. He was the same
as over. The same yellow face, black bead-like eyes,
innumerable wrinkles, fixed grin; the same straw hat,
grass-green coat, white trowsers, and big stick—his
unvarying costume ever since I had known him. How
you do ? ' was his salutation to me. Ver well since I
saw you lasso?' 1 had not seen him- for fifteen years.
He chatted, and talked, and drank tea. He was asked
whence he had come? From Rome. Whither he was
going? To Stockholm. He was charming; yet we
could not help feeling, all of us, as though we were
sitting in the presence of a facetious phantom—of a
jocular ghost. It was rather a relief when he skipped
away, and was seen no more. 1 wonder whether. he
will ever turn up again. It is clear that Estremadura
is ninety, if he be a day old; yet I dare say he will read
the account of my death, if anybody takes the trouble
to adverse that fact in the newspapers, and say, Aho !
and so he die. Eh ! I know his good papa Ter' well:—
All the Year Round.

ABSINTIIE.—We have mentioned the word absinthe,
familiarly called abs, in speaking of the Cabaret Niquet.
Widely aslthe custom has prevailed lately of drinking
the pernicious spirit, its consumption is nowhere steadily
prsevered in as at a certain dram-shop in the Quartier
Saint Jacques, where, from four to six o'clock every
afternoon, no matter whether it be wet or fine, twenty
young men, the members of a- society called Le Club des
Absintheurs, assetuh;e to drink as much absinthe. as
' their heads will carry. On entering the club,, which is
' restricted to tWenty, who cause vacancies only by death
—a condition, probably, of frequent occurrence—each
new member smears, as his co-mates have done, never to
drink or get drunk on anything but absinthe and this
oath they strictly keep. We have heard much of this
fatal liqueur. M. Delvau describes its effects in these
' words drunkenness eaused'by absinthe resembles
no.other drunkenness known. It is not the heavy in-
toxication of beer, the tierce madness caused by brandy,
or the jovial-humour produced by wine. No! It takes
you off yourlegs at the first glass, it 'fastens on your
shoulders wings of the widest sweep,. and you sail off
into a country without limit or horizon, but, at the same
time, without light or poetry. You think, like all great
dreamers, that you are stretching away towards the
infinite, and like.all great ruminants you are only tend-
tug to the incoherent. Great dreamers are great explorers,
and bring back some treasures from these excursions
into the land of the ideal, but the absinthe-drinker
returns from his, journey into the Sahara laden only
with imbecility; if not with madness.' There are five
hundred- of these gulfs of perdition in Paris.—,All the
Year Itous:d.

A. SCENE. FROM ITALY—When October has. come
round, and the grapes of olives hAve been gathered in,
there is a general stir in the hamlets on the mountains
of the Abruzzi and the Neapolitan highland's. The
fierce hot is now over,, and the poisonous malaria of
the. plains is yielding to. the fresh autumn. breeze. It is
time to bring the flocks to the valleys and low-lying
pastures,, where they may roam undisturbed until the
month of May drives them back to the hills. The note
of preparation is sounded among the shepherd families,
and z: icor few 7 days of preparation all. is made ready for
the journey. It cannot,. however,. be said that they
leave their household goods behind them, for the simple
reason that they carry, their household along with them.
First in the procession come the sheep, for whose benefit
the entire march has been. undertaken, guarded by dogs,
whose names' Fidele," Pecorone and such like suffici-
ently indicate- deft- qualities anefunetions. Then the
men, each after his own charge.- The women and!chil-
dren, laden With the utensils and little nece,sary
domestic property, bring up the rear. We may be
certain, that they have classed under the latter head of
necessary articles, huge necklaces, each bead of which
isas large as.a pigeon's egg, heavy pendants for the ears,
and flaming red and green.gowns,.to,make a,brave show
on Sundaysand. festivals. In this. order they leave( the
stre ts of the village), and wind along, the mountain
roads, novr-iii a chestnut forest, now emerging from its
shady depths, now resting near some rustic chapel,
where;the 'women.- &Tango. the wild flowers they have
gathered on the way. At length. they arrive at the
appointed pastures; the sheep are turned out, and in a
short time the who!e plain is dotted with their white
fleeces: The shepherds then put up their huts; some
building in solitary places, others .sociably neat each
ether.. Thus, settled for the season, they move_ about in
search ofnew pastures when the wants of the flocks render
such a. step necessary. FOr a circuit of about six miles
round Rome, the vast expanse of meadow is inhabited
:or six or eight months of the year by this nomadic popu.
ation.—Once a IVeek.

AN EXILED IVIONARCH,—A private letter from a
recent visitor at Rome sayathat tme ex-King of Naples
is living at Albano, in a very small house. Ile is. an
uglYy. mean. looking fallow; we often saw him, and it
singular enough no one bows to him, not even the
koorest contadino.'
Slit, CHARLES TREVELYAN.—Thiw gentleman, to the
surprise of the public, has been appointed Mr. Laing- s
successor, as the Indian: Chancellor of Exchequer in
Bengal. Truth is stranger than fiction. Who. would
have expected when gir Charles Trevelyan was
recallethfrom his Government of Madras, for openly and
officially. opposing Mr. Wilson's scheme of taxation, that
he would'soon be appointed to fill the same post as that
so satisfactorily filled by both Mr. Wilson and his suc-
cessor, Mr. Laing. r Charles Trevelyan's acceptance
of a subordinate post is a proof, at least, of his anxiety
for public employ, partly because he is conscious of his
gre..t expentnce of Indian affairs and his knowledge of
the natives, and loves occupation, and partly, perhaps,
because he would gladly wipe away a slight cloud
upon Ins reputation -as a public' servant. Certainly, his
oanductat Madras was .a sad. mistake ;' but we are right
glad. to find; that this,truly able and honest public mait
is to be once more in a position to benefit his countrt
by his rare zeal, ability, and knQwledge.—Cor.:'

Tan AMERICAN jounsArasT.—Everybody on board
was pe4fectiv acquainted not only with every particular
respecting Ate prince, but also with every detail respect-
ing his aiees de-camp and friends which possessed the
slightest i,ne idotal or historic interest. The heavy labours
of the American press on the princely voyage commenced
the very day that the Jerome Napoleon cast anchor in
New York roads. Instead of the beplumed and em-
broidered authorities who, in any other country, would
have come on board to offer their compliments and
services, the vessel was overrun, the instant it arrived,
by a crowd of busy gentlem, n, who set to work to
measure its length and breadth, to count the cannon and
the crew, to note the names of the sailors and passengers,
to interrogate everybody they could lay hands upon as
to the ages of the prince and princess, their height, the
colour of their hair, their daily habits: not forgetting the
Duchesse d'Abrantes, who was the special object of
marked curiosity and interest. These were agents of
the New York journals; their numbers may be estimated
from the fact, that in the state of New York alone there
are more than six hundred daily papers. From that
moment, the scattered features gleaned by ocular inspec-
tion, by direct questions, by approximation, by corre-
spondence from Europe, relative to the prince, the
princess, and their suite, took definite form and shape,
after a thousand contradictory changes, in a compact
and almost official body of information. It was a half

traversed transmitted from one to the other. And since,

American literature of the second order—the journals
principally—is unequal in its heaviness, being made up
of crude compilations, weighty accumulations or false or
veritable facts, ridiculous hoaxes, childish declamation,
without judgment, wit, or intellect. You see that, before
all Considerations,' copy' must be had to till the twenty
