articles.text:
Ir!jcifiet—Aoitit

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 15, 1862.

SUMMARY.
FOREIGN.

GARIBALDI has been removed from the Gulf'
of Spezzia to Pisa, where the climate is sup-
posed to be more favourable for his recovery.
A reply by the French government to the
request for Rome, addressed to Paris from
Turin, is now published, and discloses the pre-
sent purpose of Napoleon not to liberate the
Romans, or order his army off from the Italian
soil. The answer cannot astonish although it
may irritate the Italians. Ratazzi's cabinet
will adopt another declaration. Papers occupy
time; all that Ratazzi can want.

The skirmish between some Austrian and
Italian soldiers on the frontier was an accident,
and will not be followed by any political
results.

Greece lives under a provisional Government,
which may probably turn into a iepublic.
Britain, France, and Russia, agreed at the
commencement of Grecian independence that
no prince of one of their royal families should
occupy the Greek throne. According to that
article in the negotiation s, rumours respecting
Prince Alfred and a Russian duke are set

aside. Perhaps Garibaldi might not make a
bad King of Greece—would make a good one—
if he did not consider himself bound to turn
crusader against the Turks.
The assassination of the Chief Commissioner
of Police for Warsaw, in a barbarous manner,
has given the Russian Government an oppor-
tunity of billtding closer round the 'capital of
Poland all the fetters that its masters may deem
necessary for its repose.
A strange fancy for Russia, its customs and
habits, prevails in the American States, where
the worst of Russian practices nd apt
imitators, but the western admirers of the
Romanoff would make unhappy citizens of

Warsaw.
The King of Sweden has been engaged this
week in opening a railway between dothenburg
and Stockholm, which practically brings his
capital nearer our shores. The King of Den.•
mark has given both Houses of his Parliament
a dinner, and made a most patriotic speech,
meeting as patriotic a response from. little Den-
mark against big Germany.
The King of Italy is busied by reviews of his
soldiers. The King of Spain—king by courtesy
—has dislocated his arm, and the Spanish
Government have achieved atriumph in squeez-
ing an apology for the destruction of the
Blanche on the Cuban coast, and a promise to
punish the captain, if necessary, out of the
Government at Washington,
Louis Napoleon has invited Mr. Slidell, the
Commissioner from the Southern States, to
his littlepalace at Compiegne ; and it has become
apparent that if the Federal Government de-
cline the French Emperor's proposal for a six
months armistice, he will, more openly than
heretofore, favour the Confederated republic.
Napoleon's plan is now published; Russia has
consented to be one of three powers for its
delivery at Washington, if Britain will be the
other, but Viscount Palmerston hesitates, ac-
cording to the day's rumours. He evidently
remembers Mexico, and suspects a trap. At
Vesent the paper is plausible—just such a
paper as Mrs. Gurney might have handed to
President Lincoln when she went to Washing-
ton and congratulated the Chicago lawyer on
his position among prairies on fire; which
may be wafted to his own home by a change of
wind; but Napoleon might make something
out of it if the Federals refused to hear the
Ambassadors, or hesitated over our counsel and
ended by its refusal. A Cabinet council was
held here on Tuesday afternoon, but the
result is not exactly known.
The Aboriginal Committee of London had an
interview with some of the Ministry here last
week, for the purpose of impressing on the
Government the propriety of leaving three-
parts of the world in the possession of savages,
particularly of not exercising a protectorate
over Lagos. This week we observe that the
King of Dahomey proposes the invasion of
Lagos, with the intent of having a good sacri-
fice of human beings made there. We cannot
say that one and the same Lagos shares the
attention of our Aborigines —and the Daho-
meyite Aborigines—but if a strong Government
would take all Africa under its protection, and
especially the King of Dahomey, humane
people would have reason to be thankful.
From New York intelligence of the elections
is waited for impatiently, as the Government
beaten at Indiana, in Ohio, and even Pennsyl-
vania, would be completely embarrassed by the
loss of Massachusets and New York.
Another defeat near Charleston has been
sustained by the Federals, under General
Mitchell, and they claim a battle gained in
Mississipi. The armies of Confederates and
Federals were in dangerous proximity, on the
3rd current in Virginia. The Alabama, or No.
290 Confederated Steamer, has captured several
more mercantile ships belonging to the Federals,
and when last heard from was in the line of the
Californian steamers on the return voyage.

articles.title: COLONIA.L.
articles.text:
COLONIA.L.

At a dinner given on Wednesday evening to
Mr. R. G. W. Herbert, Chief Secretary for
Queensland, in Willis Rooms, St. James's; Sir
C. Nicolson stated that the young colony, when
last heard from, had a revenue of £400,000 per
annum from a population of 40,000, who were
increasing at the rate of 1,000 persons per month
Mr. Herbert referred with some bitterness of
feeling to the talk in this country of cutting off
the colonists; and while it was right in his
place to express his feelings and those of his
friends in Queenland and other Australian
colonies, yet we have no cause for making
much of a miserable theory, advanced by a few
failing philosphers. The people generally do
not share this nonsense. 1.4 .2 I

Mr. Herbert promised a large quantity of
cotton from Queensland in 1863 of admirable
quality, and he will be able to keep his word.
The sugar-cane also thrives in Queensland,
which like Natal produces, in a climate favour-
able to European labour, all the leadingproduc-
tions of the tropics. _
_ _

The West Indian letters and papers refer
cheerfully to the prospects of the crops and
the general position of the islands, which are
once more taking the lead in the sugar trade,
and hopes are entertained that they will take
a good part of the cotton trade.
The mail steamer for India, which left yes-
terday, takes to the east, and chiefly for Bombay,
more than one million sterling in bullion for
cotton.

This is the largest shipment of bullion, so far
as we remember, ever made from this country
in a single vessel. The Bombay merchants
expect to continue their supply of cotton at a
rate equal to the present importations, through
the greater part of next year. This intelligence
staggers speculators, who are allowing prices to
droop in Liverpool, and the existing high
rates must be soon farther reduced, unless
spinners in considerable numbers re-commence
work.

The intelligence from British Columbia is
perfectly checquered, and comes in black and
bright spots, like some chintz patterns; the
good news is good, and the bad news is too bad
for weak people.

The assertions and denials of good returns
for labour are alike true. Gold is plentiful,
but in mining districts food is scarce. The
roads to them are worse than "corduroy :" they
are a succession of galleys and ruts. Agricul-
ture is a thing unknown within a great many
miles where gold sparkles, not deep, yet at some
depth under the surface. An active govern-
ment would at once make roads and charge for
them, but British Columbia is a crown colony,
and has absolutely little or no revenue. In
n'eaxly similar circumstances Queensland, which
will have a colonial existence of two years in
January next, has an income of £400,000.

The circumstances are only similar in reference
to the age of the two colonies, perhaps of
their population, and the time during which
they have been noticeable localities.

In other respects their circumstances are
quite dissimilar. Queensland is semi-tropical,
pastoral partly, and for the balance of its
business, hopes in cotton and sugars. British
Columbia is temperate, or a little lower, with a
frozen winter; great forests, high mountains,
broad, deep, long lakes, and rapid rivers, with
Scenery inaccessible to bad travellers, but splen-

didin itsmature ; apparently rich in its material,
having the price of continents among its sub-;
terranesra resources. One writer complains;
that gentlemen by birth
.or education earn a
dollar a day in shelling peas in the town ofi
Victoria; but that is not so bad, showing first
plenty -of peas, and next of people able to pay '
for them.

Miners, ploughmen, road-makers, with a ,
little money, will do well in British Columbia;
at present there are a sufficient number ail
clerks to shell peas.

articles.title: DOMESTIC.
articles.text:
DOMESTIC.

Miss Rye has sailed for New Zealand with a
migration of young females under her care, butt
the accommodation is said to have been bad,
and this lady who has undertaken to superin-
tend :female emigration from the best ot•
motives, should have the advice and assistance
of some experienced persons in her next
voyage.

-Lo-rd Mayor's day was exceptional, being
bright and clear; the pageant, like others of its
kind, with rather over the common_ number of
banners; and the festival in the Guildhall was as
good as money could make it, but money could
not make Viscount Palmerston speak out, and'
he would not; while few foreign diplomatists
were present, and a gentleman from Honduras
represented them, and Lord Brougham alone
gave full value for his dinner in a sensible:
speech.

- Any marked demonstrations in respect to
the majority of the Prince of Wales, occurring
on the same day, were deferred until his mar-
riage.

Consols continue at ma to 93i, the value of
money is.un changed._

Subscriptions tOr the relief of the Lancashire
distress continue to arrive at the Mansion
House, and Manchester, in considerable sums,
but we hold them to be generous--extremely
generous—yet inadequate for the object. For
that we claim a national rate, in payment of a
national debt. Disease is added to starvation
in some of the towns.

THE COLONIES ANI) THE WORKING-
CLASSES.

The working-classes need a policy, clear,
defined, distinct, on the public questions that
affect them. They have already a fixed opinion
that reform is necessary, and that a great ex-
tension of the suffrage is due to those who are
now unenfranchised. Complete suffrage is the
best reform that we can obtain, and should be
made the object of an earnest struggle, yet we
object to the intrauction of other grievances
or purposes, direct taxation or indirect taxa-
tion, Confederalism or Federalism, Garibaldi or
the Pope, Greek or Turk, church-rate or pew-
rent, into associations devised to carry complete
reform. A good rule directs us on great in-
terests so far as we are agreed to walk together
in one mind, and it is applicable even to politics.
Different opinions are entertained by the
friends of organic reform on political economy,
and its various topics. Let us not, therefore,
weaken this agitation by the introduction into
associations formed for its attainment of the
great cab question, or the distinction betvreen
annuities, professional incomes, and rents, at
least as elements of its business, for an asso-
ciation is not committed to the illustrations
used at its meetings, but only by its own
resolutions or rules.

The working-classes need, however, a policy
on other matters in addition to their opinions
on reform. Competition has been carried so
far as to become a preference to other nations
in some particulars, and a protection in others.
Any measure that cheapens goods beneath
their real value, protects capital against in-
dustry. Our national means and sympathies
have been frequently misdirected bi an ostenta-
tions and spurious cultivation of foreign
relatious, and a neglect of what are really
domestic resources. When Mr. Bright in
1858, and in some subsequent years, appealed to
the position of the then United States as an argu-
ment for reform, he slightly perilled the cause
of the unenfranchised. Many persons in this
country declined to place our cause on any ,
comparison, but claimed the suffrage on
"our own merits," without reference to those '
of any other people; some of them adding that
if our legislators required a guarantee for good
government at home, under an enlarged elec-
toral roll, they could turn to Africa, America,
Asia' the Australian groupe, and wherever,
they found enfranchised colonies they would I
meet a security for the good behaviour of our
race." The colonies furnish the best reply
that can be given to all those parties who
tremble at the consequences to come on them
by doing justice to their neighbours.
Our colonies and India contain over a fourth
of the world's population and more than a
fourth of its soil. The North American pro-
vinces have, from the Atlantic to the Pacific,
four millions of people, and land for two
hundred millions more. The West Indian
Islands and Guiana have nearly one and a
half millions, and Guiana could accommodate
thirty millions more. British Africa and the
Mamitius have over a million and a half, and
they can take an indefinite number of millions,
for South Africa will push north to the springs
of the Nile, as its land becomes occupied
and its people grow strong in capital and
numbers. The Australian groupe of colonies
have a million and a half of popu-
lation, and they will probably end 1872
with six or seven millions; but they have the
material of homesteads for two or three hun-
dred millions. The colonists number eight or
nine millions of people, with an abundance of
land, in nearly all imaginable climates, and
they sympathise with all the difficulties, as
they share in all the advantages, of the empire.
India stands by itself with its almost illimitable
resources, its two hundred millions of indus-
trious and skilful craftsmen and peasantry,
too gigantic as a possession, to be considered
one of many colonies that, still passing through
their first, second, and the eldest only its
third century, cannot take rank with an empire
that has its traditions lost in the darkness of
unwritten history.

Distress has -fallen on one great section of
our manufacturing population and, unsolicited
by any, relief has come from all our colonies.
Bombay endeavours to reach a subscription
equal to one half of all that London has yet
collected for Lancashire. Calcutta, deriving
no direct benefit from the cotton trade, sent
substantial subscriptions by almost the first
mall after this famine in Lancashire was known
to Bengal. The Indian payments to the al-
leviation of this great grief will reach a wonder-
ful sum —larger than any benevolent con-
tribution ever previously made out of our own
island.

The Australians receive European intelli-
gence at distant periods, and the arrival of the
monthly mail is an important event with them.
Clouds have been gliding over the political
horizon. Hostilities with the Federal States
had threatened the colonies, and anxiety for
news was common in New South Wales,
in Queensland, South Australia, and Victoria.
One mail came with tidings of the gloom that
had fallen like a pall over the once busy towns

!at home;; and another mail did not leave
without artindly response to this sad tale. Not
only rich merchants ia the large cities, but the
miner in the diggings, the shepherd in the bush,
the farmer in his fields, ;and domestic servants ,
in the towns, hasteneta to help the suffering
population in one section of the old country.
Along the lake coats and river sides of
, Canada, in houses becoming comfortable and
prosperous by industry, men have watched
, political events with anxious hearts for many
, months; knowing that a great population
across the river, or beyond the lake, were armed
in a proportion never !known on that continent
before, and envious of the clearances in the
Canadian forests. To them also came the
tidings of our trials here, and from them too
have come the proofs of sympathy in trouble.
given by a people whose means are raised
from a cumbered soil, brought intc cultivation
by persistent labour, for Canada has struck no
gold 'vein so bright as its fields of wheat. From
east, south, west, alike—from every colony
have come and are coming hard won earnings,
carefully gathered savings--cheerfullygiven be-
cause homes five, ten, sixteen thousand miles
away are cold, and children are hungry, and
hearts are sinking under the heavy pressure of
want.

We desire to maintain these good feelings,
to draw closer the connections between the
mother country and these great lands, to have
honest alliances with any State, but a partner-
ship with these infant empires which are pas-
sing into strength through a prosperous
voutlL

- Twelve months have not gone by since there
arose a danger of hostilities along the Canadian
frontier, and over all the ocean. These Cana-
dian farmers sought not to purchase peace by
closing their connection with ihome. A short
resolution of their Parliament would have
saved them. No man proposed to say the word.
Homes and fields were in danger—fields gained
by industry, homes built by hardly requited
toil, but their owners did not think of insuring'
them, by a cowardly or even a very prudent con-
cession. Party spirit lives there as it lives here,
but there as here it disappeared inthe face of real
danger. "Of a sudden" only one party occupied
the land, or existed in these provinces. The
reply to an insult on their flag rung out by
Halifax and St. John's, was taken up by
Quebec and Montreal, was echoed in the
Northern capital by the Ottawa, and re-echoed
by the sea-like lake in Toronto, sped on over
the waves of Lake Superior, was heard by the
Lake of the Woods—passed over the broad
plains and rocky mountains to the gold land
of the Eastern Pacific, and after the sun over
the broad waters, to break out again in clear
defiant notes from the infant cities of the Aus-
tralian colonies; to be as distinctly given in
the old populous and rich ports of India, to
gather strength for its Atlantic journey on the
pastoral slopes and broad plains of Southern
Africa, and return back to the borders of the
American continent, lingering among the
sunny islets of the South-west.
This deep, enduring feeling of attachment
to the empire, and sympathy with all the
interests, objects, trials, triumphs of the old
country; this appropriation even of our suffer-
ings will be fostered and maintained by the
working classes, as a matter at once of duty
and profit. The power of the colonies is the
development of democracy on firm good ground.

THE LANCASHIRE DISTRESS AND
MR COBDEN, M.P.
It is no unusual thing for parties to engage
in a good cause, and under favourable aus-
pices, and yet fail in the attainment of the
object proposed, not from want of means, or
because of inadequate agencies, but simply for
want of that dash and boldness required to
confront and subdue eventful circumstances.
It was this Fabian policy, without Fabian
intentness, which gained for M'Clennan defeat
and failure, though accompanied into Vir-
ginia by a sp!endid army and ammunition of
war. A similar failure, though, perhaps, if
anything under more disgraceful circum-
stances, was announced the other day through
the lips of Mr. Cobden in the cotton metropolis.
With ample public subscriptions, and the
hearty promise of more, if required, with manu-
facturers and squires ad libitum to act upon
relief committees throughout the county, for
the purpose of distributing their grants, the
Manchester Central, which set out on the holy
mission of preventing pauperism, and keeping
the workhouses empty, have succeeded, accord-
ing to Mr. Farnall's report, in filling the Lan-
cashire unions with the flower of industrial
labour, while their funds are safely housed in
the Manchester Bank. A more egregious
blunder never was committed unless we were
to recount M'Clellan's examo3, or our own
Crimean experience. To think that caution
and secretiveness, two very excellent virtues in
their place, should have stepped into the
charitable enterprise of rescuing hungry and
naked souls who, for no fault of their own,
are suddenly deprived of their usual employ-
ment, consigned in fact to Rnwilling idleness,
and prevented from earning their bread; and
that these virtues, which generally promote the
success of business in other bramhes of social
life, should have been so exercised as to
actually bring about the very disasters they
were intended to obviate. For three months
after its start the Manchester Central could
only "see its way to distribute weekly £300."
We have read from an unquestionable autho-
rity, that "blindness in part" happened unto
Israel; but here is total want of vision
falling on the optics of a host of Chris-
tian men in a large city of modern times,
boasting itself to be, par excellence, " a
place where wisdom's senators resort"
What inference are we to draw from these
premises? Is it that Manchester blunders;
not only in losing her cotton but in relieving
her unfortunate work-people thrown out of em-
ploy? The press of last week also brings us
the astounding intelligence that these wise men
of Gotham, despite the distressed condition of
170,000 operatives, not yet in the workhouse,
but on the brink of falling into its tender care,
actually took the trouble to meet and distribute
£4OO out of £87,000 given them for im-
mediate use. We think we have now said
enough of the Manchester Central. Mr. Cob-
den dares not tell them the broad fact of their
egregrious failure, but simply proposes a re-
organisation of the executive, as well as of the
whole scheme. It is acknowledged that, as at
present provided by the funds, if distributed ac-
cording to £25,000 monthly, only five per
cent, of the indigent will be relieved, and that
a fund of one million is the lowest figure he
could mention as adequate for present wants;
whereas the sum of ten millions is mentioned
as necessary to tide the population over the
next six months. We will not dispute Mr.
Cobden's figures. Our own opinion is the com-
mon conviction of all out of Manchester, that
an adequate supply of cheap cotton, and a re-
vival of weekly wages, is the only scheme likely
effectually to relieve the kingdom in general,
and Lancashire in particular, from the burden
of this iiisiress. If the Queen in Council

were to decree a monopoly of traffic in cotton
to India and the colonies for the next five
years, on cond_tion tkat cotton was to be sold
by them at a low price, within the reach of
the mill-owners (forbidding all export from
the United Kingdom, as well as all specu-
lation in cotton), the result might be
a rich Indian exchequer—a rich cotton
growing Indian empire, a plentiful supply of
cheap and good cotton, and a well-employed
work-people in Lancashire. The Indian ryot
requires an ample guarantee that he shall not
suddenly be brought into competition with the
South American States, for if so, and he
should spend his labour in the cultivation of
cotton, the same ruin would visit him which
now is inflicted upon the Lancashire opera-1
tives ; with this diffe,renee, that he would find'
himself surrounded with cotton bales he could
not find a purchaser for, owing to the preference
generally given to American kinds. This
material guarantee the Indian Government
alone could afford, but a monopoly is distasteful,
although until some earnest measures be taken,
Lancashire will be left without cotton, and
India without trade. But what should be done
with the defunct Manchester Relief Fund?
Mr. Cobden advises its re-construction upon a
wider and broader basis. This is as absurd as
"closing of the stable-door when the steed is
stolen." The hope of saving the operatives is
entirely gone. They are in the workhouse, or
supported with out-door relief. The only
course left is to hand the subscriptions over to
the Lord Mayor's Fund and the East Lancashire,
which supplement all other aid; or transfer it
at once to the guardians of Manchester, who
will apply it to the relief of the surrounding
pauperism. Let this be a warning to all public
bodies who raise subscriptions upon certain
trusts, to beware of sloth and illiberality. The
Manchester Central set out with the idea of
saving the cotton operatives from falling into
pauperism, but they kept the funds instead of
distributing them, and now know not which
way to face the duped subscribers. They have
"let the steed starve," while they were choosing
"a fine" pasture for food.

CONGREGATIONAL COLLECTIONS

FOR LANCASHIRE.

Dr. ITNIELE's congregation in Liverpool
have set an excellent example in undertaking
the support of twenty-five families in one town,
and twenty-five in another, during the cotton
famine. This congregation promise that each
member of these families shall be allowed at
least 2s. 6d. weekly, until employment be re-
sumed.

We have urged first, a national loan as the
proper means of relief; second a voluntary
rate imposed by the local authorities, but only
collected from those householders who do not
refuse payment; and this congregational
system of relief may be regarded as the third
in efficiency. The country must have twenty
thousand congregations capable of giving a
little help; but ten thousand, taking four
families each, would relieve at an aver-
age of five members in - each family
two hundred thousand persons, or if •the
guardians of the poor would assume a payment
of is. 3d. per week for each individual, drop-
ping restrictions, inapplicable to the case, four
hundred thousand persons.
The cost would be £1 ss. per week for each
congregation, and if any one were disposed to
inquire why the burdens should be placed on
them, we answer it would be assumed n ot
placed; and quote the words, " Inasmuch as
ye have done it unto one of the least of these
my brethren, ye have done it unto me.

articles.title: JURY TRIALS.
articles.text:
JURY TRIALS.

OUR readers will generally remember the
fatality which occurred by the fall of a scaffold
in St. Martin's Hall. The representative of
one workman who was killed by its fall, brought
an action against the employer, but the jury
could not agree. A second action was brought
and the jury, in the week before last, did agree
in finding for the defender, who immediately
received a request in writing from one of the
jury for remuneration because they had found
for him. The application must have been re-
sented by the employer, or the letter could not
have been produced. It was equally resented
by some of the jurymen and mentioned
publicly. Mr. Serjeaut Parry deemed it ade-
quate ground of a motion for a new trial, but
the court declined to entertain this request.
The juryman sought remuneration from one
of the parties, for not perjuring himself; if the
verdict accorded with his judgment, or the
reward of perjury, if be gave a false verdict.
In either case be was either ignorant and knew
nothing of his duty; or he deserved punish-
ment for attempting to obtain money on false
pretences.

Tug PurNcEss's.—A drama, entitled One Good
Turn Deserves Another,' was produced here on Mon-
day evening, with great success. Messrs. G. Vining
and Miss Amy Sedgwick sustained the principal cha-
racters with considerab:e vigour and effect.
OLYMPIC.—A new piece, in three acts, by Mr.
Watts Phillips, was brought out here on Monday last,
under the title of' Camilla's Husband.' rhe principal
characters were sustained by Messrs. H. Neville, H.
Wigan, Robson, and Mrs. L. Murray. The piece was

SURREY.—A new piece, dramatised from one of
Southey's poems, called 'St. Ann's Night,' was pro-
duced here last Monday, and was very successful.
The other theatres are still running the pieces that
have appc.:are 1 in their bills for months past.

THE CHELSEA INSTITUTE FOR IVORKING-MEN.—qll
Friday evening, the 7th inst., a meeting was held in
the Boys' school-room, King-street, Chelsea, the Rev.
G. Blunt in the chair. The Chairman explained that
i
the objects for which they were assembled was to n-
vite the co-operation of working-men to establish a
reading clans on the same principle as the one now in
operation in Westminster, to be opened every evening
(Sunday excepted,) from 7 till 10. The subscription
to be one penny per week. The meeting was addressed
by the Rev. F. Blunt and several gentlemen connected
with the Chelsea Literary Institute, on the economy
and social benefits derivable from such institutions,
and stating that they were willing to assist as honorary
members, and invited the meeting to appoint a com-
mittee of themselves, to assist in arranging details.
A goodly number entered their names, and the meeting
adjourned with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.—
On Monday evening, the rev.gentlemen and friends met
the committee elect, and twelve honorary and twelve
working meiroer , with three officers were appoin; ed.
The rules, necessary to be observed were discussed,
and arrangements for opening this Saturday evening,
at 7 o'clock. The gentlemen from the Literary In-
stitute having promised the loan of several papers,
periodicals, and a selectinn of books, to commence with.
The promoters distinctly stated they had but one
object—the elevation of working-m9n-Tand being
entirely free from anything like sectarianism, we may
hope that the working-men of Chelsea will show, by
their numbers and their conduct, they are worthy of
the benefits derivable from such an institution.
MEETING OF GREEKS
L9NIJox.--The Greeks resi -
dent in London held a meeting on Saturday last at 3,
Gloucester-square, Hyde Park, for the purpose of
taking into consideration the political events of Greece.
Several speeches were then made in the same spirit,
and a iesolution was proposed and unanimously
adopted that a committee be appointed consisting of
twelve members, in order that they should send ,
a congratulatory address to the Provisional Govern-
ment in Athens, and that they should moreover con-
sider by what means the Greek community in London
could best concur in prom-ating the welfare of the
common country.

FRANCE AND AIfRRICA.

DISPATCH OF THE FRENCH GOVERNMENT
ON MEDIATION IN AMERICA.

Piaui, Nov. 13.
The Moniteur of this morning publishes a dispatch
of M. Drouyn de Lhuys, dated October 30; proposing
to the cabinets of London and St. Petersburg to comer
to an understanding, in order to cause a cessation of
the hostilities now waging on the American Con-
tinent.

M. Drouyn de Lhuys says that those hostilities
provoke sacrifices and efforts of a nature to inspire
a high idea of the perseverance and energy of both
peoples. The minister recalls that France has con-
sidered it a duty to observe a strict neutrality, and
continues But far from imposing upon the powers
an attitude resembling indifference, neutrality should.
dispose theta to render themselves useful to both par-
ties, and aid them to emerge from a position which at
present appears without issue.'
The dispatch proceeds to state that the situation of
the belligerents does not permit a hope of marked
advantage likely to accelerate the conclusion of peace,
but points out the opportunity for an armistice, to
which, in the present state of things, no strategic in-
terests appear to make an obstacle. M. Drouyn de
Lhuys continues thus :—' Dispositions favourable to-
peace begin to manifest themselves in the North as
well as in the South, and would second steps for the,
conclusion of a truce. The Emperor has charged me to
propose to the Cabinets of London and St. Petersburg to
come to an understanding to employ their influence at
Washington and in the Confederate States, in order to
bring about a suspension of hostilities for six months,
during which all direct or indirect acts of war sh ould cease
both on sea and land. These overtures would imply no
judgment upon the origin or issue of the quarrel, and no
pressure upon negotiations which might be conducted.
Our part would solely be to smooth away difficulties,
and only to intervene in the measures determined upon
by both parties. The accord of the three powers would
impress the step they might take with an evident cha-
racter of impartiality. If our counsels were not Hs-
tened to, we should have fulfilled the duties of
humanity; and even in remaining wit hout result our:
efforts would not be entirely useless, for they might
encourage in American public opinion a movement
towards conciliatory ideas, and assist in hastening the
moment when the return of peace might become pos-
sible.'

REFUSAL OF THE FRENCH

OFFER OF MEDIATION BY THE ENGLISH

GOVERNMENT.

Late last evening a despatch was sent by the Foreign.
Secretary, Earl Russell, to the French Government, to-
the effect that her Majesty's Government saw no just
reason for their joining in the proposed mediation,,
which they thought would be both useless and mis-
chievous.

PRUSSIA.

BRESLAU, Nov. 13.

To-day the trial took place of the proprietors of the.
Breslau newspapers, prosecuted by the Government
for having published an appeal, signed by Herren Lass-
witz and Sturn, merchants of this city, calling upon
their fellow-citizens to contribute to the national fund
in aid of the defenders of the Constitution. The trial
resulted in the acquittal of the accused.

MR. COBDEN, M.P., IN BLACRBURN.—Mr. Cobden
visited Blackburn on Wednesday last, to carry out the
proposition which he has made to the Manchester
Central Executive Committee.

THE BANK PAPER ROBBERY AND FORGERY.--The
examination of the prisoners George Buncher, Robert
Cummings, William Burnett, Richard Brewer, Jame
Griffiths, and Henry Williams, who are charged with
the above offence, was resumed yesterday before the
Lord Mayor. Very few additional facts were proved
in evidence and the prisoners were again remanded.
It is expected that at the examination the case for the
prosecution will be brought to a conclusion.

_
THE REWARD OF SUFFERING.—A disgraceful case is
reported from Rochdale. Twenty-five of the starving
operatives there were summoned for non pa ym ent of
poor, rate, and the magistrates, who said they could do
nothing in the way of excuse without the consent of
the guardians, issued distress warrants against all who
had not paid the rate. One man, a sample of the lot,
said he had a family of six, that he was working for
2s. 10d. a week, that he got from the guardians Bd. a
week, and a little bread and meat from the soup kitchen.
This was all he had.

REPRESENTATION OF SOLTHAMPTON.—A large meet-
ing was held last evening at the Royal Hotel, which
resulted in a complete reunion of both sections of the
Liberal party. A large and influential committee was
formed, and a strong determination expresse4 to place
Captain Mangles at the head of the poll. This union,
of Liberals completely shuts out all chance of a Con-
servative candidate being returned; and it is now much.
doubted whether Lord Mayor Bose will persevere in
soliciting the suffrages of the electors.

AMERICA AND THE DzsmEss.—A.-Crowded meeting
was held in the People's Hall of Leeds on Wednesday
evening, to petition the gov rnznent for a grant from
the consolidated fend in aid of the distressed operatives
of Lancashire. The speakers at the meeting all argued
that the war in America was the cause of the privation
in these distziets, but they equally insisted on holding
strictly to the doctrine of non-intervention. The
ground of their application to government was that,
the distress had outstripped the limits of private
lAnevolence.

'THE CONVICT GARDINER.-.-Our readers. will share
the regret, and, we must say the disappointment, felt
by us in announcing that the Home Secretary has.
seen no sufficient reason to justify the commutation of
the sentence of the convict Gardiner. By an answer
addressed to the Messrs. Lewis, of Ely-place, sir
George Grey has declined to interfere with the course,
of law. The unhappy man is thus left for death.
A member of the legal firm whom we have
named communicated the adverse result to the prisoner,
who heard his doom with resignation, but still, in the
most solemn manner, protested his innocence. •
ENGLISH SYMPATHY WITH AMERICAN ABOLITIONISM.
—We are glad to be able to atanounce the establish-
ment of an association which, under the name of the
Emancipation Society, is designed to counteract the
alleged sympathy of England with the pro-gavery
Confederacy, and to encourage the Federal Government
and people in the prosecution of a thoroughly free
i labour policy. This society will not n the least
intermeddle with such questions as the abstract or
constitutional right of secession ; but will direct all its
efforts to the development of that healthy anti-slavery
sentiment which has so honourably characterised the
people of the United Kingdom. A number of members
of Parliament, eminent ministers of religion, and
leading politicians, have promised their support ; and
an appeal to the general public will be prepared with-
out delay.

TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

THE CAMBERWELL FRIENDLY SOCIETY
OF CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

The above society held its anniversary supper on
Saturday evening, November Bth, at the Ship and
Blue-coat Boy,' Waiworth-road. Mr. Everst pre-
sided, and Mr. Hamlyn occupied the vice-chair.
After the cloth had been withdrawn, the Chairman
proposed Success and Prosperity to the Camberwell
Friendly Society of Carpenters,' coupling with it the
name of Mr. George Lake, one of ita oldest members,
and who, for many years, had filled the office of trea-
surer, but was now an employer' and for whom the
members had great respect. The Chairman proceeded
to say that their society had now been in existence
nearly thirty years, it baying been formed just before
the general Union in 1834. They had taken part in
nearly all the movements tending to benefit the trade
and ameliorate their condition. He hoped that they
Should continue to give their assistance to any move-
ment that had for its object the advancement of the
working classes.
Mr. Lake in acknowledging the kindness they had
shown in drinking his health, assured them that
although he was now a small employer be felt proud
in being a member of that society, and he should
always feel happy in promoting its interest.
The Chairman then proposed the health of Mr.
Potter, and prosperity to the Trade Societies of the
United Kingdom. He said that the presence of Mr.
Potter amongst them that evening was an additional
pleasure; for the members of that society had much
appreciated his services during the last few years in his
efforts to reduce their hours of labour. He hoped Mr.
Potter would long be spared to render further services
and ultimately those services would be rewarded.
Mr. Potter, in responding, kindly thanked the mem-
bers for their good wishes towards him, and assured
them that what he had done was solely with the view
to benefit his class and raise them morally, socially,
and intellectually. Mr. Potter then pointed out a few
of the reasons that hindared their progress, and pre-
vented them from obtaining those objects for which
they had struggled; and concluded by• urging the
members of that society to use their individual influ-
ence in furthering the progress of the BEEHIVE news-
paper, which was established for the purpose of
representing them in the press, and giving them the
Opportunity of expressing their opinions on social and
political subjects.
The Chairman then gave success to the BEEnrvE.
They held ten shares in it, and most of the members
had taken it from the first number. It was worthy of
their support, and he hoped that it would be a com-
plete success.
Mr. Hatnlyn responded to the toast, and proposed
the health of the Chairman, which he briefly acknow-
ledged; and the meeting, which was exceedingly in-
teresting, terminated.

articles.text:
THE TIN-PLATE WORKERS.

A special meeting of the members of the tin-plate
workers and gas meter makers' societies was held on
Wednesday evening, at the Sussex Hotel, Bouveric-
street, to consider the distressed condition of the Lan-
cashire tin-plate workers. Mr. T. Stowe was called to the
chair, and briefly explained the business the meeting
was convered for, after which

Mr. Dunn, of 'Manchester, Secretary to the Union
of all the Lancashire Societies, addressed the meeting,
when it was resolved that a voluntary subscription be
raised by the tin-plate workers of London weekly, to
be forwarded to Mr. Dunn's Committee, to be distri-
buted when most needed. The following Committee
of six was appointed to sit at the Bell Inn, Old Bailey,
every Saturday evening, from 8 to 10, to receive
subscriptions :—Messrs. Bawdon, Provo, Hurst, S.
Phillips, W. Thomas, and E. Corras.

articles.title: 3IETECLEY MINERS' COAL STRIKE.
articles.text:
3IETECLEY MINERS' COAL STRIKE.

If ever any cause could prove the necessity of union
among operative miners, that of Methley might be
cited. In 1858 the miners had no union, nor had they
been united for years, when the masters' association
gave notice of a reduction. The men then united,
struck, and after a terrible fight of six months, they
conquered, and having succeeded, they broke up their
temporarily formed union, and, against warning, they
earned good wages and spent them. About sia weeks
ago another alarm of reduction was sounded; and then
without provision or funds they struck again. Again
the Masters' Coal Association affirmed to the necessity
of Messrs. Briggs' change—Stating, however, it was not
a reduction to efficient' men. After a stand ef four
or five weeks we are glad, however, to report that the
matter was settled on the Bth by a compromise. The
old terms was 13d. per ton for getting large and small
coal. The proposed terms were 15d. for large, and 9d.
for small coal, the men to separate. This the men
refused to work for; but tonic at last the terms of 15d.
for large, and lid. for small, being a rise and fall of 2d.
per ton upon the several kinds. Thesmen say this is a
reduction; hut having no funds, it is better than
standing. Let the capitalist ask plenty, and half the
difference, and they succeed in a reduction in the end.
In the meantime labour, not united, thinks it does well
by halving the lowering. How long will they be thus
played with by capital A subscription of pence
weekly would save shillings, besides securing positive
certainty of peace and order. Against war, the best
security is being well armed and drilled; and against
the danger of a strike, a strong union is the surest
protection.
In connection with the above strike, Messrs. Briggs
served forty notices to quit on the men in occupa-
tion of cottages belonging to the firm. The occupants
refused to leave, and were summoned to the Wakefield
Court House to answer for their refusal. It turned
out the notices were not in the legal form, and there-
fore the summonses were dismissed.

articles.text:
AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF CAR-
PENTERS AND JOINERS.

TO THE EDITOR OF TILE DEMME.
SIR,—My attention has been drawn to an advertise-
ment in your journal calling upon the trade to support
J. Lea, as the general secretary of the above society.
Now, sir, as an officer of the society I am not aware
that any such prson as Mr. Lee exists as the secretary;
the general secretary of the society is Robert Apple-
garth. J. Lea certainly was general secretary, but
inasmuch as he committed himself in a base, mean,
end contemptible manner, and violated the rules in
every shape and form, the Executive Council dis-
missed him as unfit for the office. 'Tis true that he
clamoured aloud for a general council, and 'tis also
true that ten branches out of thirty-five supported him,
but some of the ten have joined since June last,—how
then can they judge of his abilities ? The rules say
that a member must be in the society two years before
he is eligible to sit at a general council ; but it mattered
not to J. Lea; the rules were as nothing to him; he
meant having a general council at all hazards; but,
Sir, the society knows well that in June last, J. Lea
ate very nigh the whole dust of the earth to be
re-elected, and I really think he would eat it
over again if we would have him. So I sup-
pose they will not wonder at this last act of
gross usurpation; but, sir, they, no doubt, do won -
be prevailed upon to come from afar to
der that men—intelligent rnen—could, by his cajolery
and chicanery,
presumption to dictate to a vast majority
sit at a 'mock general council,' and there have the
preposterous
of the society, and recommend a man as general secre-
tary who in daylight will shake you by the band, but
in darkness stab you in the back. I would, sir, invite
the trade to treat with contempt anything emanating
from the sapient committee of two of a mock general
council.

I hope, sir, you will find me a corner in your yell],
able journal, by so doing you will greatly oblige me
and a great number of your readers.
1 am, sir, yours respectfully,
BENJAMIN MUNDAY, Sec. No. 23 Branch.

This has been manifestly shown in 'A. J's.' letter, as he
refers to a job done by boiler makers not a hundred
yards from the Triton, which job he says cost £6 or
more per plate; the job referred to is the caisson at the
entrance of the dock, it being repaired by boilermakers.
Now, the man that did the work with two labourers
cut out four old plates and put in four new ones (with
the exception of rivetting) in six days; it would take
any six shipwrights twelve days to accomplish the
same amount of work. He also mentions the Princess
Alice, steam-tender, requiring an • alteration at the
bow; but it is not convenient for him to let the public
know that the shipwrights were attempting to repair
her in the dry dock for two months previous to the
'boilermakers going on her; and when they called her
finished she was taken out of dock and placed down by
the admiral's yacht, but not to remain there long, as she
biked so nauell they were obliged to bring her back and
dock again. Then application was made to the master
smith to send some of his men to stop the leakages;
and he went to one man and told him to go on board
and see what he could do by it, and the man told him
that he would, if the shipwrights were kept from the
job; but if they had anything to do with it, be would
not. So the report was made to the admiral, and he
decided that the shipwrights we not to go near her,
but that the dockyard smiths were to:repair the imper-
fections of the shipwrighta ; and during the time the
smiths were at work a foreman of shipwrights eame by
and told the smith that he was to be sure and use
plenty of red lead, as it was impossible to make it
water-tight without it; and the reply the smith made
was, that he was not a boilermaker, but he knew they
did not use red lead. So the smiths did what the
shipwrights attempted to do, and the boilermakers put
a new stern to her, which A. J.' says they were a
fortnight about; but to correct him, as it is excusable,
they were only nine days and a quarter—a job the
shipwrights were not capable a performing at all.
Nov. 12, 1862. F. B.

articles.title: TO THE EDITOR OF InME BEEHITE.
articles.text:
TO THE EDITOR OF InME BEEHITE.

SIR—As several letters have appeared in the BEE-
HIVE respecting the dispute in the Ship Building Trade,
nearly all of which are upon ,:xie side of the question,
I have felt somewhat surprised that they have met with
no reply (with one exception) from the other side; and
as it is difficult for your readers to form a correct
opinion by looking at one side of the question, 1, out of
no to the iron ship builders, but in the spirit
of impartiality and fair play, beg to make a few remarks
on the letter of your correspondent, J. 37, with re-
spect to the dispute in Messrs. Wigram's yard, Black.
wall. In the first place, 'J. J.' states, Messrs. Wigram
finding themselves defeated have contracted with
Messrs. Westwood and Co., to do that part of the
work for them the wooden ship builders are not capa-
ble of doing. So far from being defeated Messrs.
Wigram appear to be perfectly satisfied with the
wooden ship builders, both vritk regard to the quan-
tity and quality of their work, and J. J.' has omitted
to state that Messrs. Wigram have not the facility for
making the keel of so large a ship as he alludes to, for
that is the part that Messrs Westwood and Co. will do.
He has also omitted to state that Messrs. Wigram
adopted the same course when the iron ship builders
worked in the yard, as in the case of the steam ship,
Ripon.
In the next place, J. J.' ctates that the wooden
ship-builders cannot build an iron ship by themselves,
but require the assistance of the smiths. Can the iron
ship-builders build a ship by themselves? do not they
require the assistance of both shipwrights and smiths?
What the wooden ship-builders said they could do,
they certainly have done; and who can blame a elms
of men, when they see their trade decreasing, and their
numbers increasing, for taking employment at a trade
that they say is easily mastered, and highly remunera-
tive. I certainly coincide with the remark you made;
some time since, that it is a great pity that they cannot
come to some amicable arrangement, as nothing has ;
ever appeared more destructive to the interests of the
working class than dissensions among themselves.
Poplar, Nov. 10. J. J.

of the prosperity which now characterises the flax and

articles.title: CORRESPONDENCE
articles.text:
CORRESPONDENCE

THE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

SIR, —As Chairman of the Birmingham Working
Men's Committee, which is now engaged in raising
funds in aid of the distressed operatives of Lancashire,
I have to solicit a small portion of your space for the
purpose of replying to the strictures which appeared in
your paper of Saturday last. A Mr. Peacock there
states that, upon inquiries made, it is discovered that
the Birmingham Working Men's Committee is merely
a sham to decoy the working classes into subscribing
towards the Mayor's fund, which is sent to the Man-
chester Central.' The writer then adds that he hopes
the working men of Birmingham will not submit to
such mode of treatment, but resent it in a becoming
spirit, &c.'
I have not, in turn made any inquiries' respecting
Mr. Peacock, but I find in his letter quite sufficient evi-
dence to prove that he is utterly wanting in the art of
using proper language, whatever other good qualitiss
be may possess. With respect to our committee, I beg to
inform your readers that it consists exclusively of working
men, that it is receivingcontributions from work- people
of about 170 different houses, that it has already raised
about £9OO, that it is at present collecting about £l5O
a week, that several of the houses are pledged ulti-
mately to subscribe their £25, £lO, £5O, and £6O, that
the Committee decide all questions without interference
of the Mayor or any other gentleman, and that the
present prospect is of our raising at ieast £2,000. As
all our efforts and our contributions are made with the
view of helping our fellow workmen of Lancashire,
with considerable sacrifice to ourselves, both of time
and money, I think the facts here stated ought to he
held as testifying rather strongly in our favour,
whatever Mr. Peacock or any other person may say
to the contrary. Moreover, I will add, that it is any-
thing but creditable to Mr. Peacock that he seeks to
throw the apple of discord among a body of men who
are with excellent unanimity of purpose doing their
best to carry out succeesfully a great work of charity.
As to the disposal of our funds, all I have to say is,
they go to augment the general collecticn which is
being made by the people of Birmingham.

This colleCtion ilovi amounts to— about £7,000, in
addition to sums reaching in the aggregate about
£l,OOO more, separately raised by the ladies, the
Wesleyans and the Foresters. As the gentlemen who
have the direction of this generous subscription have
affirmed their sympathy for the cotton operatives by
themselves contributing their fifties, their hundreds,
and their two hundreds of pounds, and as they are
moreover towlsmen in whose honour and virtue we
can implicity trust, I confidently submit that in unit-
ing with them, we have formed a union which is of
value in aiding the efforts of both, and which is best
calculated to ensure a right mode of distribution for
the funds which we may succeed in raising. I may
add, in conclusion, that our committee is formed of one
member from the worltpeople of every subscribing
house, that it meets publicly every week, and that ita
proceedings are regularly reported in the local press,
so that it is by no means a small conclave or one that
exercises any power except such as it derives from the
general voice of workpeople of Birmingham.
I am, Sir, your obedient servant._

HENRY BrsEror,
Chairman of the Birmingham Working Men's Corn
mittee of the Cotton District Relief Fund.

Birmingham, 12 November, 1862.

CABMEN AND MAGISTERIAL INJUSTICE.

articles.title: THB EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE,
articles.text:
THB EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE,

SIR,—It is now becoming a recognised fact that
neither hackney carriage proprietors nor drivers re-
ceive that consideration or justice at police courts to
which they, in common with all other classes of the
community, are entitled. I wish to call your attention
to a case in which I was concerned as complainant re-
cently before Lord Mayor Cubitt at the Mansion
House. I obtained a summons against a carman in
the employ of Mr. Prescott, of King's Head-yard,
Borough, for using language of an abusive and dis-
gusting character to me in the hearing of three ladies,
whom I was driving in my cab over London Bridge to
the station. When the case was called on, the defen-
dant appeared, but said he had been wrongly sum-
moned, as he was not the driver of the van alleged to
have used the bad language. He was dressed in black,
and held a handkerchief partly up to his face. When
asked by the Lord Mayor whether I could identify
him, I at first hesitated, as be looked very different to
when in his usual .gurb. The case was dismissed.
On closer examination of the man I said I was pre-
pared to swear he was the man; but the Mayor would
not further entertain the case, or grant me another
summons unless I had a witness to prove he was the
man. The magiArate further said: Although the
name might be wrong, we cannot compel a master of
cart, van, or waggon to produce his driver hero; but
if it was a cab or omnibus case, we could compel the
roaster to produce the driver or conductor. Now,
Sir, is not this a piece of monstrous injustice ? And
does not such an observation, coming from the lips of
the highest magistrate in London, prove a case for
Legislative interference? Why, Si; should a man
paying a large duty to Government be badged and
fettered, whilst those careless, reckless drivers and
their boys—bullies I may honestly term them—
insult with impunity those who come in proximity
with them, accidentally or otherwise? I was
thus at the loss of my costs and time, as cabmen
generally are, whether they are complainants or are
proved to have been unlawfully and wrongfully sum-
moned. I tender my thanks, and those of cabmen
generally, to the REM-LIVE, for the manner in which
it has supported us in our late movement to obtain
redress, and trust we shall, if we have not already
proved to our fellow labourers in union amongst other
trades, that we are, us a body, reasonable and intel-
ligent men; men, not the indomitable beasts' that
the editor of Lloyd's paper said we were. There are
plenty of men in our ranks better men, in every sense,
than the proprietor of that journal—the Lumley case,
to wit. Congratulating myself, and workmen gene-
rally, that they have such an organ as the BEEHIVE,

J. T. GOODWIN, a Shareholder and Subscriber.
15, Sidney-street, Mile-end East.

articles.text:
ODDFELLOWS (MANCHESTER UNITY).

Slumps. The twenty-third anniversary of the
Loyal British Flag Lodge was celebrated on Monday
evening, by a public supper in the New Oddfellows'
Hall, Rudyerd-street, North Shields, at which about
eighty of the members and their friends sat down. Dr.
J. P. Bates (surgeon to the lodge) occupied the chair;
and Mr. G. P. Hall the vice-chair. On the removal of
the cloth, the Chairman gave the usual loyal and
patriotic toasts, after which short addresses were deli-
vered, interspersed by numerous songs and recitations.
This anniversary has been the most successful which
this prosperous lodge has held.

articles.title: DRUIDS.
articles.text:
DRUIDS.

HULL.—The members of the Rose of Kingston Lodge
celebrated their third anniversary on Wednesday, at the
Three Crowns, Groves, when fifty-six sat down to an
excellent supper provided by Mr. Stephenson, the
host. After the repast the chairman gave the loyal
toasts, when the secretary read the report, which stated
that since November, 1860, when the lodge opened with
only 20 members, the number has increased to 53, and
six on the list for initiation. The benefits paid to the
sick members during that period wag £3O and the lodge
fund at the present time amounted to £59. The health
of the district officers and board of directors was also
given, to which D. V. P. Thomas Bygott responded,
dwelling upon the unusual rapid SUCCCBEI of the of the
Hull district, and the efficient management of the
order by the board in London, recommending the
U. A. 0. D. as a first-class order, securing those benefits
which every working man should in prudence seek to
ensure.

articles.text:
LAW INTELLIGENC

COURT OF COMMON PLEAS.

SABEY V. STEPHENS.

Mr. Serjeant Parry moved for a rule nisi for a new
trial, on the ground that the verdict was against. the
weight of evidence, and also on the ground of miscon-
duct on the part of a juryman. Mr. Justice Blackburn
said he thought the learned serjeant would have some
difficulty in inducing the Court to think the verdict
was against evidence. He tried the first action, when
the jury were discharged without giving a verdict;
and he agreed with Mr. Justice Crompton, who
tried it last week, that the verdict which was for
the defendant was a right one. Mr. Serjea.nt Parry
urged strongly that there was negligence on the
part of the defendant in the construction of the swing-
ing scaffold in St. Martin's Hall, where the plaintiff's
son lost his life, and then referred to the conduct of
the foreman of the jury, who had sent the defendant a
letter asking for compensation in the name of the jury.
The juryman's name was known, for he had written
the demand on one of his printed circulars, which
stated he was a carman, &e. It was probable that he
had made up his mind to give a verdict for the defendant,
thinking he should gain afterwards by being employed
by the defendant. The letter was as follows : 'Dear
sir, please send me 10s. of postage stamps, and I will
acknowledge the same on behalf of the j:zry. Respect-
fully yours, the Foreman of the Jury.' The letter was
received the day after the trial. The Court ruled there
were no grounds for them to intefere. Thera was no
arrangement between the parties before the trial or any
application for renumeration made. The juryman's
conduct was very reprehensible. Rule refnsed.

COURT OF EXCHEQUER.
(Before Mr. Baron Martin and a Common Jury.)
HOLMES V. FALCONEE.-ACCIDENT.

This was an action brought by the plaintiff; an
omnibus conductor in the employ of the London
General Omnibus Company, against the defendant, the
proprietor of the Lyceum Theatre, to recover damages
for injuries sustained through the alleged negligence
of the defendant's servants. The defendant pleaded
'Not guilty.' It appeared from the evidence of the
pinintiff that about eleven o'clock on May 14th last an
omnibus pulled up on the near side of the road
nearly opposite the Adelphi Theatre. He was talking
to a passenger inside, when the defendant's coachman,
who was driving a brougham and pair, drove so cr.re-
lessly, it was alleged, that he ran the pole against the
plaintiff's knee and severely injured it. Ho was taken
to the hospital, and, after having his knee dressed,
went home, and was confined to his house for four
months, and was at the present time unable to perform
his duties. The defence was that the driver of the
plaintiff's omnibus pulled up too rapidly and without
any warnin4, in consequence of which the pole struck
the plaintiff's leg and caused the injury complained of.
It was alleged, on the defence, that the negligence
was on the part of the plaintiff in not giving a warn-
ing, and not on the defendant's coachman. The jury
returned a verdict for the plaintiff; damages, £5O.

SHERIFFS' COURT.

(Before Mr. Kerr.)

I.IACKINTOSH V. REEB.—THE FAMILY LIFE Assn-
' RA.NCE SOCIETY AGAIN—LAWORTANT DECISION.—This
was an action to recover for printing 3,000 policies,
plaintiff being a printer. Plaintiff's clerk put in an
order headed Family Life Assurance Society,' of
which the notorious J. H. Stratton was secretary, and
signed hy the chairman and defendant, who was then
one of the committee. Mr. Buchanan urged for de-
fendant that his client could not be held liable, but
that plaintiff must sue the secretary or registered officer
of the eompany.—His Honour remarked that defendant
had signed the order as a director of the Family
Life Assurance Company, but defendant handed up
a book of the rules, from which it appeared that
the society was entitled The Family Friendly
Society,' and in a second book there was a third name.
His Honour: It appears to me that Mr. Mackintosh
gave credit to the uirectors of the Family Life As-
surance Society.—Mr. Buchanan: Perhaps plaintiff
will tell us how the policies were headed?—Plaintiff's
Clerk: The Family Sick Fund Fziendly
Defendant: It is not a corporation, nor is it a joint-
stock affair. I haoe ceased to be a director, and if
plaintiff sues the registered officer he will be paid, as
there is plenty of money. Mr. Tidd Pratt says I am
not liable.—His Honour: The plaintiff sues you as
the director of the Family Life Assurance Company,
and in that form I am of opinion that he is entitled to
recover, but the defendant has-his remedy against the
society.—Verdict for the plaintiff, and costs.

On Tuesday, William Pike, a painter, ot 16; Bol-
sover-street, was brought up, on remand, before Mr.
Tyr whitt, charged with embezzling £l6 12s. Bd.,
monies belonging to the Amalgamated Association of
Operative House Painters, of which he was late secre-
tary.
Mr. Eaden, 10, Gray's-in-square, appeared for the
prosecution; Mr. Lewis, Marlborough-street, defended
the prisoner.
Christopher Clinch said: I am Secretary to -the
Brighton Branch of the Association. On the 7th of
last April, I sent a Poet-office Order, for £3 12s. id.,
to the prisoner, as the general secretary of the associ-
ation. It was made payable to him at the Tottenham-
court-road Money-order Office, and for which he never
sent me a receipt.
William Chinnery said: I was Secretary to the
Kingston Branch of the association in April last. On
the 2nd .of that month I sent a Post-office Order for ;
Bs. Bd. to the prisoner, as general secretary to the asso-
ciation. It was made payable to him at the Maryle- ,
bone-street Money-order Office. I never received an
acknowledgement for the sum from the prisoner.
I Thomas Griffin Eliman said: lam a clerk in the
Money-order Office at the General Post-office. I pro-
duce a Post-office Order for £3 12s. Id., drawn by C.
Clinch, and pay able to William Pike, atthe Tottenham-
court-road Office. It has been paid to the signature of
Wm. Pike. I also produce another Order, drawn by
Wm. Chinney, for Bs. Bd., and payable to Wm. Pike,
at the Marylebone-street Office. It has been paid to
the signature of Wm. Pike.
Robert Shaw said: I am general secretary to the
association. I know the prisoner's handwriting. The
Orders before me are signed in the prisoner's hand-
writing. It is the secretary's duty to enter all monies
received and expended in the cash ledger. The sum
sent by Post-office Orders from Kingston and Brighton
are not entered in that ledger. The prisoner absconded
on the Bth of April last. A committee was appointed
to examine his books. They delivered their reportnn
the 20th of April. The prisoner was present at that
time. I asked him if he had received the sums
mentioned, and appropriated them to his own use. He
said he had, being much pressed at the time. He was
asked to produce a statement of the sums received and
expended during the two last months he was in office.
The statement in my hand was written by the
prisoner. In it he charges himself with having appro-
priated £l6 12s. Bd.
George Carter said: I was treasurer to the associa-
tion up to June last. The sum of £8 6s. id. entered
in the book handed to me I never received, or I should
have signed for it, in the same way as I have done for
every other sum entered in the book.
Mr. Lewis, who had cross-examined the two last
witnesses, said: If your worship considers this a case
of embezzlement, you will send it for trial, so I will
not run the risk of prejudging the prisoner's case at
present.
Mr. Tyrwhitt then committed the prisoner for trial.

husband, and did some work for her living. On the
previous evening she was proceeding along High-
street, Camden-town, when prisoner and another
gentleman passed her, the former making some remark,
of which she took no notice, and went on. They
followed her, and prisoner asked her to have some
refreshment. As they pressed her very hard, she went
into the Southampton Arms, and had some brandy and
water, afterwards asking her to go to the 'Oxford.'
She said she should like to go much. They then
proceeded there in an omnibus and .remained till half-
past eleven, and on their coming out prisoner
requested her to go with him to a house in Seymour-
street. As she had to be home by twelve o'clock,
she objected, when they got into a cab, and after going
a short distance she missed her gold watch. She spoke
to prisoner about her loss, when he exclaimed, with an
oath, 'What do you mean.' The cab was stopped and
she gave prisoner in charge. In reply to Mr. Yardley
prosecutrix said she did not miss the watch till she was
in the cab. Her chain was broken. Cook, 250 S, said
the female was under the influence of liquor. She had
no idea that it was gone, neither did she see prisoner
take the watch. Prisoner, in his defence, said he had
come from Eastbourne on Saturday last, and had been
dining out with a friend named Allen. After they had
dined they strolled together and saw the female leave
an elderly gentleman. He asked her where she was
going, and after some little talk they had some drink.
It was his own foolishness got him into the present
mess, and he certainly did make use of the remark as
the female had stated because he was so indignant at
such a charge being made against him. Mr. Yardley
discharged the prisoner, observing that he had himself
to thank for the position in which he now stood by his
indiscretion in going about with strangers.

articles.title: SOUTHWARK
articles.text:
SOUTHWARK

BIGAXY.—George Barber Bayfield, a respectable-
looking man, was brought up for final examination,
charged with intermarrying with Sophia Burges, his
former wife being then and now living. It will be
remembered that prisoner was given into custody by
his second wife, and did not deny the charge. Addi-
tional evidence of the first marriage having now been
given, prisoner' who reserved his defence, was com-
mitted for trial.

articles.title: DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.
articles.text:
DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.

On Tuesday morning, about half-past two o'clock, an
alarming fire broke out in the premises of Mr. Knowles,
chemist, 319, Caledonian-road, near Huntington-
street. From the nature of the combustibles, the flames
spread with extraordinary rapidity. The fire escapes
and engines were soon on the spot, and by the well-
directed efforts of the brigade the property on either
side was saved, but the house and its contents were
totally destroyed. Shortly before five o'clock on
Tuesday morning, a fire broke out on the premises of
Mr. John Beyhie, licensed victualler and hotel pro-
prietor, 19, Park-street, Grosvenor-square. Plenty of
water having been obtained the fire was happily con-
fined to the first and second floors, and slight damage
to the bar.—Another fire, but not of a serious nature,
took place in the premises of Mr. J. Lewis, in Martin.
street, Webber-street, Lambeth, caused by a spark
flying from a lighted candle amongst some bedding.—
Late on Monday night a fire took place on the premises
of Mr. Dean, hosier and outfitter, 135, High-street,
Camden. Town, which did not succumb to the efforts of
the fire brigade until the house was completely gutted,
the stock and furniture consumed, and the premises of
Mr. Gordon, a tobacconist, much damaged. The
C4llBO of the disaster is attributed to an escape of gas.
On Thursday morning, about two o'clock, a fire
broke out on the manufacturing premises belonging to
Mr. D. Selig, cabinet maker, &c., St. John-street-road,
Clerkenwell. The following is the official report
No. 136, St. John-street, St. John's-street-road, Mr.
Selig, cabinetmaker, factory burned out, stock in open
yard destroyed, front house used as dwelling (com-
municating) seriously damaged by fire, &c.; cause of
fire unknown; contents insured. No. 124, Mr. E. G.
Sloane, watch spring maker, back front of building
severely damaged by fire, and contents by water;
contents and building insured. No. 123, Mr. T. C.
Blundell, rope and mat maker, the premises damaged
by fire, and roof of shop injured by breakage; building
and contents insured. Another fire broke out about
the same time on the premises belonging to Mr. W.
Bond, a stationer, Cross-street, Upper-street, Islington.
The fire was happily confined to the lower part of the
building, but the whole of the stock, fixtures, and other
effects are nearly destroyed. Insured.

THE LOCOMOTIVE EXPLOSION AT PADDINGTON RAIL-
WAY TEimuNts.—On Tuesday afternoon, Dr. Lankester
opened an inquiry at the Royal Saxon Tavern, Alfred-
road, Paddington, into the circumstances of the explo-
sion of the le...)motive Ptrseus, on Saturday last, at the
depot of the Great Western Railway, at Paddington,
by which three men, namely, James Wilson, aged 18;
John Eldred, 20; and Christopher Thompson, 23, lost
their lives. The court was adjourned after the jury
had viewed the premises and bodies of the deceased.
PROROGLCION OF PARLIAMENT.—At 1100 n on Thurs-
day the Lord Chancellor, accompanied by the Royal
Commissioners, attended at the House of Lords, and
the gentlereen of the House of Commons having been
summoned, were represented at the bar by the clerks
of the House. The Lord Chancellor then read the
Royal Commission, and formally prorogued Parlia-
ment until the 13th January. The Legislature is not
expected to assemble for the dispatch of business before
the first week in February.
DEATH BY •Gmtorriso.—lnformation was received on
Wednesday by the police, of the death of Mr. Cort, one
of the collectors of the Crystal Palace Gas Company,
from the effects of injuries to his throat, inflicted by
three men, who garotted ,and robligl him a few days
since in Whitechapel.
STATUE OF THE LATE JOHN FIELDEN, M.P.—A meet-
ing of the committee formed at Todmorden to erect a
statue in that town of John Fielden, late M.P. for Old-
ham, took place on Wednesday evening. Mr. Foley,
LA., the sculptor, was present, and submitted a model
of the statue for approval. The statue respresents Mr.
Fielden in a characteristic attitude, when addressing a
ten hours' meeting. He stands with his left leg thrown
slightly forward, his right hand in the arm-hole of his
waistcoat, and his left on a copy of the ten hours' bill,
which lies on a pedestal by his side.
TEE LATE LORD MAYOR.—Mr. W. Cubitt has inti-
mated to the members of the Common Council of Lang-
bourn Ward his intention of resigning his aldermanic
gown. This announcement on the part of the late Lord
Mayor has taken the ward somewhat by surprise;
several names have, however, been mentioned to fill
the vacancy, and amongst them those of Mr. Cockerell,
Mr. T wentyman, and Mr. Lusk.
MURDER. AT COSELEY.—On the 10th a man named
Henry Swinnerton, a puddler, residing in Coseley, aged
33, died in consequence of injtuies received in an assault
on him on the 4th inst. On that day Sedgeley wake
was being held, and at night the deceased left his wife
and family to go drinking. On returning home quite
drunk he was waylayed and frightfully used by some
ruffians. They attacked him on the Blue Button-bridge
on his way to Ladymoor, first of all throwing him into a
hedge; they then fetched him out, battered' his head
with life-preservers and sticks, kicking him, and gasping
his throat to strangle him at the same time. They ab-
stracted some coins amounting to 12s. from his pockets,
and threatened to throw him into the canal, and were in
the act of doing so when a voice was heard, and they
ran away. On Saturday, when told that he could not
live, deceased stated that he had been at a brothel at the
wake, and on Saturday evening he recognised two men
whom the police had apprehended as his assailants, viz.:
Jesse Watts, 28, and Wm. Henshaw, a brothel-house
keeper, both of Bilston. He related, as best as he could,
by articulations and signs, what they did, and the ruffians
did not answer a word. Swinnerton, after passing an
awful time of it, during which time ministers and others
prayed by him, died abo_ut3 o'clock on Monday in such
a.dreadful frenzy that it took a number of men to hold
him down.
