THE EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE
AGAINST A SOLICITOR.

Tuesday being the day appointed for the examination
of Mr. Whitehurst, on the charge made by Mr. Rogers,
much curiosity was exhibited, and numbers of persons
attended at Bow-street to hear the proceedings.
Mr. Sleigh appeared for the prosecution; and Mr.
George Lewis, jun., of Ely-place, for the defence.
Mr. Sleigh said it was with great pain that he
appeared to press this charge against the prisoner, who
had hitherto been regarded as a respectable member of
society and of the profession to which he belonged.
This was a painful duty both for the counsel and the
magistrate. He should call two more witnesses, and
complete this terribly disgusting and fifthy case.
Sergeant Birch, of the B division: On the 23rd tilt.
I went to Hyde-park, and. there met Mr. Holden.
That was where I saw Malcolm for the first time in
the Green-park, near Hyde-park-corner. We saw Mr.
Rogers in Piccadily, and saw him go away with Mal-
colm. I went with Mr. Holden to the top of Con-
stitution-hill, and there parted. A few minutts after-
wards, after 6 o'clock, I saw the prisoner pass Mr.
Rogers several times, walking to and fro, and then
speak to him. They walked away together very
slowly. They came down Constitution-hill very
slowly towards me. I stepped down the passage lead-
ing to Grovernor-place, and they passed and returned..
I saw them standing near a place where there were.
some bushes. I passed them and repassed them and
saw Mr. Rogers holding a letter in his hand and
showing it to Mr. Whitehurst. I heard them.
speaking but did not hear what they said. I then.
saw them proceed towards the arch. I followed close.
behind. When they got outside the park under the
lamp I saw Mr. Whitehurst with a book in his hand
writing something. I have seen it since in court—a
small book. He gave it back to Mr. Rogers. They.
then walked to the top of Grosvenor-place. I followed.
them. They turned round and met me. They stopped
close by. I walked up to them. Mr. Rogers said,
Oh, this is the gentleman.' I said, Is this the.
gentleman, Mr. Rogers, that has written the letters to
you?' He said, Yes.' The defendant heard that.
I said, I am a police-sergeant, and I shall take you.
into custody for soliciting and inciting Mr. Rogers to
commit an unnatural offence.' He did not make any
reply or observation. He never said a word. I told
him I should take him to the police-station. When I.
get him about thirty yards, he said, Oh, will you let
me go if I 4ve you my address in the City, and I will
appear at the police-court in the morning?' I said,
Certainly not.' Further down Constitution-hill
met the inspector, and told him the charge and the
defendant made no observation. I suspected where
Malcolm was, but did not exactly know.

Inspector holden, B division—On last Monday,
about six o'clock in the evening, accompanied by Ser-
geant Birch, I went to Constitution-hill. After
waiting a little while there I saw the prosecutor and
the prisoner at the bar come arm in arm together to-
wards some bushes, I saw them stop together. I.
passed on, and went further down, leaving Birch at a
certain place. Some little while after I returned on
the opposite side, being the same side as the two
parties were standing, and I met the prisoner and.
Birch together, the prosecutor following them. Birch.,
said, Oh, here is the inspector. I have got this per-
son in charge.' 1 said to Birch, What for?' He
said, 'For soliciting and inciting this gentleman,'
pointing to the prosecutor behind, to commit an.
unnatural offence.' The prisoner then said, 'lt is a
bailable case; will you take bail for me?' I said, I
have no power here; speak to the officer on duty at
the station we shall take you to?' The prisoner said,
What station am I going to?' I Baid, king-street,,,
Gardner's-lane ? Birch said, 'We will go through
the park, over the suspension-bridge.' The prisoner
said, We can't get that way—it is too late—the gates
are.closed: Su we went round Birdcage-walk.
Mr. Sleigh applied for the committal of the defend-
ant. ,

Mr. Lewis said it was now time to offer an explana- .
tion which he thought would satisfy the magistrate
that the case might end here. Mr. Lewis then entered
into a long statement, to the effect that defendant had
only acted with a Niew to discover whether the impu-
tations which had been made against Mr. Rogers were
well founded. Rogers was at the appointment for the
purpose of catching Whitehurst, and Whitehurst for
the purpose of catching Rogers. He could produce
many witnesses now present, members of parliament,
clergymen, and persons of high standing, to prove his
high moral character. He could also offer some evi-
dence of facts, but if the case was to be sent for trial
he would reserve that.

After some conversation an adjournment for further
evidence was agreed on, the prisoner being admitted.
to bail, in the same amount as before.

BA.RBA.ROUS MURDER IN VALES..

Circumstances have come to light which prove that
an atrocious and cold-blooded murder has been com-
mitted in one of the mining districts in the Rhendda
Valley. On Sunday, the 2nd inst., a young woman,
named Jane Lewis, aged 23, a servant at Tyntily,
parish of Ystradyfodwg, left her master's house about
six o'clock in the evening, for the purpose of going to
chapel. As she had not returned at a late hour the
inmates of the house became uneasy, and proceeded
to make a search for her. They had not proceeded far
from the house when they were horror struck at find-
ing the body of the young woman lying across a foot-
path in an adjoining wood, with her throat cut from
ear to ear. A razor covered with blood was found
near the body, and it was at first conjectured that
the unfortunate woman had committed suicide.
It was subsequently, however, ascertained that the
razor was the property of a fellow servant, named
Thomas Edmonds, and he was apprended on the charge
of murder. A coroner's inquest was opened on the
4th inst., at the Star Inn, Tyntily, and after a pre-
liminary inquiry was adjourned till Tuesday last. As
might naturally be expected, the event gave rise to all
manner of reports, and on the meeting of the jury on
Tuesday morning, the utmost anxiety was manifested
by the mining population in the proceedings. It ap-
peared from the evidence of Thomas Williams and his
wife (the master and mistress of the deceased), that she
left the house about half-past 5 o'clock in the evening
of the fatal day, with the intention of going to chapel,
and that the prisoner left the house about the same
time for a similar purpose. Mr. Williams had been
out during the afternoon, and on his return about
eight o'clock, he told his wife that he had been to
chapel, but bad not seen the deceased present. Soon
atter eight the prisoner returned home, and about
ten o'clock the family went to bed. Before this,
however, a young man named Thomas Williams, the
reputed sweetheart of deceased called at the house
and asked for her. He was told that she had gone
to chapel, and had not then returned. He re-
marked that lie had been to chapel but had not seen
her there, and in a jocular manner said, as he left the
house, that he supposed she had gone away with an-
other sweetheart. About eleven o'clock, the mistress,
finding that the servant had not returned, called up
her husband, and asked him to go out and look for her.
He rose, and called the prisoner to accompany him.
They procured a lantern, and first searched the out-
houses' and then proceeded down a road leading
through a wood in the direction of the chapel. Just
as they entered the wood they discovered the body of
the unfortunate woman lying across the road, with her
throat cut in the most fearful manner, and her clothes
saturated with blood. At a little distance from the
body they found a razor covered with blood, her
bonnet, and the brooch of her shawl. She was then
quite deal and cold. The master proved that the
razor and case were similar to that which belonged to
the prisoner, and it was subsequently ascertained that
prisoner's razor was not to be found in the house. The
police constable who was first on the spot examined
the prisoner's hands and clothes, but there 'w ere no
marks of blood. There were, however, some scratches
or wounds in his face, which he accounted for by •
saying that he had been cut by the horn of one of the
calves while tying it up that afternoon.
Mr. Henry Norton Davies, surgeon, said he had
examined the deceased soon after she was found, and -
had subsequently made a post-mortem examination,
assisted by other medical gentlemen. He stated that
there were four distinct cuts in the throat, the wind-
pipe being completely severed. From the fearful
nature of these wounds, and also from their appearance
generally, he was positive that they could not have •
been committed by the deceased. Her hands were
also cut, and these cuts seemed to indicate that she had
resisted. The strings of her bonnet and her collar
were also found to have been cut by a sharp instru-
ment. On opening the body it was found that deceased
was about six weeks advanced in pregnancy. He also
stated that there was no evidence of any violation
having been attempted.
At this stage the inquiry was adjourned till Wed-
nesday, as there were a number of witnesses to be
examined.

AMERICA.

NEW YORX, Oct. 30.—The Washington Star says:—
it is believed that General Lee his divided his army
into two large eorps—one under Jackson, the other
under Longstreet,—and is leaving the region in which
he has been posted since recrossing the river into Vir-
ginia. It is thought that portions of Jackson's advance
have cressed the Blue Ridge by the Gap at Front Royal,
while there ia evidence that a force of 8,000 rebels, under
Walker, known to have been for two day's past at
Upperville, are the advanced guard of Langstreet's corps.
The rebel Generals expectea probably to make a suc-
cessful dash at General Siegel's corps at and around
Centreville, on their retreat towards Gordonsville;
hence the appearance there of the troops at the
points indicated above. The army of the Potomac
is promptly in motion to meet taese rebel move-
ments, and Generals Burnside and Fitzjohn Porter are
already so close on the heels of Longstreet's army that
he will probably retrace his steps towards Wichester
and seek to retreat down the valley rather than advance
further in this direction. It will not, therefore, be
surprising to hear of a consideralle bat,le in that quarter
at any moment. The whole Federal army, with the
exception of General Sumner's corps, which remains on
Bolivar Heights, may be said to be in motion. General
Burnside's movement in Virginia has been followed by
lie corps of Fitzjohn Porter, which is now in a position
sse operate, if necessary, in the same direction. General
M'Clellan's headquarters are at Berlin, immediately
on the Potomac. The rebel pickets have again ap-
peared opposite Sharpsburg and in front of' Charles-
town, their artillery and cavalry being visible from Bo-
livar Heights. The impression increases, however, that
the main body of the rebel army has already retreated,
and that no rebels will be found at Winchester. It is
pretty well known that a considerable force of rebels
has already crossed the mountains, through the Gap at
Front Royal, and it is believed that a still larger force
is passing southwards on the other side of the moun-
tains. The forces which have been found in the vici-
nity of Snicker's Gap and Upperville are probably
watching against an attack on the flank of the main
army, 2,3 it stretched towards Gordonsville. Unless Lee's
retreat is much further advanced than is probable or
possible, it would seem that General M'Clellan has the
power by a vigorous forward movement, aided by a
similar advance from Washington, to force Lee to stop
and fight before he gains Gordonsville.
The ltieto York Times' correspondent withll'Clellan's
army still continues to assert that the generals sur-
rounding M'Clellan consider an advance on the rebels
at Gordonsville and Richmond is full or peril, and
believe that an approach by the south side of the James
River is the only and true route to Richmond, and
that if the matter was left to M'Clellan's own judgment
he would ship the whole army back to the peninsula.
The Federal General Grant officially reports further
successes against the guerillas in the different parts of
Missouri.

General Sherman has issued stringent orders for the
government of Memphis. A military commission sits
daily to try offenders under the laws of war. Vagrants
and other direputable characters are organised into
gangs and set to work in the trenches or on the streets.
Citizens are to keep indoors between tattoo and reveille,
unless attending church, places of amusement, or neces-
sary business. After midnight all persons, except guards,
must be in their houses. Assemblages of negroes are
forbidden, except by permission of the Provost-Mar-
shal.

General Buell has ordered that all persons who have
actively aided rebellion in Kentucky within the last
three months shall be arrested and sent out of Kentucky,
and forbidden to return.

The writ of habeas corpus in the case of Mr. W. H.
Winder, who is confined in Fort Warren, issued by
Judge Clifford, of the United States Circuit Court, has
not been served, because Colonel Dimmick, Commander
of Fort Warren, has refused a pass to the fort.
A large naval and military expedition is being fitted
out for Texas. The expedition is to be commanded by
General Banks.

The Republican and Democratic parties are making
most vigorous efforts throughout the state of New York
to carry the elections. Both parties are nightly holding
meetings throughout the country. The contest is very
bitter on both sides, and it is supposed the result of tbe
election_ will be very close.

President Lincoln is busily engaged on his Message to
Congress. _ _

A—commislsion has been ordered to assemble at Wash-
ington to report upon the plan of the present forts
around Washington, and upon the sufficiency of the
present defences of the capital.
The Federals have destroyed the extensive steam salt-
works erected by the Confederates at St. Joseph's Bay,
Florida. Georgia and Florida relied upon these works
for the soppy 0:1. salt for the winter's provisions for th,ir
troops.

Tile British steamer Wachuta has been captured by
the Federal gunboat Memphis. She was captured,
after a full day's chase, off the coast of North Carolina.
She threw overboard the greater portion of her cargo,
and so- strained her engines as to be unable to make
steam.

The Rickmond Despatch says:—
'The fight at Pocataligo resulted in a complete vic-
tory. Our loss is 15 killed and 40 wounded. The
enemy's total loss is not less than 200 killed and
wounded. The enemy's force consisted of six regi-
ments, with one field battery and two boats' howitzers.'
Her Majesty's steamers Cadmus and Racer sailed
from Fortress Monroe on the 28th, to be absent two
weeks on a cruise. The steamer Vanderbilt has re-
ceived her armament, and will leave New York in a few
days.

EVENING.—The whole army of the Potomac is in
motion towards Virginia. The accounts of the position
of the Confederate army in Virginia are conflicting. No-
thing positively definite appears to be known. The
correspondents of the Northern journals report that the
Federal forces were landed from 15 transports and gun.
boats at Mackey's Point, for an attack on the Charles-
ton and Savannah Railroad. The Federals proceeded
nine miles inland, driving the Confederates from three
positions; they were then reinforced from Charleston,
and the Federals retreated. The Federal loss was very
heavy. The committee, composed of the best Union
Men in Baltimore, which was appointed to report on
the charges of official disloyalty and corruption, has
been brokest up by General Wool, and its members have
been arrested. The Governor of Maryland has gone
to Washington to demand the release of the members.
The arrest has caused much excitement. The steamers
Tnbal Cain and Ann have been condemned.

Yrs. Eliza Gurney, widow of the late John J.
Gurney, had an interview with President Lincoln on
the 27th:—

'Site ,assured him at same length of the sympathy
which the Friends on both sides of the Atlantic felt in
him, and of the pryers which they offered up on his
behalf, and clesed her remarks with an earnest appeal
to him to trust in Divine power. The President was
sensibly effected, and replied in few but fit words, to the
effect that in the unhappy events amid his lot was east
he acknowledged the Divine hand, as controlling all
things, and considered himself only as an humble instru-
ment to work out the designs of Providence, being sure
that, whatever might happen, He who made the world
still governed it.'
Regarding the want of discipline among the Fe,derel
farces we have the following :
Too much laxity prevails with regard to soldiers
leaving their regimental camps and wandering beyond
the limits of their commands. Hereafter, not more than
two men of each company will be granted passes to
leave camps. Provost Guards will arrest all absentees
from camp without proper permits. The reports of
recent inspections exhibited a shameful neglect of duty
on the part of many officers of the higher as well as
lower grades in this army in those lesser details of disci-
pline, failure to attend diligently to which will produce
the demoralisation of any body of troops. Inspections
in many organisations are rarely made, drills are poorly
attended and unfrequent, cleanliness disregarded,
. .

the care of arms and ammunition but little attended
to, and the instruction of officers in tactics and
regulations almost entirely neglected. Brigade and
division drills in some cases are laid aside, and
the general orders published from time to time by
the War Department for the instruction and guidance
of the troops are not promulgated to the regiments and
batteries. The prompt distribution and promulgation
of orders is one of the first duties of Staff officers, and
commanding officers are responsible that Staff officers
are not neglectful in this respect. The Commanding
General is convinced that some examples of summary
dismissals of officers are necessary to insure atten
tion to this point of duty before the importance of
realised. He gives notice,
the subject will be fully
therefore, that any neglect in this respect of Staff or
Commanding Officers that comes to his notice will secure
his immediate recommendation for the summary dia-
xnissal of the delinquent.'
A duel had taken place at Charleston, in which Col.
W. R. Calhoun was shot dead by Afajor Alfred M. Rhett.
Thirty persons had been killed by a collision on the
Mississippi railway.

AN CORIGINAL SPECU-LATION.—A. letter from Naples
of the first inst., states that the Padre Pantaleo General
Garibaldi's chaplain, has been eng iged by an English
speculator, and was to leave Naples for London on
Monday last. Ile is to recount the life and campaigns
of General Garibaldi to an English audience. he
Padre accompanied General Garibaldi front Genoa to
Marsala, from Marsala to Palermo, Melazzo, Messina,
Reggio, throughout the Calabrias, and to the siege oi
Capua Re never quitted General Garibaldi during his
first campaign, and he followed his fortunes until after
the affair of Aspromonte.

THE PRINCE OF WALES'S BIRTH:

DAY.

On the 9th his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales
attained his majority, having been born on the 9th of
November, 1341. Such manifestations of public re-
joicing as would otherwise have been made while the
Court is still in mourning for the death of the Prince
Consort, wore prevented by the sacredness of the day.

articles.title: SINGULAR DISCOVER E
articles.text:
SINGULAR DISCOVER E

At Norton, in the East Riding, a system of public
drainage has just been placed in the streets. A few
weeks ago, the discovery of Roman remains on com-
mencing the works was recorded. The drainage, after
being taken along the course of the old Roman road
for a considerable distance, was eventually conducted
through a series of tertiary deposits of sand and gravel
as far as the completion of the first section of the
works, which is just finished. On passing the old road
a bed of peat was cut through, from which the section:,
of the sand and gravel beds rose at a considerable in-
cline to the highest point of the present surface. The
pipes themselves were deposited (by great exertion) in
a quicksand, the water literally boiling out' of it. In
ascending order there was first a loamy clay, above
which were layers of fines and without fossils, becoming
rougher and more gravelly as they ascended, till the
top deposit became rough gravel—in fact, waterworn
detritus of the chalk and oolitic limestones, sparingly
intermixed with fragments of older rocks. On the
crown of the coarse gravel a fragment of a Roman
road was found, on both sides of which there was every
appearance of a strong current having woshed away the
road and coarse gravel. A few yards further the gravel
was again met with, and in it were found fragments of
unbaked pottery, resembling the cinerary urns found
in the district, in Roman places of sepulture; and still
further another fragment of the Roman road was found,
with a deposit of gravel upon it. This gravel was all
deposited naturally. Just at the completion of the sec-
tion, and near the Manor-house at Norton, another bit
of the Roman road was found, but without the superin-
cumbent gravel bed. The inference is that the deposits
have been made in currents constantly increasing their
velocity, and that a partial revival ot the forces which
deposited the gravel has occurred even since the forma-
tion of the Roman road. There is, however, no trace
of any watercourse having existed, to judge from the
surface, which is now many feet above the basin of the
Derwent. Further sections of the drainage will be
commenced in the spring, along the suppomsd course of
the Roman road, when some further light may be
thrown upon this singular affair.

articles.title: PANIC.
articles.text:
A PANIC.

As the down train of the Waterford and Limerick
Railway was passing between Tipperary and Cahir on
Monday evening, it was brought to a standstill. The
screams of two young girls, piercingly loud, and their
efforts to fling themselves out of a second-class carriage,
caused this sudden stoppage. The guard, Patrick
Fitzgerald, hastened to the side of the train, where the
terrified young creatures were seen with their bodies
protruding from the open window. The doors at that
side of the train were all locked, and the shrieks of the
two young girls, who belong to a respectable class in
life, were most painful. Earn >stly they demanded to
be removed from that to another carriage, and they
clung around the neck of the guard, whose protection
they sought, and who describes the scene and the mo-
ment as being of a most trying character. From a
very unconnected tale it appeared that a young man,
'respectably dressed,' and one of four male passengers
who occupied seats in the carriage in which the girls
were, bad taken from his pocket suddenly a bottle, and
had thrown its contents in their faces. Though
thickly veiled, the fluid fell on their cheeks, which
began to smart and almost instantaneously they felt a
numbed sensation' and the feeling as if of unconsci-
ousness creeping over them. The windows of the
carriage had previously been closed by tl..e man who
had acted in so rude and mysterious a manner. Their
respectable dressed' assailant handed the bottle he
had used to the guard; but, incautiously, Mr. Fitz-
gerald threw it away. By gentle persuasion the young
women were induced to re-enter the train, under
charge of Mrs. Whiteside, wife of tho station-master
at Clonmel, who states that before they arrived at
Cahir the girls seemed to pass from one paroxysm of
terror into another. In Cahir such was their enfeebled
state that both left the train, and remained there under
the medical care of Dr. Stokes. The bottle-holder was
detained in Cahir for the night, under the surveillance
of the constabulary, and next day was brought before
Mr. Denis O'Brien, Jastice of the Peace. One of the
young girls, who had her passage paid to New Zea-
land, recovering, was permitted to proceed by the
night mail to the steamer at Waterford. The other
remained to confront the accused. The court as-
sembled, and the sworn depositions were read in
presence of a large force of police, under Mr. Fosberry,
sub-inspector, the medical gentlemen, and others, and
the magistrate required the production of the bottle to
have the contents analysed. The guard and head con-
stable were despatched to search for the missing phial,
which was fortunately discovered, and found to con-
tain can de Cologne. The accused was allowed to re-
turn to Waterfor&i a wiser if not a sadder man.

THE Lucia's ;END.—Here I am, on the extreme
verge of England: this paper is laid on a rough granite
rock, in a little recess which keeps off the wind. All this
little headland is granite, shattered and splintered as if
by lightning. The granite is in many places covered
with lichens: and here and there a bright sprig of
heather looks out from a little nook in which it has been
able to root itself. The sea is roaring eighty feet below.
Eighty feet make all the elevation; of course, the mere
height is very poor when compared with that of many
bits of the Scotch coast. The descent to the sea is
perpendicular; the sea below is not deep just at this
point. Out, a mile and a half from shore, you might
see the Longships Rocks, detached islets rising in a line
very sharply out of the sea; and running up almost into
spires. On one of them is a lighthouse. Three men
live in it. A few years ago, a youaag man who had been
absent from his family for twelve years, came back to
visit his old home hard by. His father was one of te
keepers of the lighthouse; and as it was his turn to take
charge of the lights that month, he could not come
ashore to see his son till a few days should pass. The
morning after the son's arrival, it was to stormy to go
out to the lighthouse to visit his father, and he came to
this spot to have as near a view as might be of the place
where his father was. He fell over the rocks and was
killed.—Good Words.

THE INDIAN COMHANDER-IN-CHIEF. - Sir Hugh
Rose was a popular chief. He is no longer so- He has
exhibited a went of prudence and magnanimity in his
conduct respecting the Priestley and Fitzgerald scandal
affair. Major Fitzgerald, in a private conversation with
Colonel Priestley at the Ufited Service Club, observed
that.he had no resinct for Sir Hugh Rose in his public
or private capacity. Colonel Priestley immediately
made an official report of this private gossip. As soon
as he heard of this, Major Fitzgerald explained and
apologised to the Colonel, who replied that he could
accept no apology himself, as the matter did not concern
himself personally, but the Commander-in-Chief, who
must decide the matter. The Major then made an offi-
cial apology in writing. There the affair might have
ended, but Sir Hugh Rose espoused the causa of Colonel
Priestley, when he heard that the club were considering
whether they should not dismiss him for a bralch of
their rules. Sir Hugh, as President of the Club and
Commander-in-Chief, forbade the members to dismiss
the Colonel. In spite of Sir Hugh, Colonel Priestley
was dismissed, and it is said the club were about to
request Sir Hugh to resign his post as President. Lord
Elgin has refused to interfere in the matter, and is said
to have disapproved of Sir Hugh's proceedings. Alto-
gether his Excellency has made a sad mess of it, and
in the end may find it necessary to resign, not only the
chair of the Club, but his seat in the Supreme Council
and his command of the Bengal Army.—Court Circular.

THE CONVICT NOBLElcAN.—Parting with our hos-
pitable friend, Francis Smith, we pursued our walk back
to Richmond, calling at a few houses on the way. At
one of the houses in this ra., ighbourhood, there is a person
in the capacity of a servant, a prisoner, who is the son of
an English marquis. My informant knew him when in
England. The last place in which he met with him there
was a ball-room, where his rank rendered him a person
of consideration. His first interview with him in this
land was in consequenee of some offence which had sub-
jected the prisoner to be brought before him as a magis-
trate, and punished. What was the surprise of the
magistrate (who told me the cirenntstance) to see the
ndividual whom he had once addressed as my lord'
standing before him a prisoner at the bar. He took an
early opportunity of conversing with him in private,
and learned that he and some bottle companions had
robbed a fish-pond in a, frolic, but, being apprehended
and convicted, transportation for 11 years was the
penalty. But there is great cause to presu.me that he
had become in other respects an utterly degraded and
miserable man. After the expiration of his term of strict
servitude he committed a second crime, for which 4.e was
again sentenced; and he is now serving out the period
of his bondage with, a settler, who has much difficulty
in managing him, in. consequence of his drunkenness.
The gentleman who narrated these particulars met With
another convict, whom ha had last seen at a. hunting
party, but who having taken to gambling and become a
spendthrift, to help his firyinces, resorted to forgery,
which resulted in transportation to Van Diemen's Land.
How melancholy to see persons thus throw away the
advantages of birth, education, and character, and finally
sink into degradation and vice.—Life .144 ours

articles.title: SOUTHERN BLOCKADE OF FEW
articles.text:
THE SOUTHERN BLOCKADE OF FEW

TURK.

The clipper ship Dreadnought, of this port, yesterday
arrivsd in safety from Live-pool, after making a long
detour to the northward in order to avoid the attentions
of Captain Semmes and the rebel steamer Alabama. it
' is somewhat humili iting for us to chronicle such a fact
as this, and to admit that, whereas we have been
blockading Charleston and Savannah by fleets a: the
very mouths of their harbours for IS months with the
grand net result of sending into those ports more large
foreign steamers than ever entered them before, the Con-
federates have succeeded in so thoroughly blockading
New York by a couple of steamers at the Azores as to
compel our ordinary transatlantic commerce to coast
the icy shores of Greenland for safety. The contrast
is painful, and we can but trust that it may not be
unprofitable. It certainly will not be, if the authori-
ties of the Navy Department are accessible to the
emotions of patriotic shame and indignation which the
contemplation of such a state of things must awaken in
every cii izen's bosom. But the Navy Department is not
the only branch of the Government interested in the dis-
graceful revelations of this singular long-range blockade.
It will be observed, that in receiving the news of the
arrival of the Dreadnought, we are further notified, on
good authority,' that there is no danger of any inter-
ference by the Alabama or the ` 290' (for these two
appear not to be one, s tve in the fiendish spirit of their
commanders) with our emigrant ships coming to New
York, since 'an understanding to that effect has been
had between the owners of the " 290 " and her captain.'
This is cool, certainly, as well as comforting. We are
to understand, are we, that the business of fitting out
privateers to prey upon Americ-in commerce is so open!)
an quietly carried on at Liverpool that loyal American
citizens resident there and engaged in the emigrant trade
can ascertain precisely what danger there is of any
harm coming to them and their ships by any
particular cruiser which may be on the point of
leaving port! If this be so, we beg leave respect-
fully, but firmly, to inquire of the State Department
whether we have such an official at Liverpool as an
American Consul; also, whether it can be regarded as
being wholly out of the power of such an official (sup-
posing him to exist) to ascertain facts familiar to all the
shipping world about him, or as being wholly out of
the sphere of his duty to endeavour to ascertain such
facts and act upon them when ascertained. It cer-
tainly is singular that while we are all of us bitterly de-
nouncing the British government for not putting a stop
to the armament and expedition of vessels destined
to prey upon our trade, we thould have heard nothing
of any steps taken by our own commercial agents to
require action in the premises of the British authorities.
It is the function, not of British, but of American
officials, to protect American interests. If B:itish
officials choose to wink at the violation of British
laws, that does not excuse our officials for their negli-
gence in not calling the attention of their British com-
peers to such violations. If bargains and agreements,
securing the safety of this or that class of merchant
ships, can be made at Liverpool between enterprising
outfitters of steam frigates and loyal American shippers,
it is , clear that the State Department of the United
States' Government ought to know something about the
matter. If it neither knows nor can learn anything in
reference thereto we shall not be surprised to hear before
long that the 'British and Southern Joint-stock Associa-
tion for Sweeping the Sees' has opened offices in Liver-
pool and London for the sale of safe-conducts ' to
American ships of all sorts at reasonable rates.—New
York Times of Oct. 27.

articles.title: EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE BY BOYS.
articles.text:
EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE BY
BOYS.

The triumph of boys over the effigy of Guy
Fawkes has been attended this year at Bradford with a
very aggravated act of violence. The particulars were
stated before Messrs. Alderman Rand, Brown, and
Light, and Mr. S. Smith, four of the magistrates of
that borough, on Saturday last, when no fewer than 30
boys and youths, from 13 to 20 years of age, most of
them employed in worsted factories, dye-houses, and
iron foundries, were charged with having committed a
murderous assault upon Mr. Isaac White, a respect tble
farmer, between 50 and 60 years of age, residing at
New Millerdam, Manningham township, in the
borough of Bradford. They were further charged
with stealing Mr. White's property. Mr. Ter y,
solicitor, appeared for the prosecution; Mr. J. G.
B.utchinson appeared for 14 of the prisoners, end
Mr. Cater on behalf of four others, the rest being. un-
defended. From the evidence of Mr. Granhan, chief
' constable of Bradford, it appeared that the prisoners
and other lads to the number altogether of 40 or more,
went on Tuesday night last with a hand-cart to Mr.
White's farm, for the purpose of conveying away pales
and other fencing materials to use as fuel for a bonfire.
A tre blown down by the late gales having been
pi eviously stolen by the same boys for the like purpose,
Mr. White kept watch upon the depredators, aporoachtd
them when they were engaged in their unlawful busi-
ness, and ordered them to desist. He then laid hold: of
the hand-cart, and no sooner had he done so than he was
attacked by the whole gang of boys, who, armed with
pales, sticks, and stones, struck him violently on the
head, face, and shoulders, knocked him down, kicked, ,
him, and left him bleeding on the ground and in a state
of insensibility. His son soon after wards found hiin,
and he was removed to his house, where he has been con-
fined to bed ever since. Niue of his teeth were knocked
out, and his gums, lips, face, head, and shoulders were
very severely cut and bruised. Dr. Bell was called in
to see him the samo flight, and found him in a half-
conscious state. The doctor considered Mr. White's
li.e was in danger at that time, but on visiting him on
each of the three following mornings he appeared to be
somewhat better,, although occasionally he complained
of pain in his head. In his evidence on Saturday, Dr.
Bell said ho had not visited Mr. White that morning,
but on the prelims day he was progressing favourably.
Still, if he continued to go on iavourably, he would not
be able to attend the court to give evidence before a
fortnight hence: The Bench remanded all the 30
prisoners for a week, but consented to take bail for their
appearance. Eleven of them, who were said to have
been the most active in the commission of the outrage,
were severally required to find two sureties in DO each
aild to enter into their own recognizances in the sum of
£2O, and the remaining 19 to give bail in half those
amounts fo: their appearance next Saturday. Mr.
White, the prosecutor in the case, is well known in
musical circles in the West Riding of Yorkshire, and is
much respected.

SOMETHING Nmw.—The -Veto Orleans Piclyzene says
it is customary with persons at the South who have old
negroes they wish to sell for a good price,. if they happen
to be minus a tooth or two to put kernels of Virginia
corn fiat and white, in th-ir jaws, set in red putty,

VERY DEFINITE.—An old lady was asked what
she thought of one of her neighbours of the name of
Jones, and with a knowing wink replied Why, I
don't like to say anything about my neighbours ; but as
to Mr. Jones, sometimes I think, and then again I
don't know, but after all, I rather guess he'll turn
out to be a good deal such a sort of man as I take him
to be.'

Tug GLA.OOw Mum:mt.—The convict M'Lachlan
takes the final destiny assigned to her by the Home
Secretary with some chagrin and disappointment, and
has shed tears abundantly at the prospect of penal
servitude for life. By the enthusiasm a those who
believed her innocent, and by their success in saving her
life, she had been uplifted into the notion that she was
forthwith to be set at liberty, and she has now asked if
the folk ootside canna do something mair for her.'
M'Lachlan, the husband, who we believe is a respectable
man, and much to be pitied under the eircumsttnces, is
about to emigrate in a few weeks. By the Act of
Parliament it appears that penal servitude, and not
transportation, is the doom of those who have been con-
demned to death and whose sentence has been commuted.

THE NEW ARCHBISHOP OP Yonx.—Dr. Thomson,
who has been nominated by tbe Crown to the Arch-
bishopric of York, is not only the youngest prelate in
the order of consecration, but the youngest in point of
years. He was born on the 11th of February, 1819.
He is the son of a tradesman at Whitehaven, and owes
all his distinctions, academical and professional, to his
own exertions. He is the son of Mr. John Thtmion, of
Whitehaven, and having been educated at Shrewsbury
School, was entered at Queen's, Oxford, where he
became scholar, fellow, tutor, and provost. Ire graduated
in 1840, when he took a third class in classic. In 1842..
he was ordained deleon, and was admitted into pric sL's
orders in the following year. He was curate fir,t at
Guildfor i, then at Cuddesden, and in 1848 was
appointed select preacher at Oxford. In 1858
no wai chosen to preach the B.impton lectures,
his subject being "The Atoning Work of Chrisr.'
In 1856, on the resignation of Dr. Bating now kishop
of Durham, Lord Palmerston nominated him to the ree-
torTof All Souls', Lane:ham-place ; but in the course of
a few months afterwards the Provostdiip of Queen's be-
coming vacant by the death of Dr. Fox, Dr. Thomson
was ,s!ected to it, notwithstanding some opposition
whic had met with in consequence of his successftd
exertions to destroy the closeness of the college. In
1858. he was elected preacher of Lincoln's-inn, in 1859
he was appointed one of the chaplains in or linary to her
Majesty, and in 1861, on the translation of Dr. Baring
to Durham, he was nominated to the Bishopric of
Gllueester and Bristol. The new archbishop is well
known by his work entitled •Au Outline of the Laws of
Thought, and by his preface to the work c tiled Aids
to Faith,' intended to be a counteractive to the Essays
and Reviews.' He has contrilufed a Life of Christ' to,
Dr. Smith's' Dictionary of the Bible,' and has published:
Averal minor works..

On the Bth the launch of the Poonah, a new ship,
built for the Peninsular and Oriental Company, took
place, in the presence of a large number of visitors, from
the dockyard of the Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding
Company, Blackwell. The Poonah is a vessel of the
same class and character as those already in possession
of the Peninsular and Oriental Company, with the addi-
tion of such improvements vs the most advanced expe-
rience in the art of shipbuilding has been able to suggest.
No effirt has been spat ed to make the new vessel pert': et
as a ship, or to provide those conveni-nces which s., much
contribute to the comfort of passengers in long sea
voyagEs. The launch it self was quite successful, the
ves-et starting off immediately the ways were removed,
and gliding smoothly along her groove till she reached
the water. Miss Collier pert (armed tt.e baptismal
ceremony by breaking a bottle of champagne. After
the launch the visitors, over 200 in number, took
part in a lunch to which they were invited by
the directors of the Thames Ironworks and Shipbuild-
ing Company, and which was presided over by Mr.
Rolt. The directors of the Peninsular and Oriental Com
pany were not present, as was expected, out of respect
to the memory of Mr. Wilcox, the late chairman, who
died within the last few days, owing to an unfortunate
accident. Mr. Rolt, in alluding to this sad circumstance,
remarked that it was the only drawback to the satis-
faction caused by the success of the launch, but it was a
serious one, as Mr. Wilcox was the principal original
promoter of the Peninsular and Oriental Company--a
company which has now reached such dimensions as to
be the owners of 80,000 tons of shipping.
In connection with the launch of the Poonah the
public may be interested in learning that just by the side
of the slip from which that vessel has just glided lies the
Minotaur, an enlarged and improved Warrior, building
on the same slip from which that frigate was launched.
The company are also building for the British Admi-
ralty, another iron-cased frigate, the Valiant, of 4,100
tons burden, which will be launched in the spring of
next year; her protecting armour is -similar to that of
the Warrior, viz., 18 inches of teak and 4-1,- inches
armour plates.
In an advanced state of progress we also find a float-
ing battery for the Russian Government, 220 feet in
length, 53 feet broad, and 2,800 tons, also protected by
41-inch armour plates on 9 inches of teak, and intended
to =Ty 26 66 pound guns on a draught of 14: feet.
The frames are also beginning to be erected of a
frigate, which the company have just undet taken to
build for the Spanish government, of about 5,000 tons,
with 52,1 inch armour plates; and the slip is also being
prepared for a similar frigate of 4,300 tons for the
Turkish government, making altogether nearly 23,000
tons of iron-cased shipping under construction by
one firm, and being alone a formidable fleet, superior
to what is possessed by any but the first-rate naval
powers. _ _

Besides producing the 5,000 tons of armour plates
required for these vessels, the company are also, with
the nine or ten steam hammers which they keep at work
night and day, manuf,cturincr° armour plates for the
Ocean and Royal Sovereign, having just completed
those for the Royal Oak—wooden vessels which the
Admiralty are easing with armour plates at the royal
dockyards, and they have during the present year com-
pleted and dispatched two iron-cased gunboats for the
Danish government.
The Poonah will be immediately followed by another
vessel, of nearly the same burden, for the Peninsular
and Oriental Company, to be laid down on the same slip
that company have kept occupied for themselves for
several years. Another paddle steamer for the Dublin
Trinity Corporation is rapidly approaching completion,
and by her side is a vessel to which some mystery
appears to attach, but which we believe to be intended
for a sailing yacht for Sir Alfred Tichborne, Bart., and
designed to surpass in accommodation and speed any-
thing yet afloat ; making with other smaller matters a
total of nearly 30,000 tone of shipping in course of con-
struction by this single firm.

articles.title: GENERAL BUTLER AND THE ESSEX.
articles.text:
GENERAL BUTLER AND THE ESSEX.

The following gives the latest stage of the affair at
New Orleans between General Butler and the captain of
the Prussian ship Eeses. It appears that the vigour of
the General has been further displayed by a military
seizure and removal of some of the moderate parcels of
family plate denounced as 'contraband of war,' and
that after a long illegal detention the vessel has been
allowed a clearance. The spite against the families
whose spoons, forks, or other valuables have thus been
seized having been gratified in a manner that must have
enabled the General to report his victory in the most
ample terms to the Cabinet at Washington, by whom it
may be communicated to the Northern press with the
view of counteracting the despondency occasioned by
the cavalry raid of General Stuart in Pennsylvania, and
the more recent capture of 4,000 waggons of provisions
by General Bragg in Kentucky, the Government will,
perhaps, terminate the matter by paying all damages the
Prussian Government may demand,, and transmitting to
General Butler an intimation that their approval and
admiration of him as a representative American has
experienced no diminution :-
27, Leadenhall-street, E.C., Nov. 7.
Sir,—We have received this -morning a letter enclosing
a fresh protest from captain, supercargo, and crew of the
Prussian ship Essex, from which it appears that the
parcel consisting of two packages, one valued at 3,000
dole. end one at 500 dole. both shipped by Robert Clark,
consigned to Messrs. George Green, Sons, and Co., of
Liverpool, were on the 4th of October forcibly taken
irom on board by a Custom-house officer, accompanied
by a sergeant and two armed soldiers.
Teat two eases, marked Nos. 1 and 2, shipped by J.
B. Elders, containing old silver ware, valued at 6,000
dols, consigned to Messrs. Duranty and Co., of Liver-
pool, were handed over to the Custom-house authorities
on their returning all the bills of lading for the same.
That a daily application for a clearance of the vessel
was made at the Custom-house, which was always
refused on the grJund that other contraband goods were
on board; but on the afternoon of the 6th of October a
Custom-house officer informed the captain that orders
had then been received from the military authorities to
clear the ship with those goods an board which had pre-
viously been declared contraband.
_ _

The vessel was towel out of the river on the evening;
of the Bth. On that day the arrival of the British man-
of-war Rinaldo became known, to tile evident relief ot
the British residents at that place.
• We are, dear Sir, y.airs respectfully,
KAHL BROTHERS.

' A CHINESE. FUNERAL.—AI the funeral of a mandarin,
in Canton, the procession was led by coolies carrying a
miniature temple tenanted by Tien-Hows (Queen of
Heaven). Then came coolies bearing a light stage, on
which reposed a huge roasted pig, adorned with coloured
papers. 'Next followed a priest and a friend of the
deceased, bearing a large bundle of pieces of white paper
cut into Squares, each with a gilded spot in the centre.
These were funeral favours, and were scattered right and
left as the procession went on. The body-guard of the
dead mandarin came next, each person carrying his
implement or sign of office. The gardener had a hoe, the
butcher a long knife, the executioner a list of victims.
A party of musicians succeeded, and then , came the
coffin, very like an English packing-case. Mourners and
mandarins brought up the rear, and very little of sorrow
was exhibited. The son of the deceased, so long as the
procession was moving, appeared unable to support his
grief, but at any temporary halting place he laughed
and chatted and became as lively as his neighbours.
THE SALMON FisHEILIES or CUMBERLAND.-The
beneficial results of the English Salmon Fisheries Act
passed last year have been experienced in a marked
decree this season in Cumberland. In the Eden the
lessees of the firheries reaped the advantage of the
abolition of the stake nets on the English shore of the
Solway Frith, and took large quantities of salmon in the
early part of the year; but no very wonderful exploits
were performed with the rod till the last week of the
season, which closed after the Ist of November. The
weather was not favourable for rod-fishing during
the greater part of the year; but the extended weekly
close time for nets gave anglers a better chance when
opportunity occurred for trying their luck. The ne's
having been thrown off, according to the provision.s of
the new Act, on the Ist of September, the salmon, no
longer stopped by the stake nets in the estuary, had a
free run, and between that time. and the close Of the

reports are equally. gratifying, the salmon having never
I.aNm so plentiful since the days when it was a common
of food. On. Saturday, the Ist, one gentleman
cured four salmon, weighing together 701 b., and there
were several others caught weighing about 201 b. A
great many more were hooked, which succeeded in
getting off ag.dn ; and, of course, imagination gave
fabulous dimensions to some of these. An obstruction
in the Derwent at Fitz Weir is now about to be rendered
passable to the breeding fish,
and if poaching can be
kept down the rivers will in a very few years be restored ,
to their pristine productiveness.

large bed of oysters, estimated by the fishermen at
the value of £5,000, has just been discovered about
three miles off the mouth of Dartmouth Harbour.
SUDDEN. DEATH OF DR. JOHN BELL.—We have to
announce the sudden death of Dr. John Bell, one of the
Inspectors-General of Hospitals, which took place at
Jedburgh on Tuesday. Dr. Bell served in the Crimea,
and at the close of the war came to reside in Jedburgh.
Dr. Bell was a brother of the late William Bell, Esq., of
Menslawr was much respected in the district—.
.Edinburs.,„ .

THE DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

THE MANSION-11011SE COMMITTEE.
On the Bth, the Mansion house Relief Fund had
amounted in all to £125,000 in round numbers, sub-
scribed in less than eight months, of which as much as
£6,700 and upwards was received during that day and
the preceding one. The subacriptions for the week end-
ing Thursday amounted to £16,130.
METROPOLITAN TABERNACLE.
The Rev. C. H. Spurgeon preached two sermons on
the 9th on behalf of relieving the distress now being
endured by the opt-ratives in the North. Notwithstand-
ing the unfavourable state of the weather the building
was filled on both occasions. Collections were made at
the. elose of each sermon, and the sum contributed
amotutted to £713 6s. 9d.
WIGAN.

The work of the Bo :rd of Guardians continues
steadily to increase, no less than 252 new applicants
having been phced upon the books of the relieving
officers during the pa,t iv. ek. The number of out-do6r
poor is thus made 4,648—an increase of 2,325 on the
corresponding week of last year. The expenditure was
£31195. 5d., an increaseofllBl 12s. 6d. on 1861, and of
£8 Is. Id. on last week. The cold weather of the paEt
few days has considerably influenced the workhouse
returns 24 new inmates h vying entered the house since
the end of last week. The number now is 494, and 54
vagrants were also relieved during the week. Adding
these figures to those published by the relief com-
mittee, we have a grand total of 15,565 persons re-
ceiving relief in the Wigan Union—au increase on the
week, in spite of a small decrease in the figures
of the committee, of 244. In addition to the relief
thus distributed, we may state that much is done unos-
tentatiously by several of the large firms of the town in
the way ot providing soup and bread for the operatives
they formerly employed. At the mills of Messrs. Eck-
ersley and Sons, Messrs. Woods and Sons, and Messrs.
Woods and Co. soup and bread are distributed several
days each week, and an ample supply given to every
one who worked in the mills, and who chooses to apply
for food. Probably between £5O and £6O will he spent
each week in this manner. Fever, happily not of a ma-
lignant character, is said to be prevalent, but the cases
are not yet very numerous._

articles.title: PRESTON.
articles.text:
PRESTON.

The report issued on Saturday by the Charitable
Relief Committee again shows a lamentable increase in
the amount of distress. There are not fewer than 477
cases, comprising 1,516 persons, in receipt of relief more
than there were last week; and the increase in the
value of the relief given is £49 3s. The entire number
of cases now on the books is 8,617, including 34,227
persons, relieved at a cost of £903. Mr. Johnson, the
newly elected schoolmaster to the unemployed opera-
tives on the moor, commences his duties to-day (Mon-
day) with 150 pupils. The arrival of parcels of clothing
is pretty considerable and exceedingly well-timed,
according to the stat meats of the relief visitors.

articles.title: BLACKBURN.
articles.text:
BLACKBURN.

The returns of ouc relief presented to the guardians
on Saturday showed that in the Union during the week
no fewer than 21,55.1 persons had been relieved with
£1,066 us. 4d., being a large increase over the previous
week. In the workhouse there are 610. inmates, against
373 last year. During the week 24,000 persons have
been relieved by the relief committee, many of whom
were also relieved by the guardians. These have that
relief supplemented by the committee with a third to the
va!ue of 6d. Mr. Commissioner Farnall met the relief
committee on Saturday evening to give them the benefit
of his experience.

articles.title: BURNLEY.
articles.text:
BURNLEY.

The Mayor presided at the weekly meeting of the
Relief Committee held on Thursday evening in the
Council Chamber. The committee granted £375 14s. id.
for the relief of the general public, £3l 10s. Id. for the
industrial school, and £3l 12s. 10d. for the purchase of
materials for the sewing classes. Notice was given of a
motion to increase the relief from Is. 9d. to 2s. per head
per week. A bale of clothing was reported to have
been received from the Central Committee:

STOCKPORT.
The guardians, fearing that they will not be able to
meet the rapidly increasing distress, have petitioned the
Rome Secretary for a grant of money out of the
Consolidated Fund. They state that, including iron-
founders and hat manufacturers, the total number of
persons out of work in the borough is about 12,000. The
number of paupers in the Union is rapidly increasing,
paving last week reached 11,125, of whom 8,138
were in the town of Stockport. In addition to this the
relief committees last week assisted 15.,,984 persons,
the largest number yet on the-books ; so that there are
now 24,122 persons in the town in the receipt of either
parochial or private relief.

articles.title: CIIORLEY.
articles.text:
CIIORLEY.

Distress is on the increase here. Not fewer than 246,
additional persons have, during the past week, applied to
the relief committee for assistance. The Guardians' returns
show an increase of 108 outdoor paupers during the
week. There are now receiving outdoor relief from the
union funds 3,542 persons. Some load cases of fever,
arising from atrophy have occurred in the older pottion
of Chorley parish.

articles.title: CLITHEROE.
articles.text:
CLITHEROE.

A. committee has just been organised by the distressed
overlookers employed at thecotton mills at Clitheroe and
Low Moor to raise funds for relieving those of their own
class. With respect to general distress in the town, it
is a subject of much comment that the gentry, taken as
a whole, living in and about Clitheroe, are strangely
apathetic.

articles.title: HASLINGDEN.
articles.text:
HASLINGDEN.

Mr. H. B. Farnall, Special Commissioner from the
Poor Law Board, visited Haslingden on Frid'ty after-
noon and attended the meeting of the guardians. It
appears that one-third of the current rate could not
be collected, in consequence of the poverty of the small
tenement holders at Newchurch. They had failed in
the introduction of the Small Tenements Act. The
Chairman asked Mr. Fanaall's advice. The Commis-
sioner said, if one third of the rate could. not be
got in they must lay another on the solvent ratepayers.
That might appear a hard course; but the parish of
Newchurch, in the event of spending more than 9d. in
the pound quarterly on the net rateable value, would
be able to throw the excess on the common tund, and
when all the other townships had spent above that sum,
then they could borrow money on the rateable value, of
the union to be paid back in seven years. If the whole
union spent anything at the rate of above Os. in the
pound during the quarter, then the excess could be
thrown on the whole county. He did not believe that
the distressed operatives could live under 2s. per head
per weak. While the Haslingden Guardians had acted
liberally by raising the scale of relief when that course
was considered necessary, yet he would caution them
against being so liberal as to tempt persons not to work
when they could. _

articles.title: COLNE.
articles.text:
COLNE.

This town,. which, from its contiguity to Yorkshire,
has participated in the advantages of the worst d trade,
has now begun seriously to feel the effects of the cotton
famine. A committee was appointed to collect the
necessary funds, Subscriptions to cover six months
were promised, altogether amounting to £7OO.
_ _ _ _ CARLISLE.

Above 3,400 persons w—e-re---r—elievcd by the Carlisle
Relief Committee during the past week, at a cost of
about £6O. The amount subscribed to the fund is
£1,186, of which sum £323 has been already extended,
so that there only remains a balance of £863. During
the week the committee had a very gratifying instance
of liberality from a former resident in Carlisle, who,
under the name of an absent friend,' sent £lOO through
the Dean of Carlisle.

articles.title: BRISTOL,
articles.text:
BRISTOL,

The subscription opened in this city by the Mayor
for the relief of the sufferers by the cotton famine
amounted on Saturday to nearly

-NORFOEK.

On Sunday mornin't—he-M;;;;"and Town Council of
Norwich attended Divine service at the Cathedral, as
did the local Volunteers, when an appeal was made on
behalf of the distressed operatives in Lancashire.

articles.title: }ISSEX.
articles.text:
}ISSEX.

The Independent congregation of Maldon have sub-
scribed £47 Bs. 5d.; Messrs. Jade, Coop, and Co.,
£100; the congregation of All Saints Church, Hockerill,
£4O ; the officers of the force of Royal Artillery sta-
tioned at Warley barracks, £l4; and a number of other
parishes and private persons smaller amounts.
LINCOLNSHIRE.

A choral festival in St. Martin's Church, Stamford,
resulted in a balance of £5O 15s. 3d., available for the
relief of the Lancashire distress. The amount has been
duly remitted by the Rev. C. J. Dyer. A similar
festival at Bourn produced the sum of .£lB as., and
several ladies and gentlemen of the neighbourhood have
agreed to make weekly contributions. The same course
has been adopted at Brigg. At Barton-on-Humber col-
lectioßs after sermons have realised £45.

HUNTINGDON.
Collections made in the parish churches of Huntingdon
have realised £46. At St. Ives a weeky offertory has
been establish,-d in the parish church, and for the fast
hree weeks the proceeds are to be remitted to Lanca-
shire.

Da. VOGEL—lnformation has just reached Malta
from the coast of Barbary which gives some faint reason
to hope that Dr. Vogel, the African traveller, who had
been given up as lost, is still alive, though 'a captive of
the Sultan of Wadai. Lieutenant You Beuraman, of
the Prussian Artillery, who went in search of the tra-
veller's papers, arrived at Muzruk on the 20th of June,
and was to leave for Wadai on the 22nd. Since that
period the rumours which have reached Bennzi reg d •
ing him have been such as to lead to the ?ear that he
was plundered on the road, if not murdered. The
Prince of Prussia while at Valetta evinced a lively
interest in the fate of these travellers, and an earnest
desire to obtain every information respecting them.

articles.title: POST OFFICE ROBBERIES.
articles.text:
POST OFFICE ROBBERIES.

It is very satisfactory to find that the recent altera-
tion in the regulations of the General Post Office rela-
tive to the registration of letters, and, the reduction in
the amount of the fee charged for registering them,
has been found to work most satisfactorily in one re-
spect—namely, by most materially reducing, if not
altogether annihilating, the offiince of stealing Nei
letters containing money or valuables. This crime, ae
the public is aware, was formerly carried on to a vary
great extent, and hardly any session of the Central
Criminal Court took place—and the same observation
applies to the Assizes—without five or six postmen
being charged with stealing letters that were entrusted
to them to deliver, or which they purloined during aka
process of sorting.
Those cases where detection took place did, not by
any means represent the total extent of the crime, as
complaints were continually made to, the head office oi
the loss of letters containing money and valuable pro-
perty, but the circumstances. were such as toafford. no
clue to the detection of the guilty party.

The cases where detectiolt6ol pface were always
of a very painful character, as it is known that the
Post Office authorities are very strict in making in-
quiries relating to the persons whom they take into
their service; and many of the unfortunate postmen
who could not resist the temptation of purloining a
letter given to them to deliver, which contained money
or other valuables, were persons who up to that time
had borne a most irreproachable character; and the
sentence of penal servituele, which the judges felt it
invariably to be their duty to pass upon them, was
attended not only with ruin to tlnm,elves, but to every
one connected with them and the Rev. Mr. Davis,
the chaplain of Newgate, and the other officials of
that prison, have frequently, in their reports, stated
that these are the must painful &set.' ption of cases
that came within their notice. Various schemes
were adopted with a view to put a atop to the
crime, but the mode that was usually carried out
was ,by making use of what is called a test'
letter, addressed to a fictitious person in the
district from whence complai,.ts of the loss of letters
containing money had been made. The effect of this
proceeding, however, was merely to detect the guilty
party; but, although the postmen were pezfectly
aware that such means were employed to discover
those who were guilty of a breach of trust, it, did not
appear to have any effect in deterring them from com-
mitting the crime, and they trusted to the chance of
being able to destroy the letter, and get rid of the coin
contained in it, before any inquiry should be made.
The crime, therefore, instead of diminishing, was un-
doubtedly on the increase The recent regulation,
however, appears almost completely to have put a stop
to the offence, and it operates in the following, manner.
The public is aware that the fee for registering letters
containing money cr valuables was formerly Is., but by
the"new regulation the fee is reduced to 4d., and all
persons sending money or other property in a letter are
cautioned as to the necessity of registering it. In ad-.
dition to this the Post-office authorities have the power
in all cases where a non-registered letter evidently con-
tains coin to register it themselves, and the party to whom
it is addressed is required to pay a double registration
fee of eightpence before the letter is delivered. It is
well that the public should be aware of this fact, as
the new regulation undoubtedly tends greatly to the
protection of property passing through the Post Office,
as in, the very few instances where a post office money.
order cannot be obtained, a letter can always be regis-
tered, and the temptation to dishonesty formerly
afforded to the servants of the Post Office is almost
entirely abolished. Persons who have been in the
habit of sendiug small sums of money in letters would
also, do well not to forg,t the effect of this alteration,
as instances have occurred in which a small amount,
such as a shilling, has been sent in a letter, and the
Post Office authorities, of course not being aware
whether it was a shilling or a sovereign, have them-
selves registered it, and the person receiving the letter
has been compelled to pay eightpeuce of the amount,
as the double registratioa fee. The t ffect of the new
regulation must, however, soon become generally
known, and there is no doubt that it will be found to
work most advantageously As rPtrArdS the Suppression
of this peculiar description of crime.

LUMINOUS FLOWEIts.—The latest and at the same
time most authentic observation of luminous flowers that
has been made, is the following :—On the 18th of June,.
1.857, about ten o'clock in the evening, M. W. Fries, the
well-known Swedish botanist, while walking alone in
the botanic garden of Upsal, remarked a group of poppies,
in which three or four flowers emitted little flashes ef
light. Forewarned as he was by a knowledge that such
things had been observed by others, he could not help
believing that he was sufferingfrom an optical delusion.
However, the flashes continued showing themselves from.
time to time during three-quarters of an hour. M. Fries
was thus forced to believe that what he saw was real.
The next day, observing the same phenomenon to re-
occur at about the same hour, he conducted to the place
a person entirely ignorant that such a manifestation of
light had ever been witnessed in the vegetable world.
and without relating anything concerning it, he brought
his companion before the group, of poppies. The latter
observer was soon in raptures of astonishment and admi-
ratien. Many other persons were then led to the spot„
some of whom immediately remarked that the flowers.
were throwing out flames.'—Pliipsa4 onPhospitorescance..
FLAX CULTIVATION IN InEwtia.—The agitation in
favour of flax growing in Ireland is daily increasing. A.
well-informed writer states that Kildare, Wicklow, and.
Meath are possessed of a. soil in very many places far
superior to any in the north for flax growing; that flax
grows well on reclaimed. bog; that a good wheat soil is
a good flax soil; that it is no more exeausting as a crop.
than wheat or potatoes; and. that any exhaustion can be
counteracted by irrigating the land with the steepwater,
and using the seed as feod.. Meadows where flax has
been grown also yield excellent grass. The Northern
Whig strongly advises cultivation of flax in Tipperary,.
and mentions that it has been handed specimens raised
in that country which, for beauty of colour and silkiness
of texture, will bear comparison with the most highly
, prized parcels produced this season in any other part of
Ireland. In the present year Ulster has raised 146,432
acres of flax; Connaught, 1,490 acres; Leinster„ 8.20
- acres ; and Munster, with its six million and odd acres
; of area, included in Wlch there are vast tracts of the
finest flax lands that ever lay to the sun, only grew
1,270 acres of flax.
REMARKABLE RECOVERY OF SPEECH.—The Western
Daily 31,,ratey relates the following story of a Mrs.
Newman, an old woman, of 70 years of age, late land-
lady of the New Inn at Oreston, and eho has leen deaf
and dumb the greater part of her life, and who, .zeizeet
some time ago with paralysis, died on Wedne:day last.
It was on Wednesday that the remarkable circumstance
related occurred. While Mrs. Newman was evidently
sinking, her sister stood near the bed in a state of ex-
treme distress. Some of the friends of both, who were
in the room, made signs to Mary Dean to leave the
room, and fetch some al tide that was required for the
dying woman's use. As she did not appear to observe
these gestures, they were repeated, and then, being
greatly agitated, she suddenly exclaimed, 'Don't bother
me!' The achiev, ment appeared to astonish herself as
much as the other persons who heard her • and it is
stated that she spoke several times since. This is one
of the many cases in which persons under great excite-
ment have either acquired or recovered the use of facul-
ties which had been considered to be absent or decayed.
THE DANISH DUCHIES QuESTioN.—The Dagbladet of
Copenhagen formally calls in doubt the adhesion which,
according to the German journals, the Cabinets of the
Tuileries and of St. Petersburg have given to the last
dispatch of Earl Russell relative to the Schleswio•p ques-
tion- It declares that at the most the French and
Russian ministers at the Court of Denmark have made
some commonplace recommendations in ord sr to satisfy
a kind of tradition in diplomatic etiquette. As to the
meeting of a European conference, which has also been
spoken of, the _Daybladet holds it as being absolutely
improbable, particularly if it were to take placeuas has
been said, to the exclusion, not only of Denmark, a
principal party interested, but also of Sweden, which in
her quality
of singer of the protocol of London, of 1850,
and of the treaty of May 8, 1852, has an indisputable
right to take part. in the deliberations of the powers
relative to the position of Denmark. Such a conference,
adds the Danish journal, would not be possible, except
with the consent of Denmark, and that consent it would
be more than ever difficult to obtain after the dispatch
of Earl Russell.

space' wherein only a few ghastly trunks are gathered
y
Would it not be well to repAee the trees that once mad"
the Brompton_road greeu, taking care they did ni
relapse into the scrubby state of yore, and replenish
Chelsea Gardens as soon as may be? There are miles
of wide roadsin London similarly improvable, where,
too, as at Bkanpton, there can be no question of the
roadway being injured by drippings from their twughs.

articles.title: LATER FROM AMERICA.
articles.text:
LATER FROM AMERICA.

NEW Yonx, Oct. 31 (Evening).—The Confederates
are still in force in the immediate front of the. army of
the Potomac. General Burnside has moved down along
the eastern base of Blue Ridge Mountains, and formed a
junction with General Sigel. It is reported at General
M'Clellan's head quarters that General Bragg is on his
way to join General Lee in Virginia. President
Lincoln has released the citizens of Baltimore who were
arrested by General Wool, and has assured the loyal
people of Maryland that the affair will be adjusted to
their satisfaction.

NEW YORK, Nov. I.—Great activity is observable on
the part of the Confederates, who are in strong force
between Winchester and the Potomac. Large bodies of
Confederates are moving without baggage along the
Front Royal road, and others towards Sharnonvale
Springs and Castlenau Ferry. Federal General Stone-
man has occupied Leesburg without opposition. The
Federals have occupied Charleston, in Western Virginia
and Grand Junction, Mississippi. The Confederate;
are in force nine miles from Grand Junction. General
Curtis reports that the Confederates have been routed
near Fayetteville, Arkansas. Deserters from Richmond
report that the steamer Merrimac No. 2 is a complete
success.

The Southern journals state that Federal General
Butler has landed at Pensacola with 7,000 men. It was
e.xnected he would advance to the junction of the
Mobile, Montgomery, and Pensacola Railroad. The
Conunercial Advertiser asserts that Nashville is sur-
rounded, and.that the inhabitants are nearly starving. The
Federal Governer of North Carolina has proposed to hold
a conference with the Confederate Governor of the State,
to discuss the position of public -affairs, and the aspect of
the war. The furtherobjects of the proposition are not
stated.. Washington dispatches assert thatmany of the
Southern slaveholders are running their slaves through
the blockade, and selling them in Cuba. The New
York municipality has resolved to issue 3,000,000
dollars paper currency in amounts under one dollar.
Numerous strikes have occurred in different branches Of
trade, but employers have consented to pay the wages
demanded. It has been found impracticable to serve
the writ of habeas corpus at Fort Warren. A large
Republican 'noting has been held in New York. Ti.e
speakers declaredthe determination of the Republican
party to subjugate the South, and -endorsed Mr. Lin-
coin's proclamation.
The Times' .Queenstown correspondent telegraphs the ,
following summary of the Kangaroo's news :
QUEENSrows, Nov. 12, 7.22 aan.—Advices have
arrived, per the Kangaroo, from New York, to Novem-
ber 1. General Mitchell has suffered a severe repulse
at Mackay Point and Pocotaligo, man attempt to cut off
the railway .communication between Charleston and
Savannah. The General is blamed for his rashness by
the Northern press. The New York ship Alleghania,
bound from Baltimore to London with a cargo of guano,
was captured on Wednesday, in Chesapeake Bay, by a
party ,of Confederates from the shore, and burnt.
The -captain, mate, and pilot were taken prisoners.
General -Wool has arrested several citizens at a Union
meeting in Baltimore, for the offenee of • endeavouring
to procure signatures among his own officers for .his
removal from ,command. The President has ordered
the arrested persons to be set at liberty uncondition-illy.
It is ernocted.that General Wool will resign. Judge
Clifford, of Massachusetts. granted a writ of ,haheas
corpus in the case of Mr. W. .11. :Winder, of Philadel-
phia, detained in Fort Warren. The _sher ff was
denied-admittance to the Fort to serve the writ. The judge
has declared that he has orders to enforce the sentence.
The election of the Democratic ticket for the .State
of New York, on Tuesday, the 4th instant, is considered
certain. The -President has eixpressed his surprise and
regret at the turn which the ,elections have already
taken. The Democrats expect to carry the States of
New Jersey and Massachusetts, as well as New- York.
There has been a series of strikes among the working
men of New York for increased wages, in consequence
of the 'depreciation of the paper currency and the alarm-
ing and rapid rise in the price of the necessaries of life.
The demands of the working men have been acceded to.
General Banks is to be appointed to the command of an
expedition to Texas. General Maclemand is to co-
operate with Admiral Dupont on the Mississippi.

LATER MOVEMENTS.

NEW Tosx, .Nov. 3, Evenitig.—The advance of

the Federal army continues. Gemini Pleasantonanet
the Confederates at Thillipmont. After skirmishing
they etreated to Union, whence they were sulase-
quently ,driven by General Pleasanton, who occupied
the plaee. Heavy firing has since been heard, tux

captured :at,Corinth report that the Federals had cttp-

A rumccar was .current at Port Loyal that the Con-
federate Ram Savannah .was coming down the river.
The Confederate steamer Alabama has captured eight
more American vessels, and destroyed them all but twz,
which gave :bonds f0r86,000 dols., payable to President
Davis after the declaration of peace.

The Alabama was last seen in lat. 39, long. 69 W., off
Cape Delaware,,directly in the track of the Californian'
steamers.

The Federal cruisers have captured the British
steamers Anglina and.Beotia, off Charleston.

G.dRIBALDI AND .AXERICAIV
EL AVERY.

The following letter has been received from the
Secretary of Garibaldi by Mr. Richardson, Common
Councilman :

My dear Mr. Richardson,—This morn* the General
has read my Varignano letter as translated by you, and
begs to say it is all right,and thanks you for it. It was
of vital importance that Garibaldi should be well under-
stood on the American question. To him men of every
colour are men—are God's creatures—are brethren,
and he wishes to see them liberated. He fancies
that they consider a poor slave as a piece of iron,
which is made into machinery to work for •civilisation
and human prosperity., for intelligence, and for man-
kind. He cannot bear to sea intellect in chains, and
told and bought: but he desires to see the slaves free as
God has created them, and subject to human laws. To-
vuorrow the General will leave for Plea; the climate
there is more genial in the winter. He might possibly
have suffered more here. The Municipal Council of
Naples are discussing the desirability of the General
going to Naples. I am going to the Villa .Spinola,
thence to Turin, to assist at the opening of Pa:diament.
We hope to defeat that Ministry who seem only able
and energetic for mischief. I take my leave of you
here, dear Sir, with the conscious knowledge that I
have made the friendship of another (an Arrivabene)
noble heart; it is, moreover, a great comfort to us.
If you desire to write me, address me at Turin.
Believe me, my dear Mr. Richardson,
Yours affectionately,
Spezzia, Nov. 7, 1862. C.. AUGUSTUS VECCIEL
