articles.title: BEE-HIVE, STuRDAY, OVEMBEIi 15, 1869.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, STuRDAY, OVEMBEIi 15, 1869.

THE CITY BANK, NANCIIESTE.R.

Jonah Andrew, late manager of the Manchester City
Bank, was brought up at the City Police-court on the
11th, in order that some formal 'evidence might be taken
to complete the case apon which he was committed at
the last examination.
Mr. J. Richardson, solicitor for the prosecution, said
that the case was adjourned for the production of
formal evidence from the Union Bank, London, to prove
that the bill upon which the prisoner was committed
was never advised by him. He (Mr. Richardson) had
received a letter from his London agents, stating that
the witness from Spooner and Attwood's was willing to
come if it were absolutely necessary; but although he
had been subpcenaed, he had not come. Messrs.
Spooner and Attvb ood were, however, wdling to render
every assistance. -Under these circumstances he (Mr.
Richardson) should ask the court that the merely foimai
evidence which would be put in should be sufficient for
the present. The other witness from Spooner and AU-
Wood's could then be produced at the assizes.
Mr. Ross: If that evidence is supplied at the assizes
it will be sufficient, and we will take the ffirmal
evidence now to complete the case.
Mr. John Hill, principal at the comitry office of the
Union Bank, Princess-street, London, through whose
hands all the letters to the bank passed, said that on
Wednesday, the 22nd of October, the bank received no
instructions or advice to meet the bill produced. No
letter was received from the prisoner, nor had he any
account with their bank.
The Magistrate's Clerk: Had the City Bank any ac-
count with you?
Witness: None whatever.
Detective Sergeant Shandley said he-apprehended the
prisoner at a meeting of creditors, at the Free-trade
Hall, on Saturday evening, Oct. 25th, and read to him
the warrant charging him with illegally appropratting
to his own use £37 17s. 6d. The prisoner said, 'I have ,
nothing to say; it is merely a debt.'
The prisoner, in answer to the usual question from
-the bench, said he had nothing to say..
This completed the depositions in the case (Mr.
Lyon's).
Mr. Superintendent Maybury : I beg leave to state
that there is another charge gainst this man. He is
'charged with receiving £lO on the 16th of last month,
which should have been paid over to the Union Bank, in
London, to meet a bill due on the 17th. The money
was sent to the bank by Mr. T. Smith, ironmonger,
Oldham-street. He has no professional gentleman to
conduct his ease, and therefore the police will have to
-go through it in the best way they. can.
Mr. W. Thomas, assistant at Mr. T. Smith's, iron-
monger, Oldham-street, said that on the 16th of October
his master sent him to the Manchester City Bank with
£lO in gold End silver to meet.a bill which was due in
the Union Bank, London 'on the 17th of October.
He took it to the City Bank about 6 o'clock in the
afternoon, and s,w Mr. J. Wads uorth, the cashier, to
whom he delivered a note given to him by his em-
,ployer, and explaining the nature of his business. The
cashier gave him a form to fill up. After the ffirm was
filled up, and while the money was being paid in he
looked round and saw the pthsonerstanding by a win& w.
The form referred to was as follows :--4 Acceptances
payable at Spooner, Attwoods, and Co. Drawers,.G. and
J. Hattersley. Acceptors, Thomas Smith. Where
payable, Union Bank, London. Due Oct. 17. Amount,
.£lO, and (underneath) Is. Mr. Jonah Andrew, 31,
Market-street, Manchester. Please order payment of;
the above, and debit the account of-.'

Mr. Joseph Wadsworth, formerly, cashier at the City
Bank, said he remembered the last witness bringing £lO
to the bank on Thursday evening, the 16th October, to t
advise a bill. The usual advice form was filled up, the !.,1
money was received, andthe amount entered in the hank :1
cash-book in the usual vay. The money was placecV,
in the cash drawer, and the advice slip was handedl
over to Mr. Coulson, the corresponding clerk. No dout:,t
the prisoner saw the book before the following day, when;
he went to London.

Cross-examined by Mr. Cobbett : The balanoe in hand
that night, inclu din g cheques and cash, was £1,064 18s. 6d.
The amount of cash was small.

Mr. W. Coulson, late-clerk at the City Bank, aid he
received the prosecutor's advice note frora the last
witness and placed it on the file. He did not smite to
any one about it that night. On the 17th—the ,day
after the money was lodged—the acceptance was advised
to-the City Bank agentsin London, Messrs. Spooner and
Attwood. Money was .always advised by the .City
Bank through its agents only. The advice in this ease
was signed by the prisoner.
By the Bench: Messrs. Spooner and Co. refused to
honour the drafts of the City Bank on Monday, the 20th.
Mr. Ross: But surelythe bill would arrive in London
on the 18th if there was,no counter order?

Witness: I cannot account for it at all. it is .a
frequent occurrence. The acceptance was net pl.yable
at Spooner's, but through them.
Mr. Ross: Why did you not advise the bill the .same
day as the money was paid ?
Witness: Because 1 received instructions not to
advise it until the following day.
Mr. Ross: From whom.?
Witness: Mr. Andrew.
Mr. Ross: Did the advice go up on the 17th?

'Witness: Oh yes, certainly.
Mr. Hill, from the country office, Union Bank, Zaori-
don, proved that no instructions had ever been received
from the City Bank to pay the £lO in question.
Mr. Smith, the prosecutor, stated that on the 10th
'October he gavethe assistant the money to retire the hill;
iproduced. That bill was dishonoured, and on Monday t
-following (20th Oct.) he received from the drawers
;notice to that effect. He remitted the amount, and
ielegraphed for the dishonoured bill.
This concluded the evidence.
Cobbett, for the defence' said: After the .ease
that was before you the other day, I have been .con- '
faidering what course I should take, and I have come to
the conclusion that it would be a useless occupation of
time for me to address you upon this case; because all
I could say would be precisely what I said upon the
.other. The two cases are precisely similar in this, that
there is no evidence of an offence having been °Om-
:flitted in either case. Of course lam not venturing to
question your judgment upon the matter, but this is my
opinion, which I cannot help. That being so, it appears
to me that the proper course is iLo leave this in your
hands.

Mr. Ross reminded Mr. Cobbett.that the decision ia
the other case was the decision of the whole bench.

The magistrates (Messrs. Ros; and It Barnes) having
consulted together, the chairman :said that this case
would go for trial with the other.
Mr. ,Cobbett asked what bail would the allowed.
Mr. Ross said that this question was,cansidered by the
magistrates on Thursday last. Consideting that the
offence was one of great and serious importance to the
whole mercantile .community, they had decided that the
prisoner must find two sureties in £3OO each, and enter
into his own recognizance in £6OO.
The prisoner was then removed. This concluded the
proceedings before the magistrates.

TIM TIVDERGILOUND MAIL.---The following is printed
in the New York Titaes as an extract from a letter,
dated Say.tnnah, Oct. 11 You cannot think how
bitterly the North is ridiculed here, and all my,efforts to
defend it only -end in mortification and consciousness
that those who think otherwise have the best of the
argument. It is now the regular habit to tend so-
called " deserters " into the Union lines along the
Potomac, whenever we want to get a mail carried north.
These "deserters,' who ard generally the bravest,
sharpest, and most unscrupulous enfants perdu* in the
rebel army, enter APClellan's tines, tell him just sub
stories as they have been told .to, take the oath, and are
immediately dismissed.. They then go to Baltimore,
post their letters there, get a return mail and Are back
in Richmond within three or four days from the time of
leaving the managers of this mail line at Baltimore. It
is thus that the —anil the [two pipers ate
mentioned here, one published in New York, and one in
Baltimore] get their "late Southern news," and I can
assure you that this mail runs regularly—the carriers
many times getting across the Potomac and into Mary-
land without being once challenged; while, _if .they are
challenged, they announce themselves as " dererters,"
take the oath—though even this is not always asked of
them—and then hulry on to Baltimore, which is our
chief post-office.'

from the Bishop of Honolulu by the last mail we le.irn
the Hawaiian mi-sion at San

safe
n arrival

The Topaze frigate, in which it

sandwich Islands, was not expected at Panama for
some weeks, while a passenger ship was about to sail the
day after their arrival for San Francisco, the usual
route to the Islands. The hi hop, therefore, wisely
determined not to lose time in the unhealthy Isthmus.
Fortunately a comfortable ship was to sail from San
Francisco the day after their arrival there for Hawaii,

principal inhabitants, have called upon us since our

has been excellent, the weather wit.lout interruption
most favourable, and we are in goad spirits for our work
We la ye daily studied the language during the voyage.'
More funds are urgently required for the efficient esta-

special fund of the Bishop of Honolulu, at th-: Society
for the Propagation.. the Gospel, 79, Pall-mall.

articles.title: AJLERICzN HAYIZLIIONIAL
articles.text:
AJLERICzN HAYIZLIIONIAL

HA TTAR S.

(From the Missouri Republican.)
A few days ago we were presented with a package of
cake and some bottles of wine, with the compliments of
a newly-married couple. This was an interesting
event to us, as the occasion was doubtless interesting to
the donors. While discussing the wine and paying due
respects to the cake, we could not help indulging in
some pleasant reminiscences. We dreamed of the time
when Sol. Scott was a Benedict, and we dreamed of
many little circumstances in that connexion. We could
not help it, and may be paidoned for contemplating the
rash act of di opping a tear for Auld Lang ';,yne '—re-
gretting nothing—nor even wi,hing that 'Sol' was, as
formerly, Scot free,' but lamenting that we were not
in the same delightful bondage as he. We immediately
commenced singing—
'There's a good time coming, boys,
Wait a little longer!'
and by this me .ns we kept our spirits up, assistedhy the
grape jaice aforesaid.
The sun went down and all the land was dark' and
what wonder! for 'Sol' was eclipsed by the smiles of
his beautiful bride. Dian rose in more than wonted
splendour, and the prettiest and fullest lover's moon that
ever shone, peeped through the window of our sanctum.
There was no even the shadow of a man on her face,
and by her dreaming light we read the following notice
for the Republicsuz, which accomparned the package to
which we have referred :

MARRIED. —On Tuesday evening, 7th instant, at St.
George's Church, by the Rv. Edward F. Berliley, Sol.
Scott, jr., to Miss Maggie Ford.'
We are informed that the affair was one of the most
brilliant of the kind that has occurred in the city for a
long time. The church was crowded by gallantry and
beauty, and

Bright
The lamps shone o'er fair women and brave men;'
and what is stranger than all, in these out of joint
timcs, no battle ;occurred ti mar the harmony of the
peaceful scene, nor did the' cannon's deafening roar"'
interrupt the ceremonies.

At the house of the bride, after the marriage cere-
mony, the scene was no less enchanting. The festivities
were prolonged until the e small .hours.' We could
not pretend to describe the beautiful brunettes and
blondes, the blick eyes, blue, and hazel; the hair black,
brown, and auburn; the lithe .and graceful forms; the
gay laugh and sparkling repartee, which constituted-the
entertainment of the evening.
'Our co-mate, and brother-in exile,'
John Goodin, was fortunate enough to be master of cere-
monies, and we can rely on the word of a companion in
distress, that a more recherche -demonstration of matri-
mony he never witnessed. We have reason to believe,
however, that some of thoce brunettes and blondes—
those black eyes, blue and hagel—those curls, black,
hrown and auburn—those lithe and graceful forms, had
an exhilarating influence soil .our usually sedate and
circumspect friend. If such should be the case, we hope
e, ill endeavour to. govern himself accordingly, ar
submit to be governed, as .the case may be. To 047 X
Avarra friend we can only say, shine on!
May vernal blossom; 'neath your rays,
And'flowers and roses smile;
May Heaven grant
.you length of days,
And bright skiesall the while.

articles.title: TITAKEY.
articles.text:
TITAKEY.

The levant Herald of .the 29th deseribe,s the essclite-
ment occasioned in Constantinople by the news ‘Of .the
Greek Revolution :

'Here in Conslantinople our publication of .the news
' of the insurrection and its successful progress excited a
a very furore of enthusiasm amongst the Greek oorn7
munity. Business of every kind was suspended—oven
consolides being for the time neglected—and grogps of
excited Hellenes congratulated each other at every'
street corner. On Friday evening the liellenic,Club
adjoining the •Palais des.Fleurs was crowded with mem-
bers Of the colony, as was also the garden outside,
where the general joy .found vent in
.successive rounds
of cheers—responded to from the windows of the„club
—as the band played, over and over again, the
Greek national air. Champagne to e.very-
body ad lib. added to the jubilant effervescence„;
but no disturbance of .any kind marred the noisy har-
mony of the evening. „Similar well-controlled excite-
ment obtained throughout Saturday, but on Sunday a.
party of outside roughs' forced their w.y into the Club-
house, and insisted on taking part in the choice which
was then being made (by ballot amongst the leading
members of the community) of a deputation. to proceed
to Athens with a congratulatory address to the new
Government. The intruders were, however, at length
ejected, and the voting for deputies continued without
further interruption. Monday passed off quietly, though
the general excitement had but little abated; and,yester-
day the following gentlemen were "'declared elected
members of the deputation to Athens :—Messrs. .A.•
Baltazzi, Stephanovieh, E. Mavrogordato, Skiros,.Rattos,
,and two others. Severalavingees, who had refused King
Otho's amnesty for their .share in the late Nauplian.in-
surrectien, left by the Austrain steamer of Saturday.for
Syria, en route for Athens.

articles.text:
INGENIOUS R,013.11 B IrOYEL

P 0121'ER.

The Birmingham Gazette -narrates the followirig in-
genious robbery, and clevereapture of the offender. On
Wednesday evening last a gentleman of the name of
.Layle, a commei dal travelier, in .the employment of
Messrs. W. Dawbarn and Co,.Prince's Basin, Liverpool,
who had been staying at Wilkins's Temperance
.Moor-street,..l.3irmurgham, wishing to make a remittance
.of, £B5 to his employers, enclosed that amount to them in
notes upon the Bank of Eng,and and Gloucestemsaire
.Banking Company in a sealed and addressed envelope,
and it was given to a man named Tinley, engaged as an
out-porter at the hotel, with instructions to take the letter
to the General Post .Office, New-street, and register it.
Ile left for the purpose of doing so, and on the following
.morning resumed his work as usual, but between eight
and nine o'clock he went to the .Bailway Station, and
.did not return to the hotel that day. Next morning
Mr. Layle received a letter from his employers at Liver-
pool acknowledging the receipt of his letter, but saying
nothing about their having received the iB5. Tele-
graphing to his employers immediately, and receiving a,
reply that the money had actually- net, arrived, Mr. Layle
at once communicated with the police authorities. One
.of the Post Office clerks remembered registering ,a
letter on the Wednesday evening addressed to Messrs.
Dawbarn, also that the direction was very badly
written, and the contents were enclosed in an adhesive
envelope. Suspicion at once attached itself to a man
named Tinley, the telegraph m ires were put in use, and
Mr. Wilkins, jun., who knew the man, in consequence
of information received by the detectives,-succeeded .in
tracing him to Bristol, where he was found about to
embark on hoard a ship. In his possession was found
£73 7s. 61-d. in bank notes, gold, silver' and copper,
and also the original envelope addressed by Mr. Layle
to Messrs. Dawburn and Co. There is little doubt
that imagining rightly that the letter entrusted to him
to register contained something of value, he opened it,
and, taking out the notes, re-directed another envelope,
and enclosing the letter, .registered it. The direction is
known to be in his handwriting. tie was at once given
into custody to the police at Bristol, and -sent to Bir--
mingham.

AN ELOQUENT RAG ricKrat.--A mg-gatherer nanaed
Denout, who has been repeatedly condemned for trifling
ass,ults, disorderly ,conduct, and petty larcenies, was
charged before the Police Tribunal, Paris, with having
ott:ndeu against public decency, by appearing in the
-treets in a costume too nearly approaching a state of
nudity, in spite of the repeated warnings of several police
agents. In answer to the charge, the accused, atter
saluting the tribunal with much gravity, laid his hand
on his heart and said:—' I have always sworn to be
faithful to the dictates of honour and no.the
_Government
of the Emperor, and I conduct myself accordingly. I
limit my acquaintance to men who wear the St.
Helena medal; 1 reside in the „Passage Napoleon; I am
the authorised rag-gatherer of the Lycee Bonaparte, and
for two years I exercise my craft on the Boulevards de in
Iteine Hortense and Prince Eugene. I always wear old
pantaloons of the Imperial Guard, and though a button
m y be wanting occasionally, it is my misfortune, not
my fault, as I have.no wife to t•ew them on. The Pre-
Lident :---‘ But Jl this has nothing to do with your
obstinate resistance to the warnings of_the police.' The
accused :---‘ As to that, it is all owing to the Ist Regi-
ment of the Grenadiers of the• Guard, for I have been so
affteted on seeing them march down the street that 1
was obliged to take four glasses of brandy one after the
other to restore the equilibrium of my mind, aud yet my
feelings continued so excited that I liuev not what I
did. I can, therefore, only implore :the Indulgence of
the tribunal.' Not Aithstanding this eloquent defence,
he court declared the charged proved, and condemned
the accused to a month's imprisonment.—Galig,,ani.
The New Zealand swift moth is a truly curious insect,
not so much for its form or colours, but for the strange
mischance which often befalls the larva, ,a vegetable
taking the place of the ichneumon-fly., and nourishing
itself on the substance of the being which gives it sup-
port. A kind of fungus affixes itself to the larva, and
becomes developed on its strange bed, taking up. gra-
dually the fatty, parts and 'tissues of the• caterpillar,
until at last the creture dies under the parasite growth,
and.is converted almost wholly into vegetael matter.—
Routledge's Nair' 'Rotary.

articles.title: FRENCH COURT.
articles.text:
THE FRENCH COURT.

A letter from Compiegne says:—' The first hunt of
the season, at which both the Emperor and Empress
were present, took place three days back. The meet
was at Fort Pokier, and, as usual, attracted a large
number of spectators. Their Majesties, with a number
of the guests, arrived at balf-past one, attired in
hunting costume. The Emperor, having mounted his
horse, gave the signal for the start. While those who
took part in the hunt were in pursuit of the stag, the
spectators walked about in groups, directing their steps
where the halloo was heard, with the hope of being
present at the finish. As the stag escaped, they were
doomed to disappointment; and the curee, of course,
could not take place in the evening. The Prince Im-
perial rode a spirited little pony, and seemed quite at
home on horseback. He was dressed in the fall uniform
of the hunt. The following morning the Emperor,
accompanied by several of the guests, shot in the forest
preserves. In the afternoon an excursion was made
to the Castle of Pierrefonds. In the evening Casimir
Dalvigne's comedy of the Ecole des Viellards was
played by the company of the Theatre Francais.'
Prince Napoleon paid a visit two days back to the
Emperor at Compiegne. On the previous day his
Imperial Highness gave a grand dinner at the Palais
-Royal, to which were invited several of the editors of
the Paris journals. M. Drouyn de Lhuys has visited
his Imperial Highness.

'THE SUCCESSION TO THE DUCHY OF BE.UNSIVICX.—
The German journals had spoken of a convention, con-
cluded between the governments of Hanover and
Brunswick, with the view of assuring to the Crown of'
the former state the succession to Bruns aick, in case of
the present duke dying without children. Letters from
Berlin state that the treaty in ques ion has not received
the adhesion of the Committee of the States of Bruns-
wick, to which it had been communicated. The
; committee has expressed the desire that the duchy
should be attached to Hanover by dynastic ties only;
that it should preserve its own constitution and admi-
nistration, and lastly, that in case the present duke
ahould die before King George V., a regency shouldle
, instituted for the Duchy of Brunswick, and should
maintain its functions' during the whole of the present
king's reign.
ATTEMPT TO UPSET THE TIDAL TRAIN.—A
attempt to overturn the tidal express train on the Lon-
don Chatham, and Dover Railway was perpetrated on
Sunday evening last, ía the neighbourhood of Chatham.
Shortly before the time at whach the train was due at
the Chatham station, and after it had been sigetilled, it
was discovered that an iron rail had been placed across
the *metals of the up line, near the entrance to the
tunnel. The discovery was made by one of the servants
of the company, who happened to be on the embank-
ment, and who noticed a man hurrying away from the
.spot. Before the obstruction 'could be removed the
, train reached the spot, but, owing to the diminished
.14peed at which it was moving preparatory to its stp-
ping at the station, no harm accrued, though had the
.rail been placed a short distance down the line there is
little doubt a very serious accident would have resulted.
it is stated that the man who was seen hurrying from
the spot where the obstruction was placed can be identi-
led, and such information has been given to the police
.at Chatham as, there is way little doubt, will lead to his
.apprehension.
THE COMPIEGNE WEATHERGLASS.—The Parisians
have discovered a new political barometera called. the
'Compiegne Weatherglass.' It consists simply in a
careful analytical .eoniparison of the invitadon list
issued by his Imperial Majesty from his autumn
residence. This yeaathe scale is divided into 12 degrees
or days. M. Pereire, the banker, has been invited for
the whole term as well as Baron Rothschild. M. Deouyn
de Ihuys has been honoured with a 10 days' invitation;
and M. Felician David, the Composer, with one of four
-days. The Italian Ambassador has been asked to stay
a day, in the masquerade of la grand chasse—Spectator.
'NAVIGATION OF TILE INDUS.—Copy ,of a letter from
Mr. Bourne, the managing director olthe British Inland
Steam Navigation Company :—`.on -board the Indus,
Sukkur, October 4, 1862. I send you these few lines
from on board the steamer Indus, which is now towing

articles.title: EUROPEAN MEDIATION IN AMERICA.
articles.text:
EUROPEAN MEDIATION IN
AMERICA.

Under the above beading La _Patric publishes the
following:—
We yesterday confirmed the news already spread for
some days in England of an attempt at mediation pro-
jected by France and Russia in America. The initia-
tive of this step is due to the Imperial Government. The
proposition emanating from France has been immediately
accepted by Russia, and it is with this important adhe-
sion that the same proposition has just been made to
the British Government. What will be the reply of the
Cabinet of St. James's? Public opinion is anxious to
ascertain it. The joint action of France and of Ru-sia
might perhaps suffice to assure at Richmond and at
Washington the success of an offer of mediation. France
exercises a legitimate influence in America, due to her
conciliating and frank policy, and recently to her inter-
vention in the Trent affair. Russia, on her part, still
entertains intimate relations with the Northern States,
formed by the exchange of services the least forgotten
of which date from the Crimean war. But we do not
hesitate to admit that on this occasion the concurrence
of England is almost indispensable. The common action
of the cabinets of Paris and of St. Petersburg would be
powerfully strengthened by the adhesion of Gre.tt
Britain, whose political position is especially under-
stood on the other side of the Atlantic. Yet, if we
are to credit the still somewhat vague reports in circula-
tion, the propo.ition of France and Russia has not met
with a favourable reception at London. A Cabinet
Council is to be held on Tuesday, and at this council the
Palmerston cabinet will adopt its resolutions.

articles.title: STREET ROBBERIES.
articles.text:
STREET ROBBERIES.

Mr. D. W. Harvey, in a letter to a Contemporary,
says :—You will readily suppose, from my official
position, that my attention has been given to a subject
which now largely engages the public mind, and will
continue to be a source ot great and painful solicitude,
if not effectually met by appropriate remedies. I allude
to the burglaries and daring acts of personal violence
which are daily occurring. As there is no doubt that
many of these outrages are justly attributable to convicts
on tickets of leave, it appears to me that immediate
attention should be given to this great and growing
evil; and in aid of this object I venture to suggest
that all persons to whom tickets of leave have been
granted and are still in force should be ordered forth-
with, by competent authority, to report themselves at a
given quarter, with their names and residences, and if
need be to present themselves; and that those persons
who do not comply with such order within seven days
should lose the privilege of their tickets, to be dealt
with for disobedience; and further, that those who com-
ply with this order, and give satisfactory accounts of
themselves, should be placed in communication with the
heads of police in the district in which they reside, who
should receive instructions to afford them the counten-
ance which their conduct may deserve. I consider this
last suggestion most important, for it cannot be doubted
that the means of employment to those who are honestly
seeking it is greatly checked by the mistaken zeal of
the police, who are too ready to give intimations to their
employers of their previous nicgfaisance, which in most
cases leads to their immediate discharge, thus throwing
them back on their I:orraer associates and vicious
course. That such is the case is within my own ex-
perience.'

WAR OFFICE, Nov. 11.
The :Queen has been graciously pleased to signify her
intention to confer the decoration of the Victoria Cross
on the undermentioned Non-commissioned Officers of
the Army, whose claims to the same have been submitted
for her Majesty's approval, on account of acts of bravery
performed by them in India, as recorded against their
names, viz. :

Colour-SergeantCorneliusCoghlan, 75th Regiment.—
For gallantly venturing, under a heavy fire, with three
others, into a Serai occupied by the enemy in great
numbers, and removing Private Corbett, 75th Regiraent,
who lay severely wounded. Also for cheering and
encouraging a party which hesitated to charge down a
lane in Subzee Muudee, at Delhi, lined on each side
with huts, and raked by a cross fire; then entering with
the said,party into an enclosure filled with the enemy,
and destroying every man. For having, also, on the
same -occasion, returned under a cross fire to collect
dhoolies, and carry off the wounded; a service which
was successfully performed, and for which this man
obtained great praise from the officers of his regiment.
Dates of acts of bravery, June Bth and July 18th, 1857.
Corporal (then Private) Charles Anderson; Trum-
peter Thomas Monaghan, 2nd Dragoon Guards.—For
saving-the life of Lieutenant-Colonel Seymour, C. 8.,
commanding the regiment, in an attack made on him on
the &h of October, 1858, by mutinous sepoys, in a dtnse
jungle-ef sugar canes, from which an attempt was made
to dislodge them. The mutineers were between thirty
and forty in number. They suddenly opened fire on
Lieutenant-Colonel Seymour and his party at a few
yards .distance, and immediately afterwards rushed in
upon them with drawn (native) swords. Pistolling a
man, cutting at him, and emptying with deadly effect at
arm's length every barrel of his revolver, Lieutenant-
Colonel -Seymour was out down by two sword cuts,
when the two men above recommended, rushed to his
rescue, and the trumpeter shooting a man with his
pistol in,the act of cutting at him, and both trumpeter
and dragoon driving at the enemy with their swords,
enabled:him to arise, and .assist in defending himself
again, when the whole of the enemy were dispatched.
The oscurrence took place :soon after the action fought
near Sundeela, Oudh, on the date above mentioned.
Date af.acts of bravery, Oct. Bth, 1858.

DEATH OF MR. JONAS Ws—We have to record
the death of the renowned breeder of sheep, Mr. Jonas
Webb, late of Babraham, Cambridgeshire, which took
place on the 10th instant, at the house of his brother- in-
law, Mr. 11. Marshall, of Cambridge. About three
weeks ago, Mrs. Webb, being an invalid, was ordered
a change of scene by her medical attendants, and ex-
pressed a desire to visit hr brother, Mr. M4rshall, and
went to Cambridge accordingly. Mr. Webb, visiting
her, was induced to remain, he then being in his usual,
but not robust health. Mrs. Webb got worse, and died
on the sth instant, the anniversary of the birthday of
her son, v ho was to have been married on that same morn-
ing, but whose marriage was of course postponed. When
Mr. Webb realised the idea that all hopes of The survival
of his wife were over he fell into a nervous fever, never
rallied, and died beta een 7 and 8 p m. on Monday, on
the 66th anniversary of his own birth, and the day on
which the remains of his wife were interred. Mr.
Webb's physicians stated that they could have success-
fully combated the disease, but were powerless in regard
to the mental shock.

Sub-Editor of the BEE Hivg, respectfully informs his

Baying been for 15 years overseer and manager of one

pedition. Cards. Circulars, Trade Rules, Hand Bills,

taken at fair and reasonable prices.

R. H. during the wh,le time lie worked as a journeyman

positors, and his pen and personal services have always

LONDON OPERATIVE
ROREMAKFRS Appeal to the Metropolitan
Trades, and Trades of the United Kingdom.
ElaurnEe. Worreicso MEN: It is with a feeling of
reluctance that we,. the London Operative Ropemskers,
venture to draw your attention to our present position,
knowing as we do. the great depressian of trade in
almost every degarlment of manufacture, and yet we
feel encouraged to lay our cases before you soliciting
your sympathy and aid, by the conviction that we are
well known by thcsLondon trades, and to many trades
in the country, for our willingness to assist others in
times of difficulty.. We will thereforessimply state our
ease to you, hoping that you will deem it worthy of
your kind consideration
On the 11th. el June last one of our employers offered
a reduction of sevenpencc per day, or three and six-
pence per week, from our wages, and we, having a
well organised, trade society, could not submit to any
• reduction ~f wages, recognising, as fair workmen should
do that a fair day's work is entitled to a fair day's pay,
and having enjoyed the present rate of wages for the
last seven years, and there being no reasonable plea
given why such reduction should. take place.
Having sent deputations to the employers to reason
the matter with them and used every effort to pre-
vent a strike, but finding that the employers were
determined if possible to effect a general reduction of
wages throughout the trade, there was no other course
left us bt.t to withdi aw the whole of the journeymen
from the firm, viz.—Messrs. J. H. Baker, Bermond-
sey. This is the eighth week of the strike, and our
men are firm and in good spirits, being convinced of the
justness of their claims and ultimate success, for al-
though the firm has resorted to all kinds of misrepre-
sentation to obtain men their shop is sti 1 empty, for
as fast as the men come up from the country through
their agents and advertisements in the country, local
papers, they (the men) after having the question of
dispute explained to them, leave their work, and by
our assistance leave London again, which creates a
large expense over the actual cost of keeping our own
members on strike. We have expended over £l5O, a
large sum for only one firm, but then we are fighting
for the whole trade, for some of the other employers
have already given notice to their then, that as soon
as Messrs. Baker and Brothers get supplied with men
at the reduction that they will give no more for their
work than the Messrs. Baker's,and if We are com-
pelled to submit to this reduction we shall lose
£1,500 per year in wages (then leaving a large surplus
of men out of work), a sum you will admit worth
sti uggling for.
Having thus briefly stated our ;present position we
earnestly appeal to the sympathy of our fellow workmen
another trades. soliciting their assistance to enable us to
defend successfully our right of wages and t, ade against
these grasping employers. In appealing to our fellow
working men, we may say that we have had always a
willing heart and ready hand to assist other trades
Placed in similar circnmstances ; indeed, since 1853 there
has not been a question affecting the interest of the
working classes, or a dispute in any other trade, but
what we have supported and sustained to our utmost
ability. We therefore make this appeal ' with some
~egree of confidene, that you will r,adily respond to us
' in our present difficulties, and show to the employing
classes that there is a spirit of union and brotherhood
amongst the working men of England, that will enable
them to rally round their fellow but oppressed brother
Workmen.
We beg to remain yours very respectfully, on behalf of
the trade. Thomas Hay, Charles Howe, William Matthews,
Charles Terdre, Robert Still, committee ; Richard Bur-
ridge, treasurer; Daniel Smith, secretary.

to any society to give the information that may be re-
quired, or forward any information on the question of
dispute, by SPPI3 ing to
